subject: Applied Physiology
question: Define homeostasis.
answer_html:
Definition Homeostasis is the maintenance of a constant internal environment in the body in spite of changes in the external environment. The term was coined by the physiologist Walter Cannon; the idea of the "internal environment" came from Claude Bernard.

Examples of values kept constant

  1. Body temperature – about 37 °C
  2. Blood pH – 7.35–7.45
  3. Fasting blood glucose – about 70–100 mg/dl
  4. Blood pressure – about 120/80 mm Hg
  5. Water and electrolyte levels (sodium, potassium)

How it is maintained: mainly by negative feedback mechanisms controlled by the nervous and endocrine systems. Disease results when homeostasis fails.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Name the body fluid compartments.
answer_html:
Introduction Water is the largest component of the body – about 60% of body weight in an adult man (about 42 litres in a 70 kg man). It is about 75% in newborns and less in women, the obese and the elderly.

Compartments

  1. Intracellular fluid (ICF) – inside the cells; two-thirds of body water (about 28 L); rich in potassium
  2. Extracellular fluid (ECF) – outside the cells; one-third (about 14 L); rich in sodium. It includes:
    • Interstitial fluid – between cells; about three-quarters of the ECF
    • Plasma – fluid part of blood; about one-quarter of the ECF
    • Transcellular fluid – small amounts: CSF, synovial, pleural, peritoneal and intraocular fluids

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Define diffusion and osmosis.
answer_html:
1. Diffusion

  • Movement of molecules from an area of higher concentration to an area of lower concentration until they are evenly spread
  • Needs no energy (passive)
  • Example: oxygen moving from the alveoli into the blood; carbon dioxide moving out

2. Osmosis

  • Movement of water through a semipermeable membrane from a dilute solution (less solute) to a concentrated solution (more solute)
  • Example: water absorption in the large intestine

Applied: 0.9% saline is isotonic; a hypotonic solution makes red cells swell and burst, a hypertonic one makes them shrink – the basis for choosing IV fluids.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Explain feedback mechanisms with examples.
answer_html:
Introduction Homeostasis is maintained by feedback mechanisms. A feedback mechanism is a control loop in which the result of a process acts back on the process itself, either to stop it or to speed it up.

1. Components of a feedback loop

  1. Receptor (sensor) – detects a change (stimulus) in a controlled value
  2. Control centre – usually the brain (hypothalamus) or an endocrine gland; compares the value with its set point and sends commands
  3. Effector – a muscle or gland that carries out the response

2. Negative feedback – the most common type

  • The response reverses (opposes) the original change and brings the value back to normal
  • It keeps conditions stable
  • Examples:
    • Body temperature – when temperature rises, the hypothalamus causes sweating and vasodilation → temperature falls; when it falls, shivering and vasoconstriction raise it
    • Blood glucose – a rise in glucose stimulates insulin, which lowers it; a fall stimulates glucagon
    • Blood pressure – a rise in BP stimulates the baroreceptors → the heart slows and vessels dilate → BP falls
    • Hormone levels – a high level of thyroxine suppresses TSH from the pituitary, so thyroxine falls back

3. Positive feedback – less common

  • The response increases (amplifies) the original change until a definite end point is reached
  • It does not maintain stability, but completes a process quickly
  • Examples:
    • Labour – the baby's head presses on the cervix → oxytocin is released → stronger contractions → more pressure on the cervix → more oxytocin, until the baby is born (Ferguson reflex)
    • Blood clotting – thrombin speeds up its own formation until a clot forms
    • LH surge before ovulation (oestrogen stimulates LH)
    • Milk ejection during breastfeeding

4. Comparison

Negative feedback Positive feedback
reverses the change increases the change
maintains stability completes a process
very common uncommon
e.g. temperature, BP, glucose e.g. labour, clotting

5. Nursing importance

  • Fever, shock, dehydration and diabetes are failures of homeostasis
  • Many nursing actions – cooling, fluid replacement, insulin, oxygen – support the body's own feedback systems

Conclusion Negative feedback keeps the internal environment stable, while positive feedback drives a process to completion; both are essential for health.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Describe the stages of tissue repair (wound healing).
answer_html:
Introduction When tissue is injured, the body repairs it by:

  • Regeneration – replacement by the same type of cells (skin epithelium, liver, bone), or
  • Repair by fibrosis – replacement by fibrous (scar) tissue when cells cannot regenerate (heart muscle, brain)

Wound healing is a combination of both and occurs in overlapping stages.

1. Haemostasis (immediately after injury)

  • Injured blood vessels constrict
  • Platelets form a plug and a fibrin clot seals the wound
  • The clot forms a scaffold for later repair

2. Inflammatory phase (first 3–5 days)

  • Redness, warmth, swelling and pain
  • Neutrophils arrive first, then macrophages
  • They remove bacteria, dead tissue and debris and release growth factors

3. Proliferative phase (about day 4 to 3 weeks)

  • Granulation tissue forms – new capillaries (angiogenesis) and fibroblasts; it looks pink, moist and granular and bleeds easily
  • Fibroblasts lay down collagen
  • Epithelialisation – epithelial cells grow over the surface from the edges
  • Wound contraction – myofibroblasts pull the edges together

4. Maturation (remodelling) phase (3 weeks to 1–2 years)

  • Collagen is reorganised and cross-linked
  • The scar becomes paler, flatter and stronger, but reaches only about 70–80% of the original strength

5. Types of wound healing

  • Primary intention – clean wound with edges brought together (surgical incision); quick healing, thin scar
  • Secondary intention – gaping or infected wound; heals from the base by granulation; slow, large scar (ulcers, abscess cavities)
  • Tertiary intention (delayed primary closure) – wound left open for a few days and then closed

6. Factors that delay healing

  • Local: infection, poor blood supply, foreign body, movement of the part, pressure
  • General: malnutrition (lack of protein, vitamin C, zinc), diabetes, old age, obesity, anaemia, steroids, smoking, cancer and chemotherapy

7. Nursing role

  • Aseptic dressing technique
  • Good nutrition – protein, vitamin C, zinc
  • Control of blood sugar in diabetics
  • Rest and support of the part; relief of pressure
  • Watch for signs of infection – increasing pain, redness, swelling, pus, fever

Conclusion Wound healing passes through haemostasis, inflammation, proliferation and remodelling; good nursing care removes the factors that delay it.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Describe the cell cycle.
answer_html:
Introduction The cell cycle is the series of events by which a cell grows, copies its DNA and divides into two daughter cells. It is the basis of growth, tissue repair and replacement of worn-out cells.

1. Phases of the cell cycle The cycle has two main parts – interphase and the mitotic (M) phase.

A. Interphase – the longest part (about 90% of the cycle); the cell is very active, not "resting"

  • G1 phase (first gap)
    • The cell grows in size
    • Makes proteins, enzymes and organelles
    • A checkpoint at the end decides whether the cell will divide
  • S phase (synthesis)
    • DNA is replicated – each chromosome now has two identical chromatids
    • Centrioles are duplicated
  • G2 phase (second gap)
    • The cell checks the copied DNA for errors and repairs them
    • Makes proteins needed for division

B. M phase (mitotic phase)

  • Mitosis – division of the nucleus in four stages:
    1. Prophase
    2. Metaphase
    3. Anaphase
    4. Telophase
  • Cytokinesis – division of the cytoplasm, giving two daughter cells

2. G0 phase

  • Cells that stop dividing leave the cycle and enter G0
  • Permanent cells – mature neurons and heart muscle cells; never divide again
  • Stable cells – liver and kidney cells; stay in G0 but can re-enter the cycle when needed (after injury)
  • Labile cells – skin, gut lining, bone marrow; divide continuously

3. Control of the cell cycle

  • Checkpoints at the end of G1, the end of G2 and during metaphase stop the cycle if the DNA is damaged or the cell is not ready
  • Controlled by special proteins (cyclins) and growth factors

4. Applied / nursing importance

  • Cancer is uncontrolled cell division due to failure of the checkpoints
  • Anticancer drugs act on particular phases (S phase, M phase); radiotherapy damages DNA
  • Rapidly dividing tissues – bone marrow, gut lining, hair follicles, skin – are most affected by chemotherapy, causing low blood counts, mouth ulcers, diarrhoea and hair loss
  • Permanent cells (heart, brain) cannot regenerate, so infarcts heal by scarring

Conclusion The cell cycle consists of interphase (G1, S, G2) and the M phase, under strict checkpoint control; its loss of control causes cancer.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Describe the mechanisms of transport across the cell membrane with examples. (2 + 8)
answer_html:
(a) Introduction (2 marks)

  • Every cell is surrounded by a cell membrane – a double layer of phospholipids with proteins embedded in it (fluid mosaic model)
  • The membrane is selectively permeable – it allows some substances to pass freely, controls the passage of others and keeps out the rest
  • Small, lipid-soluble substances (oxygen, carbon dioxide, alcohol) cross easily through the lipid layer
  • Ions, glucose, amino acids and large molecules need special channels, carriers or vesicles
  • Transport mechanisms are grouped into two types:
    1. Passive transport – no energy needed; substances move down their concentration gradient
    2. Active transport – energy (ATP) needed; substances can move against their gradient

(b) Mechanisms of transport (8 marks)

A. Passive transport

1. Simple diffusion

  • Molecules move directly through the lipid layer or through protein channels, from higher to lower concentration
  • Continues until the concentration is equal on both sides
  • Examples: exchange of O₂ and CO₂ in the lungs and tissues; movement of alcohol and some drugs; sodium and potassium through ion channels
  • Rate of diffusion increases with a larger concentration difference, larger surface area, thinner membrane and higher temperature – this is why thickening of the alveolar membrane (pulmonary fibrosis, oedema) reduces oxygen uptake

2. Facilitated diffusion

  • A carrier protein binds the substance and helps it across, still downhill (no energy)
  • Shows saturation – when all carriers are occupied, the rate cannot increase further
  • Example: entry of glucose into muscle and fat cells through GLUT carriers; insulin increases the number of GLUT4 carriers – this is how insulin lowers blood sugar

3. Osmosis

  • Diffusion of water across a semipermeable membrane from a region of low solute concentration to high solute concentration
  • Osmotic pressure – the pressure needed to stop this movement; plasma proteins (albumin) exert an osmotic pull that keeps water in blood vessels
  • Examples: water absorption in the large intestine and kidney tubules
  • Tonicity of solutions:
    • Isotonic (0.9% NaCl, Ringer's lactate) – no change in cell size
    • Hypotonic – water enters cells; red cells swell and burst (haemolysis)
    • Hypertonic – water leaves cells; cells shrink

4. Filtration

  • Movement of water and small solutes through a membrane under hydrostatic pressure
  • Examples: formation of glomerular filtrate in the kidney; formation of tissue fluid at the arterial end of capillaries

B. Active transport

1. Primary active transport

  • The carrier protein itself splits ATP to move substances against their gradient
  • Sodium–potassium pump (Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase):
    • Pumps 3 Na⁺ ions out and 2 K⁺ ions in for each ATP used
    • Keeps sodium high outside and potassium high inside the cell
    • Maintains the resting membrane potential needed for nerve impulses and muscle contraction
    • Controls cell volume – without it cells would swell and burst
  • Other pumps: calcium pump (muscle relaxation), proton pump (H⁺/K⁺-ATPase) in the stomach (acid secretion)

2. Secondary active transport (co-transport)

  • Uses the energy stored in the sodium gradient created by the Na⁺/K⁺ pump
  • Sodium–glucose co-transport in the small intestine and kidney tubules – glucose enters the cell together with sodium
  • Applied: this is why ORS works – glucose in ORS increases the absorption of sodium and water from the gut even during diarrhoea
  • Amino acids are also absorbed this way

3. Vesicular (bulk) transport – for large particles and large amounts

  • Endocytosis – the membrane folds inwards and encloses material in a vesicle:
    • Phagocytosis ("cell eating") – neutrophils and macrophages engulf bacteria and debris
    • Pinocytosis ("cell drinking") – uptake of fluid droplets
    • Receptor-mediated endocytosis – uptake of specific substances such as cholesterol (LDL) and iron
  • Exocytosis – vesicles fuse with the membrane and release their contents outside
    • Secretion of hormones (insulin), digestive enzymes and neurotransmitters (acetylcholine)

Summary table

Feature Passive transport Active transport
Direction down the concentration gradient against the gradient
Energy not needed ATP needed (directly or indirectly)
Carrier sometimes (facilitated diffusion) always (or vesicles)
Examples diffusion of O₂, osmosis, filtration, glucose into muscle Na⁺/K⁺ pump, glucose absorption with sodium, phagocytosis, exocytosis

(c) Applied / nursing importance

  • IV fluid selection depends on osmosis – isotonic for volume replacement, hypotonic or hypertonic only under orders
  • Digoxin acts by inhibiting the Na⁺/K⁺ pump in heart muscle
  • Proton pump inhibitors (omeprazole) block acid secretion
  • ORS uses sodium–glucose co-transport
  • Low albumin reduces osmotic pull → oedema
  • Diuretics such as mannitol act by osmosis

Conclusion Substances cross the cell membrane by passive processes (diffusion, facilitated diffusion, osmosis, filtration) or by active processes (pumps, co-transport, endocytosis, exocytosis); these mechanisms explain many everyday treatments such as IV fluids, ORS and common drugs.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Define tonicity. Differentiate isotonic, hypotonic and hypertonic solutions with examples.
answer_html:
Definition Tonicity is the ability of a solution to make cells gain or lose water by osmosis. It is compared with the osmotic pressure of plasma (about 285–295 mOsm/kg).

Type Effect on cells Examples
Isotonic – same as plasma no change in cell size 0.9% sodium chloride (normal saline), Ringer's lactate
Hypotonic – lower than plasma water enters cells → cells swell (red cells may burst – haemolysis) 0.45% saline, sterile water
Hypertonic – higher than plasma water leaves cells → cells shrink (crenation) 3% saline, 10% dextrose, 20% mannitol

Nursing: choose the correct IV fluid as prescribed; hypertonic fluids are given slowly and preferably through large veins; 5% dextrose becomes hypotonic once its glucose is used.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Define electrolytes. Name the major electrolytes of ECF and ICF.
answer_html:
Definition Electrolytes are substances that dissociate into ions (charged particles) when dissolved in water and conduct electricity. Cations carry a positive charge; anions carry a negative charge.

Major electrolytes

  1. Extracellular fluid (ECF) – sodium (Na⁺) – the main cation (about 135–145 mEq/L in plasma); chloride (Cl⁻) and bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻) – the main anions
  2. Intracellular fluid (ICF) – potassium (K⁺) – the main cation (plasma K⁺ is only 3.5–5 mEq/L); magnesium (Mg²⁺); phosphate and proteins – the main anions

Functions: maintain water distribution and osmotic pressure, nerve and muscle excitability, acid–base balance and enzyme activity.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Define resting membrane potential.
answer_html:
Definition The resting membrane potential (RMP) is the difference in electrical charge across the cell membrane of a cell at rest, the inside being negative compared with the outside.

Values

  • About –70 mV in nerve cells and about –90 mV in skeletal and cardiac muscle

Causes

  1. The sodium–potassium pump moves 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in for each ATP used
  2. The membrane at rest is much more permeable to K⁺, which leaks out
  3. Large negatively charged proteins remain inside the cell

Importance: it makes nerves and muscles excitable; changes in potassium levels (hypo- or hyperkalaemia) disturb it and can cause muscle weakness and dangerous heart rhythms.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: What is apoptosis?
answer_html:
Definition Apoptosis is programmed cell death – a natural, orderly process by which the body removes unwanted, old or damaged cells without causing inflammation.

Features

  1. The cell shrinks, its nucleus breaks into fragments and it is packed into small apoptotic bodies
  2. These are quickly eaten by macrophages
  3. Neighbouring cells are not harmed

Examples

  • Removal of the web between fingers in the embryo
  • Shedding of the endometrium in menstruation
  • Removal of old blood cells and of cells with damaged DNA

Difference from necrosis: necrosis is accidental cell death from injury (burns, ischaemia) with swelling, bursting of cells and inflammation.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Define pH. State the normal pH of blood.
answer_html:
Definition pH is the negative logarithm of the hydrogen ion concentration – a measure of how acidic or alkaline a solution is, on a scale of 0 to 14:

  • pH 7 – neutral
  • below 7 – acidic (more H⁺ ions)
  • above 7 – alkaline (fewer H⁺ ions)

Normal pH of arterial blood: 7.35–7.45 (slightly alkaline)

Abnormal values

  • Below 7.35 – acidosis
  • Above 7.45 – alkalosis
  • Values below 6.8 or above 7.8 are usually incompatible with life

Other values: gastric juice about 1.5–3.5, urine about 6 (range 4.5–8), saliva about 6.5–7.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Explain the regulation of water and electrolyte balance.
answer_html:
Introduction Water forms about 60% of the body weight of an adult man (less in women and the elderly, more in infants). For health, the water taken in must equal the water lost, and the electrolytes must stay within narrow limits. This is called fluid and electrolyte balance.

1. Daily water intake (about 2.5 litres)

  • Drinking – about 1.5 litres
  • Water in food – about 0.75 litre
  • Metabolic water (from oxidation of food) – about 0.25–0.3 litre

2. Daily water output (about 2.5 litres)

  • Urine – about 1.5 litres
  • Skin – sweat and insensible loss (about 0.5 litre)
  • Lungs – water vapour in expired air (about 0.35–0.4 litre)
  • Faeces – about 0.1–0.2 litre
  • Loss through skin and lungs is called insensible loss; it increases in fever, hot weather and rapid breathing

3. Regulation of water

(a) Thirst mechanism

  • Rise in plasma osmolality or fall in blood volume stimulates osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus → thirst → drinking

(b) Antidiuretic hormone (ADH)

  • Released from the posterior pituitary when osmolality rises or blood volume falls
  • Increases water reabsorption in the collecting ducts of the kidney → less, more concentrated urine

4. Regulation of sodium (and therefore ECF volume)

(a) Renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system

  • Low BP or low sodium → kidney releases renin → angiotensin II → aldosterone from the adrenal cortex
  • Aldosterone causes sodium (and water) reabsorption and potassium excretion in the distal tubules

(b) Atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP)

  • Released by the stretched atria when blood volume is high; increases sodium and water excretion

5. Regulation of potassium

  • Aldosterone increases potassium excretion; insulin and adrenaline move potassium into cells

6. Other electrolytes

  • Calcium – parathyroid hormone, vitamin D and calcitonin
  • Hydrogen ion and bicarbonate – buffers, lungs and kidneys

7. Applied – nursing importance

  • Dehydration – diarrhoea, vomiting, fever, burns; signs: thirst, dry tongue, sunken eyes, low urine output, rapid pulse; treated with ORS or IV fluids
  • Fluid overload – in heart and kidney failure; oedema, breathlessness
  • Intake–output charting, daily weight and monitoring of serum electrolytes are key nursing duties
  • Hypokalaemia (weakness, arrhythmias) with diuretics, vomiting and diarrhoea; hyperkalaemia in kidney failure

Conclusion Water and electrolyte balance is maintained by matching intake and output, and is regulated by thirst, ADH, the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system and ANP; nurses support it through intake–output charting, daily weights and correct fluid therapy.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Explain oedema – its mechanism and causes.
answer_html:
Introduction Oedema is the abnormal accumulation of fluid in the interstitial (tissue) spaces. It appears as swelling, especially of the ankles, feet, sacrum and around the eyes. Pressing a swollen area may leave a pit – pitting oedema.

1. Normal fluid exchange at the capillaries (Starling forces)

  • Capillary hydrostatic pressure (blood pressure inside the capillary) pushes fluid out into the tissues – higher at the arterial end
  • Plasma oncotic (colloid osmotic) pressure, created mainly by albumin, pulls fluid back into the capillary
  • At the arterial end, outward pressure is greater → fluid leaves; at the venous end, inward pull is greater → most fluid returns
  • The small excess is removed by the lymphatics

2. Mechanism of oedema – oedema develops when this balance is upset

(a) Increased capillary hydrostatic pressure

  • Heart failure – right-sided failure causes swelling of legs and liver; left-sided failure causes pulmonary oedema
  • Venous obstruction – deep vein thrombosis, varicose veins, pressure of the pregnant uterus
  • Fluid overload – excess IV fluids, kidney failure

(b) Decreased plasma oncotic pressure (low albumin)

  • Nephrotic syndrome – loss of protein in urine
  • Liver cirrhosis – reduced albumin formation (oedema and ascites)
  • Malnutrition – kwashiorkor in children
  • Burns and protein-losing conditions

(c) Increased capillary permeability

  • Inflammation, infection, burns, allergy (angio-oedema), snake bite – proteins leak out and draw water with them

(d) Lymphatic obstruction

  • Filariasis (elephantiasis), removal of lymph nodes (after mastectomy), tumours – non-pitting oedema

(e) Sodium and water retention

  • Kidney disease, excess aldosterone, steroids, pregnancy

3. Types

  • Localised (one limb, one area) and generalised (anasarca)
  • Pitting and non-pitting

4. Nursing implications

  • Assess – site, extent, pitting (grade it), daily weight, intake–output, breathing (pulmonary oedema)
  • Elevate swollen limbs; skin care – oedematous skin breaks down easily
  • Restrict salt and fluids as advised; give diuretics as prescribed and monitor potassium
  • High-protein diet when albumin is low (if kidney function allows)
  • Semi-Fowler's position for breathlessness

Conclusion Oedema results from increased capillary pressure, low plasma proteins, leaky capillaries, blocked lymphatics or sodium retention; understanding Starling forces helps nurses assess and manage it.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Explain acid–base balance – the buffer systems, respiratory and renal regulation – and the disorders of acid–base balance. (2 + 3 + 2 + 3)
answer_html:
(a) Introduction (2 marks)

  • An acid releases hydrogen ions (H⁺); a base accepts them
  • The body constantly produces acids – carbon dioxide (from metabolism, forming carbonic acid), lactic acid, keto acids, and sulphuric and phosphoric acids from proteins
  • Yet the pH of arterial blood is kept between 7.35 and 7.45, because enzymes, nerves, muscles and the heart work properly only within this range
  • Acid–base balance is maintained by three lines of defence: buffers (seconds), the lungs (minutes) and the kidneys (hours to days)

(b) Buffer systems – the first line of defence (3 marks) A buffer is a mixture of a weak acid and its salt that resists changes in pH by taking up or releasing H⁺.

  1. Bicarbonate–carbonic acid buffer
    • The most important buffer of the ECF
    • H⁺ + HCO₃⁻ ⇌ H₂CO₃ ⇌ CO₂ + H₂O
    • Normal ratio of bicarbonate to carbonic acid is 20 : 1; the pH stays normal as long as this ratio is kept
    • It is powerful because both parts are regulated – CO₂ by the lungs and HCO₃⁻ by the kidneys
  2. Phosphate buffer
    • Important inside cells and in the urine
  3. Protein buffers
    • Plasma proteins and haemoglobin (the most important buffer inside red cells); together, proteins are the most plentiful buffers in the body

(c) Respiratory and renal regulation (2 marks)

Respiratory regulation – the second line

  • A rise in H⁺ or CO₂ stimulates the respiratory centre → deeper, faster breathing → more CO₂ washed out → pH rises
  • A fall in H⁺ slows breathing → CO₂ is retained
  • Acts within minutes, but cannot remove non-volatile acids

Renal regulation – the third and most powerful line

  • The kidneys secrete H⁺ into the urine, reabsorb filtered bicarbonate and form new bicarbonate
  • Excess H⁺ is carried in the urine with phosphate and ammonia (as ammonium) buffers
  • Slow (hours to days) but can correct the pH almost completely

(d) Disorders of acid–base balance (3 marks)

Normal arterial blood gas (ABG) values

  • pH 7.35–7.45; PaCO₂ 35–45 mmHg; HCO₃⁻ 22–26 mEq/L; PaO₂ 80–100 mmHg

1. Respiratory acidosis – pH ↓, PaCO₂ ↑

  • Causes: hypoventilation – COPD, severe asthma, pneumonia, chest injury, opioid or sedative overdose, respiratory muscle paralysis
  • Features: headache, drowsiness, confusion, flushed skin
  • Compensation: kidneys retain bicarbonate

2. Respiratory alkalosis – pH ↑, PaCO₂ ↓

  • Causes: hyperventilation – anxiety and panic, high altitude, fever, early salicylate poisoning
  • Features: dizziness, tingling of fingers and around the mouth, carpopedal spasm
  • Compensation: kidneys excrete bicarbonate

3. Metabolic acidosis – pH ↓, HCO₃⁻ ↓

  • Causes: diabetic ketoacidosis, kidney failure, lactic acidosis in shock, severe diarrhoea (loss of bicarbonate), poisoning (methanol)
  • Features: Kussmaul's breathing (deep, rapid breathing – the lungs blow off CO₂ to compensate), nausea, confusion, hyperkalaemia
  • Compensation: lungs

4. Metabolic alkalosis – pH ↑, HCO₃⁻ ↑

  • Causes: prolonged vomiting or nasogastric suction (loss of HCl), diuretics, excess antacid or bicarbonate intake, hypokalaemia
  • Features: shallow slow breathing, muscle cramps, tetany, confusion
  • Compensation: lungs (hypoventilation)

Summary

Disorder pH Primary change Common cause
Respiratory acidosis ↓ PaCO₂ ↑ COPD, opioid overdose
Respiratory alkalosis ↑ PaCO₂ ↓ anxiety, hyperventilation
Metabolic acidosis ↓ HCO₃⁻ ↓ DKA, kidney failure, diarrhoea
Metabolic alkalosis ↑ HCO₃⁻ ↑ vomiting, NG suction

Nursing implications

  • Take ABG samples correctly (heparinised syringe, no air bubbles, ice if delayed, pressure on the site for 5 minutes)
  • Observe breathing patterns, level of consciousness and signs of tetany
  • Give oxygen, IV fluids, bicarbonate or insulin as prescribed; for anxiety-related hyperventilation, calm the patient and coach slow breathing

Conclusion Acid–base balance keeps blood pH at 7.35–7.45 through buffers (mainly bicarbonate–carbonic acid in a 20 : 1 ratio), the lungs (CO₂ removal) and the kidneys (H⁺ excretion and bicarbonate formation); failure leads to respiratory or metabolic acidosis or alkalosis, recognised by ABG analysis.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: List the lung volumes and capacities with their normal values.
answer_html:
Introduction Lung volumes are measured by spirometry. They help assess lung function in asthma and COPD.

Lung volumes (adult)

  1. Tidal volume (TV) – air breathed in or out in a normal breath – about 500 ml
  2. Inspiratory reserve volume (IRV) – extra air breathed in after a normal inspiration – about 3000 ml
  3. Expiratory reserve volume (ERV) – extra air breathed out after a normal expiration – about 1100 ml
  4. Residual volume (RV) – air left in the lungs after the deepest expiration – about 1200 ml

Lung capacities

  • Vital capacity = TV + IRV + ERV – about 4.6 litres
  • Inspiratory capacity = TV + IRV – about 3.5 litres
  • Functional residual capacity = ERV + RV – about 2.3 litres
  • Total lung capacity – about 5.8–6 litres

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Define bronchiectasis.
answer_html:
Definition Bronchiectasis is a permanent, abnormal dilatation (widening) of the bronchi due to destruction of the muscle and elastic tissue of their walls.

Causes: repeated or severe infections (tuberculosis, whooping cough, measles pneumonia), bronchial obstruction, cystic fibrosis.

Features

  1. Chronic cough with large amounts of foul-smelling, purulent sputum, worse in the morning and on changing position
  2. Haemoptysis (coughing up blood)
  3. Clubbing of fingers
  4. Repeated chest infections

Nursing care: postural drainage, chest physiotherapy, good oral hygiene, antibiotics as ordered.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: What is periodic breathing? Give examples.
answer_html:
Definition Periodic breathing is an abnormal breathing pattern in which periods of breathing alternate with periods of apnoea (no breathing).

Types

  1. Cheyne–Stokes breathing
    • Breaths gradually become deeper and faster, then shallower and slower, followed by a pause (apnoea); the cycle repeats
    • Seen in heart failure, brain damage, stroke, raised intracranial pressure, at high altitude, and in dying patients
  2. Biot's breathing
    • Irregular groups of quick, shallow breaths separated by periods of apnoea
    • Seen in meningitis and brainstem damage

Note: Cheyne–Stokes breathing may be normal in sleeping infants and the elderly.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Define hypoxia, cyanosis and dyspnoea. Explain the types of hypoxia.
answer_html:
Introduction Every cell needs a continuous supply of oxygen. Failure at any step – breathing, gas exchange, transport by blood or use by cells – leads to hypoxia.

1. Definitions

  • Hypoxia – deficiency of oxygen at the tissue level
  • Cyanosis – bluish discoloration of the skin and mucous membranes, seen when the reduced (deoxygenated) haemoglobin in capillary blood is more than about 5 g/dl
    • Central cyanosis – lips, tongue, mucous membranes; caused by lung or heart disease
    • Peripheral cyanosis – fingers, toes, ear lobes; caused by cold or poor circulation
    • May not appear in severe anaemia (too little Hb) and is prominent in polycythaemia
  • Dyspnoea – difficult or laboured breathing of which the person is aware
    • Causes: lung disease (asthma, pneumonia, COPD), heart failure, anaemia, anxiety, heavy exercise
    • Orthopnoea – breathlessness on lying flat
    • Paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea – waking at night breathless (left heart failure)

2. Types of hypoxia

A. Hypoxic (arterial) hypoxia

  • Low oxygen tension (PO₂) in arterial blood
  • Causes: high altitude, airway obstruction, pneumonia, pulmonary oedema, respiratory depression (opioids), hypoventilation
  • Cyanosis is usually present
  • Responds well to oxygen therapy

B. Anaemic hypoxia

  • Arterial PO₂ is normal, but the blood cannot carry enough oxygen
  • Causes: anaemia, haemorrhage, carbon monoxide poisoning (CO binds Hb more strongly than O₂)
  • Cyanosis is absent; CO poisoning gives a cherry-red colour

C. Stagnant (circulatory or ischaemic) hypoxia

  • Blood flows too slowly to the tissues
  • Causes: shock, heart failure, embolism, cold exposure, tight bandage or plaster
  • Peripheral cyanosis is common

D. Histotoxic hypoxia

  • Oxygen reaches the tissues, but the cells cannot use it
  • Cause: cyanide poisoning (blocks the cell's respiratory enzymes)
  • Oxygen therapy is of little use; specific antidote needed

3. Summary table

Type Defect Example
Hypoxic low arterial PO₂ high altitude, pneumonia
Anaemic low O₂-carrying capacity anaemia, CO poisoning
Stagnant slow blood flow shock, heart failure
Histotoxic cells cannot use O₂ cyanide poisoning

4. Nursing importance

  • Observe the lips and tongue for central cyanosis and the nail beds for peripheral cyanosis
  • Monitor SpO₂ with a pulse oximeter (falsely normal in CO poisoning)
  • Position breathless patients upright; give oxygen as prescribed

Conclusion Hypoxia may be hypoxic, anaemic, stagnant or histotoxic; cyanosis and dyspnoea are important signs, and the treatment depends on the type.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Explain the transport of oxygen and carbon dioxide in the blood.

diagram.caption: Oxygen-haemoglobin dissociation curve
labels: shift to the right with raised CO2

answer_html:
Introduction Blood carries oxygen from the lungs to the tissues and carbon dioxide from the tissues to the lungs. Most of this transport depends on haemoglobin inside red blood cells and on the enzyme carbonic anhydrase.

A. Transport of oxygen

1. Forms

  • Combined with haemoglobin (about 97–98%) – as oxyhaemoglobin
    • Each Hb molecule has four haem groups and can carry four O₂ molecules
    • 1 g of Hb carries about 1.34 ml of O₂
  • Dissolved in plasma (about 2–3%) – small but important, because it sets the PO₂

2. Loading and unloading

  • In the lungs, the high PO₂ (about 100 mm Hg) saturates Hb almost fully – about 97%
  • In the tissues, the low PO₂ (about 40 mm Hg) makes Hb release oxygen – venous blood is still about 75% saturated (reserve for exercise)

3. Oxygen–haemoglobin dissociation curve

  • An S-shaped (sigmoid) curve showing % saturation of Hb at different PO₂
  • Shift to the right – Hb gives up O₂ more easily; caused by increased CO₂, increased H⁺ (fall in pH), increased temperature and increased 2,3-BPG – conditions found in active tissues (Bohr effect)
  • Shift to the left – Hb holds O₂ more tightly; caused by the opposite changes, carbon monoxide and foetal haemoglobin

4. Normal values: arterial PO₂ about 95–100 mm Hg; SpO₂ 95–100%.

B. Transport of carbon dioxide

1. As bicarbonate – about 70%

  • In red cells, the enzyme carbonic anhydrase speeds up: CO₂ + H₂O → H₂CO₃ → H⁺ + HCO₃⁻
  • HCO₃⁻ moves out into the plasma, and Cl⁻ moves into the red cell to keep electrical balance – the chloride shift
  • H⁺ is buffered by haemoglobin

2. As carbamino-haemoglobin – about 20–23%

  • CO₂ combines with the protein (globin) part of haemoglobin

3. Dissolved in plasma – about 7%

4. Haldane effect – deoxygenated haemoglobin carries more CO₂; so in the tissues (where Hb gives up O₂) CO₂ uptake increases, and in the lungs (where Hb takes up O₂) CO₂ is released.

C. Applied / nursing importance

  • Carbon monoxide poisoning (charcoal stoves in closed rooms, fires) – CO binds Hb about 200 times more strongly than O₂; the pulse oximeter may read falsely normal; give high-flow oxygen
  • Anaemia reduces oxygen-carrying capacity – patients tire and become breathless easily
  • Fever and acidosis shift the curve to the right, so tissues get more oxygen but blood picks up less in the lungs
  • CO₂ retention in COPD causes respiratory acidosis

Conclusion Oxygen is carried mainly as oxyhaemoglobin, and carbon dioxide mainly as bicarbonate; the dissociation curve and the Bohr and Haldane effects help oxygen reach the tissues that need it most.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Explain the regulation of respiration.
answer_html:
Introduction Breathing goes on automatically, day and night, without our attention, yet it can be changed voluntarily when we speak, sing or hold our breath. The rate and depth of breathing are adjusted continuously to keep the arterial O₂, CO₂ and pH normal. This control is both nervous and chemical.

1. Nervous regulation – respiratory centres in the brainstem A. Medulla oblongata

  • Dorsal respiratory group – the basic inspiratory centre; sends rhythmic impulses through the phrenic and intercostal nerves to the diaphragm and intercostal muscles
  • Ventral respiratory group – mostly inactive in quiet breathing; active in forced breathing (exercise)

B. Pons

  • Pneumotaxic centre – limits the duration of inspiration and increases the rate
  • Apneustic centre – prolongs inspiration

C. Higher centres

  • Cerebral cortex – voluntary control (speaking, singing, breath-holding); cannot override the chemical drive for long
  • Hypothalamus and limbic system – emotions and temperature change breathing (fast breathing in fear, panting in heat)

D. Reflexes

  • Hering–Breuer (inflation) reflex – stretch receptors in the lungs send impulses through the vagus to stop inspiration and prevent over-inflation
  • Irritant receptors – cough and sneeze
  • Proprioceptors in moving joints and muscles increase breathing in exercise
  • Pain and temperature stimulate breathing

2. Chemical regulation A. Central chemoreceptors – in the medulla

  • Respond to an increase in CO₂ / H⁺ in the CSF
  • Provide the main, moment-to-moment drive for breathing in a healthy person
  • A small rise in CO₂ greatly increases breathing

B. Peripheral chemoreceptors – carotid bodies (at the carotid bifurcation) and aortic bodies (on the aortic arch)

  • Respond mainly to a fall in arterial O₂ (below about 60 mm Hg); also to a rise in CO₂ and H⁺
  • Send impulses through the glossopharyngeal and vagus nerves
  • Become important at high altitude and in chronic lung disease

3. Applied / nursing importance

  • COPD patients with long-standing CO₂ retention may depend on low oxygen (hypoxic drive) to breathe; give controlled oxygen (target SpO₂ about 88–92%) and watch for drowsiness
  • Opioids and sedatives depress the respiratory centre – count respirations before giving morphine; naloxone reverses opioid depression
  • Head injury and raised intracranial pressure cause abnormal breathing patterns
  • Hyperventilation in anxiety washes out CO₂ → tingling, dizziness; rebreathing calmly helps

Conclusion Breathing is set by centres in the medulla and pons, adjusted by higher centres and reflexes, and controlled chemically mainly by CO₂ acting on central chemoreceptors and by low O₂ acting on the carotid and aortic bodies.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Describe the mechanism of respiration and the factors affecting respiration. (2 + 4 + 2 + 2)

diagram.caption: Inspiration and expiration
labels: alveolar pressure below atmospheric (air in); diaphragm relaxes and domes up

answer_html:
(a) Definition and stages of respiration (2 marks) Respiration is the process by which oxygen is taken from the atmosphere to the body cells and carbon dioxide is removed from the cells to the atmosphere. It takes place in stages:

  1. Pulmonary ventilation (breathing) – movement of air into and out of the lungs
  2. External respiration – exchange of gases between the alveoli and the blood in pulmonary capillaries
  3. Transport of gases in the blood – O₂ to the tissues, CO₂ back to the lungs
  4. Internal respiration – exchange of gases between the blood and tissue cells
  5. Cellular respiration – use of O₂ by the mitochondria to release energy (ATP) from food, producing CO₂ and water

(b) Mechanics of breathing (4 marks) Air moves because of pressure differences between the atmosphere and the alveoli. These differences are created by changing the volume of the thoracic cavity (Boyle's law – when volume increases, pressure falls).

1. Inspiration – an active process

  • Diaphragm contracts – its dome flattens and moves down about 1.5 cm in quiet breathing (up to 7–10 cm in deep breathing); this increases the vertical diameter of the chest and accounts for about 75% of quiet breathing
  • External intercostal muscles contract – lift the ribs upward and outward
    • Pump-handle movement of the upper ribs increases the front-to-back diameter
    • Bucket-handle movement of the lower ribs increases the side-to-side diameter
  • The chest volume increases → the intrapleural pressure becomes more negative → the lungs expand with the chest wall
  • Alveolar pressure falls below atmospheric pressure (by about 1 mm Hg) → air flows into the lungs
  • In deep or laboured inspiration, accessory muscles help – sternocleidomastoid, scalenes, pectorals

2. Expiration – passive in quiet breathing

  • The diaphragm and external intercostals relax
  • The elastic recoil of the lungs and chest wall reduces the chest volume
  • Alveolar pressure rises above atmospheric pressure → air flows out
  • Forced expiration (coughing, exercise, asthma) is active – internal intercostals pull the ribs down and abdominal muscles push the diaphragm up

3. Factors that help breathing

  • Surfactant – secreted by type II alveolar cells; lowers surface tension and prevents the alveoli from collapsing at the end of expiration
  • Lung compliance – the ease with which the lungs stretch; reduced in pulmonary fibrosis and pulmonary oedema, so breathing becomes hard work
  • Airway resistance – depends on the diameter of the bronchi; increased in asthma and bronchitis
  • Negative intrapleural pressure – keeps the lungs inflated; lost in pneumothorax

(c) Exchange of gases (2 marks)

  • Gases move by simple diffusion from higher to lower partial pressure
  • The respiratory membrane (alveolar wall + capillary wall) is very thin (less than 1 µm) and has a huge area (about 70 m²)
  • In the lungs:
    • Alveolar PO₂ (about 104 mm Hg) > venous blood PO₂ (40 mm Hg) → O₂ enters the blood
    • Venous blood PCO₂ (45 mm Hg) > alveolar PCO₂ (40 mm Hg) → CO₂ leaves the blood
  • In the tissues the gradients are reversed: O₂ diffuses into the cells and CO₂ into the blood
  • CO₂ diffuses about 20 times more easily than O₂, so in lung disease low oxygen appears before high CO₂

Normal respiratory rate

  • Adults: 12–20 per minute
  • Newborns: about 40–60 per minute; children in between
  • Minute ventilation = tidal volume × rate = about 500 ml × 12 = 6 litres per minute

(d) Factors affecting respiration (2 marks)

  1. Age – faster in infants and children
  2. Sex – slightly faster in women
  3. Exercise – increases rate and depth
  4. Emotions, anxiety and pain – increase the rate
  5. Body temperature – fever increases the rate; hypothermia decreases it
  6. Altitude – low oxygen at high altitude increases breathing
  7. Drugs – opioids and sedatives depress breathing; stimulants increase it
  8. Sleep – breathing becomes slower and more regular
  9. Body position – lying flat limits chest expansion; Fowler's (upright) position eases breathing
  10. Diseases – asthma, pneumonia, COPD, heart failure, obesity, abdominal distension, ascites; metabolic acidosis (diabetic ketoacidosis) causes deep, rapid Kussmaul breathing
  11. Haemoglobin level – anaemia increases breathing on exertion
  12. Voluntary control – speaking, singing, breath-holding

(e) Nursing points

  • Count respirations for a full minute, preferably without telling the patient (they may change their breathing)
  • Note rate, depth, rhythm, effort and use of accessory muscles
  • Position breathless patients upright; give oxygen as prescribed
  • Teach deep breathing exercises, coughing and incentive spirometry after surgery to prevent lung collapse
  • Avoid tight abdominal binders that limit diaphragm movement

Conclusion Respiration includes ventilation, gas exchange, transport and cellular use of oxygen. Inspiration is active (diaphragm and external intercostals) and quiet expiration is passive (elastic recoil); many physical, emotional and disease factors alter breathing, so careful observation of respiration is a basic nursing skill.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: What is surfactant? State its functions.
answer_html:
Definition Surfactant is a lipoprotein mixture (mainly the phospholipid dipalmitoyl lecithin) secreted by the type II alveolar cells. It lines the inner surface of the alveoli. It begins to be produced in the fetal lungs in the second half of pregnancy and is usually adequate by about 34–35 weeks.

Functions

  1. Lowers surface tension of the fluid lining the alveoli
  2. Prevents collapse of alveoli (atelectasis) at the end of expiration
  3. Increases lung compliance – makes breathing easier
  4. Keeps alveoli of different sizes stable
  5. Helps prevent pulmonary oedema

Applied: lack of surfactant in premature babies causes respiratory distress syndrome; mothers in preterm labour are given antenatal corticosteroids to speed its production, and surfactant can be given into the baby's trachea.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: What is lung compliance?
answer_html:
Definition Lung compliance is the stretchability (distensibility) of the lungs – the change in lung volume for each unit change in pressure (ΔV/ΔP). It shows how easily the lungs expand.

Normal value: about 200 ml per cm H₂O for the lungs alone (about 100 ml/cm H₂O for the lungs and chest wall together).

Factors

  • Depends on the elastic tissue of the lungs and on surfactant

Applied

  • Decreased compliance (stiff lungs, hard to inflate) – pulmonary fibrosis, pulmonary oedema, respiratory distress syndrome, pneumonia, chest wall deformities
  • Increased compliance – emphysema (loss of elastic tissue; lungs inflate easily but do not recoil, so air is trapped)

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Define dead space. Name its types.
answer_html:
Definition Dead space is the part of the inspired air that does not take part in gas exchange.

Types

  1. Anatomical dead space – the volume of the conducting airways (nose, pharynx, larynx, trachea, bronchi down to the terminal bronchioles); about 150 ml in an adult
  2. Alveolar dead space – alveoli that are ventilated but not perfused with blood (normally very small)
  3. Physiological dead space – anatomical + alveolar dead space; nearly equal to anatomical dead space in healthy people, increased in lung disease (e.g. pulmonary embolism)

Applied: rapid, shallow breathing is inefficient because a larger share of each breath stays in the dead space; deep, slow breathing improves alveolar ventilation.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Define asphyxia.
answer_html:
Definition Asphyxia is a condition of severe lack of oxygen (hypoxia) together with excess carbon dioxide (hypercapnia) in the blood and tissues, caused by obstruction of the airway or failure of breathing.

Causes

  • Choking on a foreign body, drowning, hanging and strangulation, smothering, crowding in closed spaces, poisonous gases

Stages

  1. Stage of hyperpnoea – rapid, deep breathing, rise in BP and pulse
  2. Stage of convulsions – loss of consciousness, convulsions, cyanosis
  3. Stage of exhaustion – breathing stops, pulse fails, pupils dilate; death follows in a few minutes unless relieved

Applied: immediate first aid – clear the airway, back blows and abdominal thrusts for choking, CPR.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: What is the Hering–Breuer reflex?
answer_html:
Definition The Hering–Breuer (inflation) reflex is a protective reflex that stops inspiration when the lungs are over-stretched.

Mechanism

  1. Stretch receptors in the walls of the bronchi and bronchioles are stimulated when the lungs inflate
  2. Impulses travel through the vagus nerve to the respiratory centre
  3. The centre inhibits inspiration and allows expiration to begin

Importance

  • Prevents over-inflation of the lungs
  • Helps regulate the depth and rate of breathing
  • Important in newborns; in adults it acts mainly when the tidal volume is large (for example during exercise)

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Explain the oxygen–haemoglobin dissociation curve and the factors affecting it.
answer_html:
Introduction The oxygen–haemoglobin dissociation curve shows the relationship between the partial pressure of oxygen (PO₂) and the percentage saturation of haemoglobin with oxygen. It explains how haemoglobin loads oxygen in the lungs and unloads it in the tissues.

1. Shape of the curve – sigmoid (S-shaped)

  • When one haem group binds oxygen, the others bind more easily (cooperative binding), giving an S shape
  • At a PO₂ of 100 mmHg (arterial blood), haemoglobin is about 97–98% saturated
  • At a PO₂ of 40 mmHg (venous blood at rest), it is still about 75% saturated – a reserve for exercise
  • P50 – the PO₂ at which haemoglobin is 50% saturated – is about 26–27 mmHg

2. Significance of the shape

  • Upper flat part – even if alveolar PO₂ falls (high altitude, mild lung disease), saturation stays high – a safety margin for loading
  • Steep middle part – a small fall in tissue PO₂ releases a large amount of oxygen to the tissues

3. Shift to the right – haemoglobin holds oxygen less tightly, so more oxygen is released to the tissues (P50 increases)

  • Increased CO₂ and increased H⁺ (acidosis) – the Bohr effect
  • Increased temperature (fever, exercise)
  • Increased 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate (2,3-BPG) – in anaemia, high altitude
  • Exercise – all the above occur in active muscles

4. Shift to the left – haemoglobin holds oxygen more tightly, releasing less to the tissues

  • Decreased CO₂, H⁺, temperature and 2,3-BPG (alkalosis, hypothermia)
  • Fetal haemoglobin (HbF) – helps the fetus take oxygen from the mother's blood
  • Carbon monoxide – binds haemoglobin about 200 times more strongly than oxygen and also shifts the curve to the left

5. Applied importance

  • Pulse oximetry measures saturation; because of the curve, a saturation of 90% corresponds to a PO₂ of only about 60 mmHg – values below 90–92% are a warning sign
  • Carbon monoxide poisoning (charcoal stoves, generators in closed rooms) – oximeters may show falsely normal readings; treat with 100% oxygen
  • Fever and acidosis increase oxygen delivery to tissues, while hypothermia and alkalosis reduce it

Conclusion The sigmoid oxygen–haemoglobin dissociation curve ensures nearly full loading of oxygen in the lungs and easy unloading in the tissues; it shifts to the right with more CO₂, acid, heat and 2,3-BPG, and to the left with fetal haemoglobin, carbon monoxide and cold.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Explain the exchange of gases in the lungs and tissues.
answer_html:
Introduction Gas exchange is the movement of oxygen and carbon dioxide between the alveoli and blood (external respiration) and between blood and tissues (internal respiration). It occurs by simple diffusion, from a region of higher partial pressure to a region of lower partial pressure.

1. Partial pressures (approximate values)

Site PO₂ (mmHg) PCO₂ (mmHg)
Atmospheric air 160 0.3
Alveolar air 100–104 40
Venous blood reaching lungs 40 45–46
Arterial blood 95–100 40
Tissues 40 or less 46 or more

2. Exchange in the lungs (external respiration)

  • Oxygen diffuses from the alveoli (PO₂ about 100) into the pulmonary capillary blood (PO₂ 40)
  • Carbon dioxide diffuses from the blood (PCO₂ 46) into the alveoli (PCO₂ 40)
  • Exchange is completed in a fraction of a second, well within the time blood spends in the capillary (about 0.75 second at rest)

3. Exchange in the tissues (internal respiration)

  • Oxygen diffuses from arterial blood (PO₂ 100) into the cells (PO₂ 40 or less)
  • Carbon dioxide diffuses from the cells (PCO₂ 46 or more) into the blood

4. Factors affecting diffusion across the respiratory membrane

  • Partial pressure difference – larger gradient, faster diffusion
  • Surface area – about 70 m²; reduced in emphysema, lung removal
  • Thickness of the membrane – normally about 0.5 µm; increased in pulmonary oedema, fibrosis and pneumonia
  • Solubility of the gas – CO₂ is about 20 times more soluble than O₂, so CO₂ diffuses easily even with a small gradient
  • Ventilation–perfusion ratio – normally about 0.8; mismatch (as in pulmonary embolism or pneumonia) reduces exchange

5. Applied importance

  • Oxygen therapy raises alveolar PO₂ and increases the gradient
  • Pulmonary oedema and fibrosis thicken the membrane – hypoxia
  • Emphysema reduces the surface area
  • Positioning – good lung down in unilateral disease improves matching

Conclusion Gases are exchanged in the lungs and tissues by diffusion down partial pressure gradients; the rate depends on the gradient, surface area, membrane thickness, solubility and ventilation–perfusion matching.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Explain the respiratory changes during exercise.
answer_html:
Introduction During exercise, working muscles need much more oxygen and produce more carbon dioxide, heat and acid. The respiratory and cardiovascular systems adjust quickly to meet these needs.

1. Pulmonary ventilation

  • Ventilation increases from about 6 litres per minute at rest to many times higher in heavy exercise
  • At first the depth of breathing increases, then the rate
  • Sudden rise at the start – due to impulses from the motor cortex and from receptors in moving joints and muscles, even before blood gases change
  • Gradual further rise – due to increased CO₂, H⁺ (lactic acid), temperature and adrenaline stimulating the respiratory centre

2. Oxygen consumption and CO₂ production

  • Oxygen uptake rises from about 250 ml per minute at rest to several litres per minute in trained athletes
  • The maximum oxygen uptake (VO₂ max) is a measure of fitness

3. Oxygen delivery to muscles

  • Cardiac output increases several times (higher heart rate and stroke volume)
  • Blood is redirected to the working muscles; muscle capillaries open up
  • The oxygen–haemoglobin dissociation curve shifts to the right (more CO₂, acid and heat), so more oxygen is released
  • Myoglobin in muscle supplies stored oxygen

4. Oxygen debt

  • In heavy exercise, muscles also use anaerobic glycolysis, producing lactic acid
  • After exercise, extra oxygen is taken in (oxygen debt) to remove lactic acid, rebuild ATP and creatine phosphate and restore myoglobin oxygen – hence breathlessness continues for some time after stopping

5. Effects of regular training

  • Stronger respiratory muscles, larger vital capacity, slower resting heart and breathing rates, higher VO₂ max and better oxygen extraction

6. Applied importance

  • Exercise tolerance is assessed in heart and lung disease (6-minute walk test)
  • Graded exercise and breathing exercises in pulmonary rehabilitation (COPD) and after surgery
  • Patients with heart or lung disease become breathless on exertion early

Conclusion During exercise, ventilation, oxygen uptake, cardiac output and oxygen release to the muscles all increase, and an oxygen debt is repaid afterwards; regular training improves these responses.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Write any four functions of the liver.
answer_html:
Introduction The liver is the largest gland of the body and its "chemical factory".

Functions of the liver

  1. Metabolism – stores glucose as glycogen and releases it when blood sugar falls; forms new glucose (gluconeogenesis); breaks down fats; converts ammonia into urea
  2. Secretion of bile – needed for digestion and absorption of fats
  3. Synthesis of plasma proteins – albumin, globulins and clotting factors (prothrombin, fibrinogen)
  4. Detoxification – breaks down drugs, alcohol, toxins and hormones
  5. Storage – glycogen, vitamins A, D, B12, iron and copper
  6. Defence – Kupffer cells remove bacteria and old cells
  7. Heat production and formation of blood cells in the foetus

subject: Applied Physiology
question: List the functions of saliva.
answer_html:
Introduction Saliva is secreted by the salivary glands – about 1–1.5 litres a day, pH about 6.8.

Functions

  1. Digestive – salivary amylase (ptyalin) starts breaking starch into maltose
  2. Lubrication – mucin moistens food and forms a smooth bolus for swallowing
  3. Taste – dissolves food so that taste buds can detect it
  4. Cleansing and protection – washes the mouth and teeth; lysozyme and IgA kill bacteria
  5. Speech – keeps the mouth and tongue moist
  6. Excretion – of some drugs, heavy metals and viruses (rabies)
  7. Water balance – a dry mouth produces thirst

subject: Applied Physiology
question: State the composition and functions of bile.
answer_html:
Introduction Bile is secreted continuously by the liver (about 500–1000 ml a day) and is stored and concentrated in the gall bladder.

Composition

  • Water, bile salts, bile pigments (bilirubin, biliverdin), cholesterol, lecithin, electrolytes, mucin

Functions

  1. Emulsification of fats – bile salts break fat into tiny droplets for lipase to act on
  2. Absorption of fats and fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E, K
  3. Excretion of bilirubin, cholesterol, drugs and toxins
  4. Neutralises acid chyme (alkaline)
  5. Stimulates intestinal movements (mild laxative)

Applied: in obstructive jaundice, stools become clay-coloured and vitamin K absorption falls – bleeding tendency.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Explain the mechanism of hydrochloric acid secretion in the stomach.

diagram.caption: Parietal cell - HCl secretion
labels: CO2 + H2O to H2CO3 to H+ and HCO3-
HCO3- / Cl- exchange into blood (alkaline tide)

answer_html:
Introduction Hydrochloric acid (HCl) is secreted by the parietal (oxyntic) cells of the gastric glands in the fundus and body of the stomach. It makes gastric juice strongly acidic (pH about 1.5–3). The acid is produced inside the cell from carbon dioxide and water and pumped out against a huge concentration gradient – about a million times more H⁺ than in blood.

1. Steps in the formation of HCl

  1. Formation of H⁺ – inside the parietal cell, CO₂ (from cell metabolism and blood) combines with water under the enzyme carbonic anhydrase: CO₂ + H₂O → H₂CO₃ → H⁺ + HCO₃⁻

  2. Secretion of H⁺ – H⁺ is pumped into the canaliculi (gland lumen) by the H⁺/K⁺-ATPase (proton pump) in exchange for K⁺; this uses ATP

  3. Removal of HCO₃⁻ – bicarbonate passes into the blood in exchange for chloride; blood leaving the stomach after a meal becomes alkaline (alkaline tide), and urine may also become alkaline
  4. Secretion of Cl⁻ – chloride ions move into the lumen through chloride channels
  5. Formation of HCl – in the lumen, H⁺ + Cl⁻ = HCl

2. Stimulants of acid secretion

  • Acetylcholine – released by the vagus nerve
  • Gastrin – hormone from G cells
  • Histamine – acts on H₂ receptors of parietal cells; strengthens the effect of the other two

3. Inhibitors

  • Low pH in the stomach (somatostatin), secretin, GIP, sympathetic activity

4. Functions of HCl

  • Converts inactive pepsinogen into pepsin and provides the acid pH it needs
  • Kills bacteria swallowed with food – a defence barrier
  • Denatures (softens) proteins
  • Helps absorption of iron and calcium
  • Stimulates the release of secretin when acid chyme enters the duodenum

5. Applied / nursing importance

  • Proton pump inhibitors (omeprazole, pantoprazole) block step 2 – the most powerful acid-reducing drugs; given before breakfast
  • H₂ blockers (famotidine) block the action of histamine
  • Antacids neutralise the acid already formed
  • Excess acid plays a part in peptic ulcer and GERD
  • Achlorhydria (no acid) occurs in pernicious anaemia and atrophic gastritis

Conclusion Parietal cells produce H⁺ from CO₂ and water using carbonic anhydrase and pump it out with the proton pump, while chloride follows to form HCl; this mechanism is the target of the commonest acid-reducing drugs.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Describe the movements of the small intestine and their significance.
answer_html:
Introduction The small intestine shows different types of movement that mix chyme with digestive juices, bring it into contact with the mucosa and push it towards the colon. These movements are controlled mainly by the intestine's own nerve plexuses (enteric nervous system), and are increased by the vagus and decreased by sympathetic nerves.

1. Segmentation (mixing) contractions

  • Rhythmic contractions of short rings of circular muscle that divide the intestine into segments
  • The contracted rings then relax and new rings form in between, so the chyme is chopped and mixed back and forth
  • About 11–12 per minute in the duodenum, fewer in the ileum
  • Significance: mixes chyme thoroughly with pancreatic juice, bile and intestinal juice; brings it in contact with the villi for absorption

2. Peristalsis (propulsive movement)

  • A wave of contraction behind the food with relaxation in front of it, moving chyme towards the colon
  • Usually weak and travels only a short distance
  • Chyme takes about 3–5 hours to pass through the small intestine
  • Peristaltic rush – a strong, fast wave in infection or irritation; sweeps contents rapidly and causes diarrhoea
  • Significance: moves chyme forward at a rate that allows complete digestion and absorption

3. Pendular movements

  • To-and-fro, swaying movements of loops of intestine
  • Significance: help mixing

4. Movements of the villi

  • Villi shorten and lengthen and sway from side to side
  • Significance: stir the fluid near the surface and pump lymph out of the lacteals, helping fat absorption

5. Migrating motor complex

  • Strong sweeping waves that pass along the intestine every 1–2 hours during fasting
  • Significance: clear leftover food, mucus and bacteria – the "housekeeper" of the gut

6. Reflexes affecting movements

  • Gastro-ileal reflex – food in the stomach increases ileal movement and opens the ileocaecal valve
  • Intestino-intestinal reflex – over-distension of one part inhibits movement in the rest
  • Gastrocolic reflex – food in the stomach triggers mass movement in the colon (urge to defecate after meals)

7. Applied / nursing importance

  • Paralytic ileus after abdominal surgery – movements stop, bowel sounds are absent, the abdomen distends; keep the patient nil by mouth with NG aspiration until bowel sounds return and flatus is passed
  • Intestinal obstruction – colicky pain, vomiting, loud high-pitched bowel sounds
  • Diarrhoea in infections – peristaltic rush
  • Early ambulation after surgery helps bowel movements return

Conclusion Segmentation and pendular movements mix the chyme, peristalsis moves it forward and villous movements aid absorption; assessing bowel sounds is the nurse's bedside check on these movements.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Describe the composition, functions and regulation of pancreatic juice.
answer_html:
Introduction Pancreatic juice is the most important digestive juice because it contains enzymes for all three main foods – carbohydrates, proteins and fats. It is secreted by the acini of the pancreas and enters the duodenum through the pancreatic duct.

1. Volume and properties

  • About 1–1.5 litres a day
  • Clear, watery and alkaline (pH about 8) because of its high bicarbonate content

2. Composition

  • Water and bicarbonate (from duct cells)
  • Proteolytic enzymes – secreted in inactive form to protect the pancreas:
    • Trypsinogen → activated to trypsin by enterokinase of the duodenum
    • Chymotrypsinogen → chymotrypsin (activated by trypsin)
    • Procarboxypeptidase → carboxypeptidase
  • Pancreatic amylase – starch → maltose
  • Lipolytic enzymes – pancreatic lipase (fats → fatty acids and monoglycerides), phospholipase, cholesterol esterase
  • Nucleases – break down nucleic acids
  • Trypsin inhibitor – prevents early activation of trypsin inside the gland

3. Functions

  • Neutralises acid chyme coming from the stomach, so intestinal enzymes can work and the duodenal lining is protected
  • Digestion of proteins into peptides and amino acids
  • Digestion of carbohydrates – starch to maltose
  • Digestion of fats (with the help of bile)

4. Regulation of secretion A. Cephalic phase (about 20%)

  • Sight, smell and taste of food → vagus → small amount of enzyme-rich juice

B. Gastric phase (about 10%)

  • Distension of the stomach and gastrin → vagovagal reflexes

C. Intestinal phase (about 70%) – the most important

  • Acid chyme in the duodenum → S cells release secretin → large volume of watery, bicarbonate-rich juice (neutralises acid)
  • Fats and proteins in the duodenum → I cells release cholecystokinin (CCK) → enzyme-rich juice and contraction of the gall bladder (bile enters at the same time)

5. Applied / nursing importance

  • Acute pancreatitis – enzymes get activated inside the gland and digest it (autodigestion); severe epigastric pain going to the back, raised serum amylase and lipase; patient kept nil by mouth to rest the pancreas
  • Chronic pancreatitis and cystic fibrosis – lack of lipase → bulky, oily, foul-smelling stools (steatorrhoea); pancreatic enzyme capsules are given with meals
  • Gallstone blocking the ampulla can trigger pancreatitis

Conclusion Pancreatic juice is an alkaline, enzyme-rich secretion that digests all main foods; it is controlled mainly by secretin (bicarbonate) and CCK (enzymes) in the intestinal phase.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Explain the digestion and absorption of carbohydrates, proteins and fats.
answer_html:
Introduction Digestion is the breakdown of large food molecules into small, absorbable units by enzymes. Absorption is the passage of these units through the intestinal lining into blood or lymph. Most digestion and nearly all absorption take place in the small intestine.

1. Carbohydrates

  • Mouth – salivary amylase begins to break starch into maltose
  • Stomach – amylase continues briefly inside the bolus until acid stops it
  • Small intestine
    • Pancreatic amylase – starch → maltose
    • Brush-border enzymes: maltase (maltose → glucose), sucrase (sucrose → glucose + fructose), lactase (lactose → glucose + galactose)
  • End products: glucose, fructose, galactose
  • Absorption: glucose and galactose by sodium co-transport (secondary active); fructose by facilitated diffusion → portal blood → liver

2. Proteins

  • Stomach – pepsin (in HCl) breaks proteins into proteoses, peptones and polypeptides
  • Small intestine
    • Trypsin, chymotrypsin, carboxypeptidase (pancreatic) – polypeptides → smaller peptides
    • Brush-border aminopeptidases and dipeptidases → amino acids
  • End products: amino acids (and some di- and tripeptides)
  • Absorption: active transport with sodium → portal blood

3. Fats

  • Mouth and stomach – lingual and gastric lipase digest a small amount
  • Small intestine
    • Bile salts emulsify fat into tiny droplets
    • Pancreatic lipase → fatty acids and monoglycerides
  • Absorption
    • Products form tiny micelles with bile salts and enter the cells
    • Inside the cells they are re-made into triglycerides and packed as chylomicrons
    • Chylomicrons enter the lacteals → lymph → thoracic duct → blood

4. Summary table

Food Enzymes End products Absorbed into
Carbohydrates amylases, maltase, sucrase, lactase glucose, fructose, galactose portal blood
Proteins pepsin, trypsin, chymotrypsin, peptidases amino acids portal blood
Fats lipases (with bile salts) fatty acids, monoglycerides lymph (lacteals)

5. Absorption of other substances

  • Water – about 8–9 litres enter the gut daily; most is absorbed in the small intestine, the rest in the colon
  • Iron and calcium – mainly duodenum
  • Vitamin B12 – terminal ileum, needs intrinsic factor
  • Fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) – with fat; need bile

6. Applied / nursing importance

  • Lactose intolerance (lactase deficiency) – bloating and diarrhoea after milk
  • Removal of the ileum or lack of intrinsic factor → B12 deficiency anaemia
  • ORS uses sodium–glucose co-transport to rehydrate
  • Obstructive jaundice → poor fat and vitamin K absorption

Conclusion Carbohydrates are digested to monosaccharides, proteins to amino acids and fats to fatty acids and monoglycerides; sugars and amino acids enter the portal blood, while fats enter the lymph.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Describe the composition, functions and phases of gastric juice secretion. Add a note on peptic ulcer. (2 + 2 + 4 + 2)
answer_html:
Introduction Gastric juice is the digestive juice secreted by the gastric glands of the stomach. It begins protein digestion, kills microbes and helps the absorption of vitamin B12. Its secretion is closely controlled by nerves and hormones so that acid is produced when food is present and stopped when it is not.

(a) Composition (2 marks)

  • Volume: about 1.5–2.5 litres a day
  • Reaction: strongly acidic, pH about 1.5–3
  • Water – about 99%
  • Hydrochloric acid – from parietal cells
  • Pepsinogen – from chief cells; activated to pepsin by HCl
  • Gastric lipase – small amount; digests some fat
  • Mucus and bicarbonate – from mucous cells; protect the stomach lining
  • Intrinsic factor – from parietal cells; needed for vitamin B12 absorption
  • Electrolytes – Na⁺, K⁺, Cl⁻, H⁺
  • The hormone gastrin (from G cells) is released into the blood, not into the juice

(b) Functions (2 marks)

  1. Digestive
    • Pepsin breaks proteins into proteoses, peptones and polypeptides
    • Gastric lipase breaks some fats (important in infants)
  2. Functions of HCl – activates pepsinogen, provides acid pH, kills bacteria, softens proteins, helps iron and calcium absorption
  3. Protective – a layer of mucus and bicarbonate (the gastric mucosal barrier) protects the stomach wall from acid and pepsin
  4. Haemopoietic – intrinsic factor allows absorption of vitamin B12, needed for red cell formation
  5. Liquefies food into chyme

(c) Phases of gastric secretion and their regulation (4 marks) Gastric secretion is divided into three phases according to where the stimulus acts.

1. Cephalic phase (about 30% of secretion)

  • Stimulus: sight, smell, taste, chewing or even the thought of food
  • Mechanism: impulses from the brain (cerebral cortex, hypothalamus, medulla) travel through the vagus nerves → acetylcholine directly stimulates the gastric glands and also releases gastrin from G cells
  • Proof: in Pavlov's sham-feeding experiments gastric juice flowed even when food never reached the stomach
  • Inhibited by anxiety, depression and loss of appetite
  • Practical meaning: attractive, well-presented food helps digestion

2. Gastric phase (about 60% – the most important)

  • Stimulus: food entering the stomach
  • Mechanisms:
    • Distension of the stomach stretches its wall → local nerve reflexes and long vagovagal reflexes → more secretion
    • Protein digestion products (peptides, amino acids), caffeine and alcohol stimulate G cells in the pyloric region to release gastrin into the blood
    • Gastrin reaches the glands through the blood and strongly stimulates parietal cells (acid) and chief cells (pepsinogen)
    • Histamine from enterochromaffin-like cells adds to the effect
  • Self-regulation (negative feedback): when the pH in the pyloric region falls below about 2, somatostatin is released and gastrin secretion stops – this prevents excess acid

3. Intestinal phase (about 10%)

  • Stimulus: chyme entering the duodenum
  • Early stimulatory part – partly digested proteins release a little "intestinal gastrin"
  • Mainly inhibitory:
    • Acid, fat and hypertonic chyme in the duodenum release the hormones secretin, cholecystokinin (CCK) and GIP (gastric inhibitory peptide)
    • They inhibit gastric secretion and slow gastric emptying
    • The enterogastric reflex (nervous) also inhibits the stomach
  • Purpose: gives the duodenum time to neutralise and digest the chyme before more arrives

Summary

Phase Stimulus Main mediator Share
Cephalic sight, smell, thought of food vagus (acetylcholine) about 30%
Gastric food in stomach (distension, peptides) gastrin, local reflexes about 60%
Intestinal chyme in duodenum secretin, CCK, GIP (mostly inhibit) about 10%

(d) Note on peptic ulcer (2 marks) Definition: a peptic ulcer is a break (ulcer) in the mucous membrane of the parts of the gut exposed to acid and pepsin – mainly the stomach (gastric ulcer) and the first part of the duodenum (duodenal ulcer).

Cause: imbalance between aggressive factors and protective factors

  • Aggressive: excess acid and pepsin, Helicobacter pylori infection, NSAIDs (aspirin, ibuprofen), smoking, alcohol, stress, irregular meals
  • Protective: mucus, bicarbonate, good mucosal blood flow, prostaglandins

Clinical features

  • Burning epigastric pain
    • Gastric ulcer – pain soon after meals; weight loss
    • Duodenal ulcer – pain when hungry and at night, relieved by food
  • Nausea, heartburn, bloating

Complications: bleeding (haematemesis, black tarry stools – melaena), perforation (sudden severe pain, rigid abdomen), pyloric obstruction (vomiting).

Management and nursing

  • Proton pump inhibitors; eradication of H. pylori with antibiotics
  • Stop NSAIDs, smoking and alcohol; small regular meals; reduce stress
  • Watch pulse, BP and stool colour for signs of bleeding

Conclusion Gastric juice is an acidic secretion rich in HCl and pepsinogen whose flow is controlled in cephalic, gastric and intestinal phases by the vagus, gastrin and duodenal hormones. When the balance between acid and mucosal protection is lost, peptic ulcer results.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Describe digestion in the mouth. (2 + 3 + 3 + 2)
answer_html:
(a) Introduction (2 marks)

  • Digestion begins in the mouth (oral or buccal cavity)
  • Here food is broken down mechanically by chewing and chemically by saliva, and shaped into a soft, moist bolus that can be swallowed easily
  • Food stays in the mouth only for a short time, so chemical digestion is limited, but chewing and saliva are essential for the rest of digestion
  • Structures involved: teeth, tongue, cheeks, lips, palate, muscles of mastication and salivary glands

(b) Mechanical digestion – mastication (3 marks) 1. Teeth

  • Incisors – cut food
  • Canines – tear food
  • Premolars and molars – crush and grind food
  • Adults have 32 permanent teeth; children have 20 milk (deciduous) teeth

2. Muscles of mastication

  • Masseter, temporalis, medial and lateral pterygoids
  • Supplied by the mandibular branch of the trigeminal (5th) nerve
  • Move the lower jaw up, down, forward and from side to side

3. Role of tongue, cheeks and lips

  • Keep turning the food and placing it between the teeth
  • The tongue mixes food with saliva and shapes the bolus

4. Importance of chewing

  • Breaks food into small particles and increases the surface area for enzymes
  • Mixes food with saliva
  • Forms a smooth bolus that is easy to swallow
  • Releases flavour, which reflexly stimulates saliva, gastric juice and pancreatic juice
  • Prevents injury to the oesophagus from large hard pieces

(c) Chemical digestion – saliva (3 marks) 1. Salivary glands: parotid, submandibular and sublingual, plus many small glands in the mouth.

2. Properties

  • Volume about 1–1.5 litres a day
  • pH about 6.8 (slightly acidic to neutral)

3. Composition

  • Water – about 99.5%
  • Organic: salivary amylase (ptyalin), lingual lipase, mucin, lysozyme, immunoglobulin A, blood group substances
  • Inorganic: sodium, potassium, chloride, bicarbonate, calcium, phosphate

4. Enzyme action

  • Salivary amylase
    • Acts on cooked starch and breaks it into maltose, maltotriose and small dextrins
    • Works best at pH about 6.8
    • Its action continues for some time inside the bolus in the stomach, until gastric acid penetrates and inactivates it
  • Lingual lipase – begins the digestion of a small amount of fat; continues in the stomach
  • Mucin – lubricates the bolus

5. Regulation of salivary secretion – entirely nervous (no hormones)

  • Parasympathetic – facial nerve (to the submandibular and sublingual glands) and glossopharyngeal nerve (to the parotid) → large volume of watery saliva rich in enzymes
  • Sympathetic → small amount of thick, viscous saliva – the mouth feels dry in fear
  • Unconditioned reflex – food touching the mouth and tongue (taste)
  • Conditioned reflex – sight, smell or even the thought of food (Pavlov's experiments on dogs)

6. Deglutition – oral stage

  • After chewing, the tongue pushes the bolus upward and backward against the palate into the oropharynx
  • This first stage is voluntary; after the bolus touches the pharynx, swallowing continues as a reflex

(d) Applied aspects (2 marks)

  • Dry mouth (xerostomia) – in dehydration, fever, mouth breathing, anxiety, atropine and other anticholinergic drugs, and after radiation to the head and neck; such patients need frequent mouth care
  • Parotitis – infection of the parotid in dehydrated, unconscious or post-operative patients with poor oral hygiene; prevented by good mouth care and adequate fluids
  • Mumps – viral infection of the parotid glands
  • Excess salivation – in organophosphorus poisoning, rabies, teething and some drugs
  • Elderly patients with missing teeth or ill-fitting dentures chew poorly – offer soft, moist food
  • Patients on nil by mouth still need mouth care to keep the mucosa healthy
  • Good chewing habits and oral hygiene support digestion and prevent dental caries

Conclusion In the mouth, food is chewed into small pieces and mixed with saliva, whose amylase begins starch digestion and whose mucin lubricates the bolus; salivary secretion is controlled purely by nervous reflexes, and good oral care preserves these functions in sick patients.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: What is the enterohepatic circulation of bile salts?
answer_html:
Definition The enterohepatic circulation is the recycling of bile salts between the liver and the intestine.

Steps

  1. The liver forms bile salts from cholesterol and secretes them in bile
  2. In the small intestine, bile salts help digest and absorb fats
  3. About 95% of bile salts are reabsorbed in the terminal ileum
  4. They return to the liver through the portal vein and are secreted again
  5. The pool of bile salts recirculates several times a day; only a small amount is lost in faeces and replaced by new synthesis

Applied: removal or disease of the terminal ileum (Crohn's disease) causes loss of bile salts and fat malabsorption (fatty stools); drugs such as cholestyramine bind bile salts and lower cholesterol.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Name the gastrointestinal hormones and state their functions.
answer_html:
Introduction Hormones produced by cells of the stomach and intestine regulate digestion.

Hormones and functions

  1. Gastrin – from G cells of the stomach (antrum); stimulates HCl secretion and gastric movements
  2. Secretin – from the duodenum when acid enters it; stimulates bicarbonate-rich pancreatic juice and inhibits gastric secretion
  3. Cholecystokinin (CCK) – from the duodenum when fat and protein enter it; causes gall bladder contraction and enzyme-rich pancreatic juice; produces a feeling of fullness
  4. Glucose-dependent insulinotropic peptide (GIP) – stimulates insulin release; inhibits gastric secretion
  5. Motilin – stimulates intestinal movements between meals
  6. Ghrelin – from the stomach; stimulates hunger

subject: Applied Physiology
question: What is the gastrocolic reflex?
answer_html:
Definition The gastrocolic reflex is an increase in movements of the colon (mass movements) when food enters and stretches the stomach.

Features
