  1. It pushes faeces into the rectum and produces the urge to defecate shortly after a meal
  2. It is strongest after the first meal of the day (breakfast)
  3. It is controlled by the myenteric nerve plexus, the autonomic nerves and hormones such as gastrin

Applied

  • Explains why infants often pass stool after feeds
  • Used in bowel training – encourage patients to use the toilet after breakfast
  • Ignoring the urge repeatedly leads to constipation

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Mention the functions of the stomach.
answer_html:
Introduction The stomach is the widest part of the alimentary canal, between the oesophagus and the duodenum.

Functions

  1. Storage of food – acts as a reservoir, allowing intermittent meals
  2. Mechanical digestion – churning movements mix food with gastric juice to form chyme
  3. Chemical digestion – pepsin begins protein digestion; gastric lipase acts on some fats
  4. Hydrochloric acid – kills microbes, activates pepsinogen, helps iron absorption
  5. Intrinsic factor – essential for absorption of vitamin B₁₂
  6. Mucus – protects the stomach wall from acid
  7. Absorption of small amounts of water, alcohol and some drugs (aspirin)
  8. Gastrin secretion and controlled emptying of chyme into the duodenum

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Explain the mechanism of deglutition (swallowing).
answer_html:
Introduction Deglutition (swallowing) is the process by which food is moved from the mouth to the stomach. It is a complex act involving more than 20 muscles, controlled by the swallowing centre in the medulla and lower pons. It has three stages.

1. Oral (voluntary) stage

  • Food is chewed and mixed with saliva to form a bolus
  • The tongue presses against the hard palate and pushes the bolus backwards into the oropharynx
  • This stage is under voluntary control

2. Pharyngeal (involuntary) stage – lasts about 1–2 seconds

  • Touch receptors in the pharynx trigger the swallowing reflex
  • The soft palate rises and closes the nasopharynx – food cannot enter the nose
  • The larynx moves up and forward; the epiglottis folds over the laryngeal inlet and the vocal cords close – food cannot enter the airway
  • Breathing stops briefly (deglutition apnoea)
  • The upper oesophageal sphincter relaxes and the pharyngeal constrictor muscles push the bolus into the oesophagus

3. Oesophageal (involuntary) stage

  • Peristaltic waves carry the bolus down the oesophagus
  • The lower oesophageal sphincter relaxes to let food enter the stomach, then closes to prevent reflux
  • Solid food takes several seconds to reach the stomach; liquids pass faster with the help of gravity

4. Nerve control

  • Afferent – trigeminal (V), glossopharyngeal (IX) and vagus (X) nerves
  • Centre – medulla and lower pons
  • Efferent – V, IX, X and hypoglossal (XII) nerves

5. Applied importance

  • Dysphagia (difficulty in swallowing) – stroke, Parkinson's disease, oesophageal cancer, achalasia (failure of the lower sphincter to relax)
  • Aspiration – if the protective mechanisms fail (stroke, unconsciousness, sedation), food enters the lungs, causing aspiration pneumonia
  • Nursing: check the swallowing (gag) reflex before oral feeding; feed stroke patients sitting upright with thickened fluids and small spoonfuls; keep the head raised for 30 minutes after feeds; use nasogastric feeding when swallowing is unsafe
  • Gastro-oesophageal reflux when the lower sphincter is weak

Conclusion Swallowing has a voluntary oral stage and involuntary pharyngeal and oesophageal stages, during which the nose and airway are sealed off and peristalsis carries food to the stomach; its failure leads to dysphagia and aspiration.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Explain the role of the liver in metabolism.
answer_html:
Introduction The liver is the largest gland of the body and its chief metabolic organ. It receives nutrient-rich blood from the gut through the portal vein and processes carbohydrates, fats and proteins before they reach the general circulation.

1. Carbohydrate metabolism

  • Glycogenesis – stores excess glucose as glycogen after meals
  • Glycogenolysis – breaks glycogen to glucose between meals
  • Gluconeogenesis – forms glucose from amino acids, lactate and glycerol during fasting
  • Thus the liver keeps the blood glucose level steady

2. Fat metabolism

  • Oxidation of fatty acids for energy; formation of ketone bodies in fasting and uncontrolled diabetes
  • Synthesis of cholesterol, phospholipids and lipoproteins
  • Converts excess carbohydrate and protein into fat
  • Forms bile salts from cholesterol, needed for fat digestion

3. Protein metabolism

  • Deamination of amino acids; converts the toxic ammonia into urea (urea cycle), which is excreted by the kidneys
  • Synthesis of plasma proteins – albumin, most globulins, fibrinogen, prothrombin and other clotting factors (factors II, VII, IX and X need vitamin K)
  • Interconversion of amino acids

4. Storage

  • Glycogen, vitamins A, D, B₁₂ and K, iron (as ferritin) and copper

5. Other metabolic functions

  • Detoxification and metabolism of drugs (first-pass effect), alcohol and toxins
  • Inactivation of hormones (steroids, insulin)
  • Bilirubin – conjugation and excretion in bile
  • Heat production

6. Applied importance (liver failure, cirrhosis)

  • Low albumin → oedema and ascites
  • Low clotting factors → bleeding tendency (check prothrombin time; give vitamin K)
  • Ammonia not converted to urea → hepatic encephalopathy (confusion, flapping tremor); protein intake adjusted, lactulose given
  • Hypoglycaemia, jaundice, reduced drug metabolism – doses of sedatives and paracetamol must be reduced

Conclusion The liver controls carbohydrate, fat and protein metabolism, makes plasma proteins and clotting factors, converts ammonia to urea, stores vitamins and iron, and detoxifies drugs; its failure produces oedema, bleeding, encephalopathy and jaundice.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Explain the physiology of defecation.
answer_html:
Introduction Defecation is the expulsion of faeces from the rectum through the anus. It is a reflex act that can be voluntarily controlled after early childhood.

1. Filling of the rectum

  • Normally the rectum is empty
  • Mass movements of the colon (often after meals – the gastrocolic reflex) push faeces into the rectum

2. Defecation reflex

  • Distension of the rectal wall stimulates stretch receptors
  • Intrinsic reflex – through the myenteric plexus, causing peristalsis in the descending and sigmoid colon and rectum
  • Parasympathetic reflex – impulses travel to the sacral spinal cord (S2–S4) and back through the pelvic nerves, strengthening rectal contraction and relaxing the internal anal sphincter (involuntary, smooth muscle)
  • The person feels the urge to defecate

3. Voluntary control

  • The external anal sphincter (skeletal muscle, supplied by the pudendal nerve) is under voluntary control
  • If the time and place are suitable, it is relaxed; if not, it is contracted and the urge passes for some time (faeces move back and the rectum adapts)

4. Act of defecation

  • Squatting or sitting posture straightens the anorectal angle
  • A deep breath is taken, the glottis is closed, and the diaphragm and abdominal muscles contract (Valsalva manoeuvre), raising intra-abdominal pressure
  • The levator ani and external sphincter relax and faeces are expelled

5. Applied importance

  • Constipation – ignoring the urge, low fibre and fluids, immobility, opioid drugs, lack of privacy
  • Straining (Valsalva) can be dangerous after a heart attack, eye surgery or in raised intracranial pressure – give stool softeners
  • Faecal incontinence – spinal cord injury, damage to the anal sphincter (third-degree perineal tear), dementia
  • Bowel training – a regular time after breakfast, privacy, a commode or toilet rather than a bedpan, adequate fibre and fluids
  • Enemas and suppositories stimulate the reflex

Conclusion Defecation is a spinal reflex triggered by rectal distension, which relaxes the internal sphincter, while the external sphincter allows voluntary control; adequate fibre, fluids, activity, privacy and regular habits keep it normal.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Describe the composition, functions and regulation of intestinal juice.
answer_html:
Introduction Intestinal juice (succus entericus) is the secretion of the small intestine, produced mainly by the crypts of Lieberkühn and, in the duodenum, the Brunner's glands. About 1.5–2 litres are secreted daily.

1. Properties

  • Slightly alkaline (pH about 7.5–8), watery, with mucus

2. Composition

  • Water and electrolytes (bicarbonate)
  • Mucus – from goblet cells and Brunner's glands
  • Enzymes – most act at the brush border (surface of the microvilli):
    • Disaccharidases – maltase, sucrase, lactase (split disaccharides into monosaccharides)
    • Peptidases – aminopeptidases and dipeptidases (split peptides into amino acids)
    • Enterokinase (enteropeptidase) – activates pancreatic trypsinogen into trypsin
    • Intestinal lipase – a small amount

3. Functions

  • Completes digestion – final breakdown of carbohydrates into glucose, galactose and fructose, and of proteins into amino acids
  • Activates pancreatic enzymes (enterokinase)
  • Neutralises acid chyme from the stomach
  • Dilutes chyme and provides a watery medium for absorption
  • Protects the mucosa (mucus)

4. Regulation

  • Local reflexes – the most important; mechanical and chemical stimulation by chyme in the intestine increases secretion
  • Parasympathetic (vagus) stimulation increases secretion; sympathetic decreases it
  • Hormones – secretin, cholecystokinin and vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP) increase secretion

5. Applied importance

  • Lactose intolerance – deficiency of lactase; bloating, gas and diarrhoea after milk; common in adults; curd is better tolerated
  • Cholera – the toxin causes massive secretion of water and salts, leading to severe watery diarrhoea and dehydration – ORS is life-saving
  • Enterokinase deficiency – poor protein digestion

Conclusion Intestinal juice is an alkaline secretion containing mucus and brush-border enzymes (disaccharidases, peptidases, enterokinase) that completes digestion; it is regulated mainly by local reflexes, the vagus and hormones.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Explain the physiology of vomiting.
answer_html:
Introduction Vomiting (emesis) is the forceful expulsion of the contents of the stomach (and sometimes the duodenum) through the mouth. It is a protective reflex that removes harmful substances, but it can cause dehydration and electrolyte disturbances.

1. Control centres

  • Vomiting centre – in the medulla oblongata
  • Chemoreceptor trigger zone (CTZ) – in the floor of the fourth ventricle (area postrema), outside the blood–brain barrier, so it is sensitive to drugs and toxins in the blood

2. Causes (stimuli)

  • From the gut – irritation or distension of the stomach and intestines (food poisoning, gastritis, intestinal obstruction) through vagal and sympathetic afferents
  • Through the CTZ – drugs (opioids, chemotherapy, digoxin), toxins, uraemia, ketoacidosis, pregnancy (hormones)
  • From the vestibular apparatus – motion sickness
  • From higher centres – unpleasant sights and smells, fear, severe pain
  • Raised intracranial pressure – projectile vomiting without nausea

3. Mechanism (sequence of events)

  • Nausea – unpleasant feeling, with salivation, sweating, pallor, fast pulse
  • Retching – rhythmic contractions of the respiratory and abdominal muscles against a closed glottis
  • Act of vomiting:
    • deep breath; the glottis closes and the soft palate rises (protecting the airway and nose)
    • the lower oesophageal sphincter relaxes
    • strong contraction of the diaphragm and abdominal muscles squeezes the stomach
    • stomach contents are forced up and out through the mouth

4. Effects of severe or repeated vomiting

  • Dehydration and loss of sodium and potassium (hypokalaemia)
  • Loss of hydrochloric acid → metabolic alkalosis
  • Aspiration of vomit into the lungs (unconscious or drowsy patients)
  • Tear at the oesophagogastric junction (Mallory–Weiss tear) causing bleeding
  • Malnutrition

5. Nursing care

  • Position the patient on the side (or sitting forward) to prevent aspiration; keep a kidney tray and suction ready
  • Observe and record the amount, colour (bile, blood, "coffee grounds"), smell and frequency
  • Oral hygiene after each episode
  • Fluids and electrolytes – small sips of ORS, IV fluids if needed; intake–output chart
  • Give antiemetics as prescribed (ondansetron, domperidone, metoclopramide), preferably before chemotherapy
  • Remove unpleasant smells; fresh air

Conclusion Vomiting is a protective reflex coordinated by the medullary vomiting centre and the CTZ, triggered by gut irritation, drugs, motion, emotions and raised intracranial pressure; repeated vomiting causes dehydration, hypokalaemia and alkalosis, so careful nursing care is needed.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Explain bilirubin metabolism and the types of jaundice.
answer_html:
Introduction Bilirubin is a yellow pigment formed from the breakdown of haemoglobin of old red blood cells. Jaundice is the yellow colour of the skin, sclera and mucous membranes due to a high level of bilirubin in the blood.

A. Bilirubin metabolism

  1. Breakdown of red cells – red cells live about 120 days; old cells are destroyed by macrophages of the reticuloendothelial system (mainly the spleen)
  2. Haemoglobin → globin (reused as amino acids) + haem; haem → iron (reused) + biliverdin → bilirubin
  3. This unconjugated (indirect) bilirubin is fat-soluble and is carried in the blood bound to albumin; it cannot pass into urine
  4. In the liver, bilirubin is conjugated with glucuronic acid (by the enzyme glucuronyl transferase) to form conjugated (direct) bilirubin, which is water-soluble
  5. Conjugated bilirubin is excreted in bile into the intestine
  6. Intestinal bacteria convert it into urobilinogen:
    • most is changed to stercobilin, which gives stool its brown colour
    • some is reabsorbed and excreted in urine as urobilin (yellow colour of urine)

Normal serum bilirubin: about 0.3–1.0 mg/dl; jaundice becomes visible when it rises above about 2–2.5 mg/dl in adults (higher in newborns).

B. Types of jaundice

1. Pre-hepatic (haemolytic) jaundice

  • Cause – excessive destruction of red cells: malaria, sickle cell anaemia, thalassaemia, incompatible blood transfusion, Rh incompatibility, physiological jaundice of the newborn
  • Bilirubin – mainly unconjugated
  • Features – mild jaundice, anaemia; urine and stool colour normal or dark (more urobilinogen)

2. Hepatic (hepatocellular) jaundice

  • Cause – liver cells damaged: viral hepatitis (A, B, E), alcoholic liver disease, cirrhosis, drugs (anti-TB drugs, paracetamol overdose)
  • Bilirubin – both unconjugated and conjugated raised
  • Features – loss of appetite, nausea, tender liver, dark urine

3. Post-hepatic (obstructive) jaundice

  • Cause – blockage of bile flow: gallstones in the common bile duct, cancer of the head of the pancreas, strictures
  • Bilirubin – mainly conjugated
  • Features – deep jaundice, dark urine, pale (clay-coloured) stools, itching (bile salts in the skin), bleeding tendency (poor vitamin K absorption)

C. Neonatal jaundice

  • Common in the first week because of high red cell breakdown and immature liver conjugation
  • Very high unconjugated bilirubin can cross the immature blood–brain barrier and damage the brain (kernicterus) – treated with phototherapy or exchange transfusion

D. Nursing points

  • Observe the colour of skin, sclera, urine and stool; relieve itching (cool baths, calamine); check for bleeding; follow hepatitis precautions; give a low-fat diet in obstructive jaundice; protect the eyes of newborns under phototherapy and maintain hydration

Conclusion Bilirubin is formed from haem, conjugated in the liver and excreted in bile to give colour to stool and urine; jaundice may be pre-hepatic (haemolysis), hepatic (liver damage) or post-hepatic (obstruction), each with typical findings.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Define cardiac output and give its normal value.
answer_html:
Definition Cardiac output is the volume of blood pumped by each ventricle per minute.

Formula and normal value

  • Cardiac output = stroke volume × heart rate
  • Stroke volume about 70 ml; heart rate about 72 per minute
  • Cardiac output ≈ 5 litres per minute in a resting adult
  • Can rise four to five times during heavy exercise

Factors affecting cardiac output

  1. Venous return (preload) – more filling, stronger contraction
  2. Force of contraction – increased by sympathetic stimulation and adrenaline
  3. Resistance (afterload) – high BP reduces output
  4. Heart rate

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Define blood pressure and pulse pressure. Give the normal values.
answer_html:
Definitions

  1. Blood pressure – the lateral pressure exerted by blood on the walls of the arteries
    • Systolic pressure – the highest pressure, during ventricular contraction – about 120 mm Hg
    • Diastolic pressure – the lowest pressure, during ventricular relaxation – about 80 mm Hg
  2. Pulse pressure = systolic − diastolic = about 40 mm Hg
  3. Mean arterial pressure = diastolic + one-third of pulse pressure ≈ 93 mm Hg

Notes

  • Blood pressure rises with age and is slightly lower in women
  • Hypertension: 140/90 mm Hg or more on repeated readings
  • Hypotension: systolic below about 90 mm Hg

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Name the heart sounds and their causes.
answer_html:
Introduction Heart sounds are produced mainly by the closure of the heart valves. They are heard with a stethoscope.

Heart sounds

  1. First heart sound (S1, "lub")
    • Caused by closure of the atrioventricular valves (mitral and tricuspid) at the start of ventricular systole
    • Long, low-pitched; best heard at the apex
  2. Second heart sound (S2, "dub")
    • Caused by closure of the semilunar valves (aortic and pulmonary) at the start of diastole
    • Short, sharp; best heard at the base (2nd intercostal spaces)
  3. Third heart sound (S3) – rapid filling of the ventricles; may be normal in children and athletes, abnormal in heart failure
  4. Fourth heart sound (S4) – atrial contraction against a stiff ventricle; usually abnormal

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Explain the conducting system of the heart with a diagram.
answer_html:
Introduction The heart has its own specialised muscle tissue that generates the impulse and conducts it in an orderly way through the heart. Because of this the heart beats on its own (autorhythmicity) even without nerve supply – a transplanted heart keeps beating.

1. Components of the conducting system

A. Sinoatrial (SA) node

  • A small mass of specialised cells in the wall of the right atrium, near the opening of the superior vena cava
  • Generates impulses at about 60–100 per minute – the fastest rate, so it controls the heart
  • Called the natural pacemaker of the heart

B. Internodal pathways

  • Carry the impulse quickly through the atria to the AV node
  • The impulse spreading through the atrial muscle makes both atria contract

C. Atrioventricular (AV) node

  • Lies in the lower part of the interatrial septum, near the opening of the coronary sinus
  • Delays the impulse by about 0.1 second – this allows the atria to finish emptying blood into the ventricles before the ventricles contract
  • Can act as a pacemaker at 40–60 per minute if the SA node fails

D. Bundle of His (atrioventricular bundle)

  • Passes from the AV node through the fibrous skeleton into the interventricular septum
  • The only electrical connection between the atria and the ventricles

E. Right and left bundle branches

  • Run down the two sides of the interventricular septum towards the apex

F. Purkinje fibres

  • Spread through the walls of both ventricles
  • Conduct the impulse fastest, so both ventricles contract almost together, from the apex upwards – squeezing blood towards the outlets
  • Can produce 15–40 impulses per minute if all higher centres fail

2. Sequence SA node → atria (contract) → AV node (delay) → bundle of His → bundle branches → Purkinje fibres → ventricles (contract)

3. Relation to the ECG

  • P wave – atrial depolarisation
  • PR interval (0.12–0.20 s) – mainly the delay at the AV node
  • QRS complex – ventricular depolarisation
  • T wave – ventricular repolarisation

4. Nerve control

  • Sympathetic nerves increase the rate of the SA node and speed conduction
  • Vagus nerves slow the SA node and AV conduction

5. Properties of cardiac tissue: automaticity, rhythmicity, conductivity, excitability, contractility.

6. Applied / nursing importance

  • Heart block – damage to the AV node (inferior MI, digoxin toxicity, ageing); slow pulse, fainting; may need an artificial pacemaker
  • Arrhythmias – atrial fibrillation (irregularly irregular pulse), ventricular tachycardia and fibrillation (cardiac arrest – defibrillation)
  • Count the apical pulse for a full minute before giving digoxin; withhold if below 60 and report
  • Cardiac monitoring in ICU shows these rhythms continuously

Conclusion The SA node starts each heartbeat, the AV node delays it, and the bundle of His, bundle branches and Purkinje fibres spread it through the ventricles; disorders of this system cause heart blocks and arrhythmias.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Explain the regulation of arterial blood pressure.
answer_html:
Introduction Blood pressure must be kept within a narrow range – high enough to perfuse the brain, heart and kidneys, but not so high that it damages vessels. Blood pressure = cardiac output × peripheral resistance. The body controls it through short-term (nervous), intermediate (hormonal) and long-term (renal) mechanisms.

1. Short-term (nervous) regulation – acts within seconds

A. Baroreceptor reflex – the most important rapid control

  • Baroreceptors are stretch receptors in the carotid sinus and aortic arch
  • They send impulses through the glossopharyngeal and vagus nerves to the vasomotor centre in the medulla
  • Rise in BP → more stretch → more impulses → increased vagal activity and decreased sympathetic activity → heart slows, vessels dilate → BP falls
  • Fall in BP → fewer impulses → increased sympathetic activity → faster heart, vasoconstriction → BP rises
  • Example: when we stand up quickly, this reflex prevents fainting

B. Chemoreceptor reflex

  • Carotid and aortic bodies respond to low O₂, high CO₂ and acidosis → stimulate vasoconstriction and raise BP

C. CNS ischaemic response

  • When blood supply to the vasomotor centre falls severely, it produces intense vasoconstriction – a last-resort mechanism

2. Intermediate (hormonal) regulation – minutes to hours

  • Renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system – a fall in BP makes the kidneys release renin → angiotensin II (powerful vasoconstrictor) → aldosterone (retains sodium and water) → BP rises
  • ADH (vasopressin) – retains water and constricts vessels
  • Adrenaline and noradrenaline – increase heart rate and force, constrict vessels
  • Atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP) – released when the atria are stretched; removes sodium and water and lowers BP

3. Long-term (renal) regulation – days

  • The kidneys adjust blood volume by changing the excretion of salt and water
  • High BP → more salt and water lost in urine (pressure natriuresis) → volume and BP fall
  • This is the most powerful long-term control

4. Local regulation

  • Arterioles adjust their own diameter (autoregulation) – nitric oxide, carbon dioxide and other metabolites dilate them

5. Applied / nursing importance

  • Postural hypotension – in the elderly and patients on antihypertensives, the baroreceptor response is slow; teach them to sit up and stand slowly
  • Antihypertensive drugs act on these mechanisms – ACE inhibitors (block RAAS), beta-blockers (reduce heart rate), diuretics (reduce volume), vasodilators
  • Shock – these reflexes cause a fast pulse and cold, clammy skin as the body tries to maintain BP; a falling BP is a late sign
  • Low-salt diet helps control hypertension

Conclusion Blood pressure is regulated quickly by the baroreceptor reflex, over hours by hormones such as renin–angiotensin–aldosterone, ADH and adrenaline, and in the long term by the kidneys through control of blood volume.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Explain the hepatic portal system.
answer_html:
Introduction Normally blood passes from arteries → capillaries → veins → heart. In a portal system, venous blood from one capillary bed passes through a second capillary bed before returning to the heart. The hepatic portal system carries blood from the digestive organs to the liver, so that the liver can process absorbed food and remove harmful substances before they reach the general circulation.

1. Organs drained

  • Abdominal part of the gut – from the lower end of the oesophagus to the upper part of the anal canal
  • Spleen, pancreas and gall bladder

2. Formation of the portal vein

  • Formed behind the neck of the pancreas at about L1–L2 by the union of:
    • Superior mesenteric vein (from the small intestine and right side of the colon)
    • Splenic vein (from the spleen, stomach and pancreas)
  • The inferior mesenteric vein (from the left colon and rectum) usually joins the splenic vein

3. Course

  • About 8 cm long
  • Passes upwards behind the first part of the duodenum
  • Runs in the free edge of the lesser omentum with the hepatic artery and bile duct
  • At the porta hepatis divides into right and left branches

4. Termination

  • Branches end in the liver sinusoids (second capillary bed)
  • Sinusoids → central veins → hepatic veins → inferior vena cava → right atrium

5. Tributaries

  • Splenic vein, superior mesenteric vein, left and right gastric veins, cystic vein, para-umbilical veins

6. Functions

  • Brings absorbed nutrients (glucose, amino acids) to the liver for metabolism and storage
  • Allows the liver to detoxify drugs, alcohol and toxins absorbed from the gut – first-pass metabolism (why some drugs are given sublingually, IV or as patches)
  • Kupffer cells remove bacteria absorbed from the gut
  • Supplies about 75% of the blood reaching the liver

7. Portal–systemic anastomoses – places where portal and systemic veins meet

  • Lower end of the oesophagus
  • Anal canal (rectal veins)
  • Around the umbilicus (para-umbilical veins)
  • Behind the peritoneum (retroperitoneal veins)

8. Applied / nursing importance – portal hypertension

  • Raised pressure in the portal system, usually due to cirrhosis of the liver (alcohol, hepatitis B and C)
  • The anastomoses enlarge:
    • Oesophageal varices – may bleed massively (haematemesis) – emergency care, blood transfusion, endoscopic banding
    • Haemorrhoids
    • Caput medusae – dilated veins radiating from the umbilicus
  • Splenomegaly and ascites
  • Nursing: watch for vomiting of blood and black stools; measure abdominal girth and weight daily in ascites

Conclusion The hepatic portal system carries nutrient-rich blood from the gut, spleen and pancreas to the liver through the portal vein, formed by the superior mesenteric and splenic veins; obstruction to this flow causes portal hypertension with varices and ascites.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Describe the cardiac cycle with its phases. (2 + 6 + 2)
answer_html:
(a) Definition and duration (2 marks)

  • The cardiac cycle is the sequence of electrical and mechanical events that take place in the heart from the beginning of one heartbeat to the beginning of the next
  • Each cycle includes systole (contraction) and diastole (relaxation) of the atria and ventricles
  • At a heart rate of 75 per minute, one cycle lasts 0.8 second:
    • Atrial systole – 0.1 s; atrial diastole – 0.7 s
    • Ventricular systole – 0.3 s; ventricular diastole – 0.5 s
  • The heart muscle therefore rests more than it works, which is why it never fatigues
  • The two sides of the heart work together; the left side is described here, the right side follows the same pattern at lower pressures

(b) Phases of the cardiac cycle (6 marks)

A. Ventricular systole (0.3 second)

1. Isovolumetric (isometric) contraction – about 0.05 s

  • The ventricles start to contract and the pressure inside them rises above the atrial pressure
  • The AV valves (mitral and tricuspid) close → first heart sound (S1, "lub")
  • The semilunar valves are still closed, because ventricular pressure is lower than aortic pressure
  • So the ventricle contracts as a closed chamber – pressure rises sharply but volume does not change

2. Ejection phase – about 0.25 s

  • When left ventricular pressure exceeds aortic pressure (about 80 mm Hg), the aortic valve opens; the pulmonary valve opens when right ventricular pressure exceeds pulmonary artery pressure (about 10 mm Hg)
  • Rapid ejection – about two-thirds of the stroke volume is pushed out quickly
  • Slow (reduced) ejection – the rest leaves more slowly as the ventricle begins to relax
  • Stroke volume – about 70 ml is ejected from the end-diastolic volume of about 120–130 ml; about 50 ml remains (end-systolic volume)
  • Ejection fraction = stroke volume / end-diastolic volume ≈ 55–70%
  • Peak pressures: left ventricle about 120 mm Hg; right ventricle about 25 mm Hg

B. Ventricular diastole (0.5 second)

3. Protodiastole – about 0.04 s

  • The ventricles start to relax; blood flow out of the ventricles slows and stops

4. Isovolumetric (isometric) relaxation – about 0.08 s

  • Pressure in the aorta and pulmonary artery is now higher than in the ventricles → semilunar valves close → second heart sound (S2, "dub")
  • The AV valves are still closed, so the ventricles relax as closed chambers – pressure falls steeply without any change in volume

5. Rapid filling phase – about 0.11 s

  • When ventricular pressure falls below atrial pressure, the AV valves open
  • Blood that has collected in the atria rushes into the ventricles
  • A third heart sound may be heard (normal in the young)

6. Slow filling (diastasis) – about 0.19 s

  • Blood flows slowly from the veins through the atria into the ventricles

7. Atrial systole – the last 0.1 s of ventricular diastole

  • The atria contract and push in the final 20–30% of ventricular filling (the "atrial kick")
  • The ventricles are now full (end-diastolic volume) and the next cycle begins

C. Summary table

Phase Valves Event Heart sound
Isovolumetric contraction AV close; semilunar closed pressure rises, no ejection S1
Ejection semilunar open blood leaves ventricles –
Isovolumetric relaxation semilunar close; AV closed pressure falls S2
Rapid filling AV open ventricles fill quickly (S3)
Slow filling AV open slow filling –
Atrial systole AV open atrial kick (S4)

D. Relation to the ECG

  • P wave – atrial depolarisation; followed by atrial systole
  • QRS complex – ventricular depolarisation; marks the start of ventricular systole
  • T wave – ventricular repolarisation; near the end of systole

E. Pressure changes (left side)

  • Left ventricle: about 0–10 mm Hg in diastole to 120 mm Hg in systole
  • Aorta: between 80 and 120 mm Hg (it never falls to zero because of the elastic recoil of its wall)
  • Left atrium: low pressure throughout

(c) Applied aspects (2 marks)

  • A fast heart rate shortens diastole much more than systole – the ventricles have less time to fill and the heart muscle gets less coronary blood (coronary flow occurs mainly in diastole); dangerous in heart disease
  • Loss of the atrial kick in atrial fibrillation reduces cardiac output and allows clots to form in the atria (stroke risk)
  • Murmurs are heard when narrowed or leaking valves disturb blood flow during particular phases (e.g. mitral stenosis – during filling)
  • A low ejection fraction (on echocardiography) indicates heart failure
  • Nursing: count the apical pulse for a full minute, note rhythm, and report irregular or very fast or slow rates

Conclusion Each cardiac cycle of 0.8 second consists of isovolumetric contraction, ejection, isovolumetric relaxation, rapid and slow filling and atrial systole; the opening and closing of the valves produce the heart sounds and ensure one-way flow of blood.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Define stroke volume and ejection fraction.
answer_html:
Stroke volume (SV)

  • The volume of blood pumped by each ventricle in one beat
  • Normal: about 70 ml (60–80 ml) at rest
  • SV = end-diastolic volume (about 120–130 ml) – end-systolic volume (about 50–60 ml)

Ejection fraction (EF)

  • The percentage of the end-diastolic volume that is pumped out in each beat
  • EF = (stroke volume ÷ end-diastolic volume) × 100
  • Normal: about 55–70%

Applied: EF is measured by echocardiography; a low EF (below about 40%) indicates a weak heart (heart failure with reduced ejection fraction).

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Define venous return. List the factors that help it.
answer_html:
Definition Venous return is the amount of blood returning to the right atrium per minute through the veins. Normally it equals the cardiac output.

Factors that help venous return

  1. Skeletal muscle pump – contraction of leg muscles squeezes the veins
  2. Valves in veins – prevent backflow
  3. Respiratory pump – the negative pressure in the chest during inspiration draws blood towards the heart
  4. Venoconstriction by sympathetic nerves
  5. Gravity – for veins above the heart
  6. Adequate blood volume
  7. The pressure gradient from the veins to the right atrium

Applied: immobility reduces venous return → DVT; leg exercises, early ambulation, elevation and compression stockings help. Soldiers standing still for long may faint.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: What is a heart murmur?
answer_html:
Definition A heart murmur is an abnormal swishing or blowing sound heard with a stethoscope over the heart, produced by turbulent blood flow.

Causes

  1. Narrowing of a valve (stenosis) – e.g. mitral stenosis, aortic stenosis
  2. Leaking valve (regurgitation) – e.g. mitral regurgitation
  3. Abnormal openings – septal defects, patent ductus arteriosus
  4. High flow states – anaemia, fever, pregnancy, thyrotoxicosis; such "functional (innocent)" murmurs are common in children and do not indicate heart disease

Types: systolic and diastolic, depending on when they occur in the cardiac cycle.

Applied: rheumatic heart disease, still common in India, causes valve murmurs.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Explain the regulation of heart rate.
answer_html:
Introduction The normal heart rate in an adult at rest is about 72 beats per minute (60–100). The SA node sets the basic rhythm, but the rate is constantly adjusted by nerves, reflexes, hormones and other factors to meet the body's needs.

1. Intrinsic rhythm

  • If all nerves to the heart are cut, the SA node beats at about 100 per minute; the lower resting rate shows that the vagus normally slows the heart (vagal tone)

2. Nervous control – the cardiac centre

  • Located in the medulla oblongata: a cardio-inhibitory and a cardio-acceleratory area
  • Parasympathetic (vagus nerve) – releases acetylcholine at the SA and AV nodes → slows the heart
  • Sympathetic (cardiac nerves from T1–T5) – release noradrenaline → increases rate and force of contraction

3. Reflexes

  • Baroreceptor reflex – stretch receptors in the carotid sinus and aortic arch; a rise in BP stimulates them → vagal activity increases → heart rate falls (and vice versa) – the basis of Marey's law (heart rate is inversely related to BP)
  • Bainbridge (atrial) reflex – stretching of the right atrium by increased venous return → heart rate increases
  • Chemoreceptor reflex – low oxygen and high CO₂ affect the rate
  • Respiratory sinus arrhythmia – heart rate rises during inspiration and falls during expiration (normal in young people)

4. Higher centres

  • Emotions (fear, anger, excitement) increase the rate through the hypothalamus; sudden shock may slow it and cause fainting

5. Hormones

  • Adrenaline and noradrenaline, thyroxine (fast pulse in hyperthyroidism)

6. Other factors

  • Temperature – fever increases the rate; hypothermia decreases it
  • Electrolytes – high or low potassium and calcium disturb rhythm
  • Exercise, age (high in infants), sex, sleep (rate falls), pain, drugs (atropine increases; beta blockers and digoxin decrease)

7. Applied importance

  • Tachycardia in fever, shock, anaemia, haemorrhage, anxiety and hyperthyroidism
  • Bradycardia in athletes, raised intracranial pressure, heart block, hypothyroidism and with beta blockers or digoxin
  • Carotid sinus massage and vagal manoeuvres can slow some fast rhythms (done by doctors)
  • Nurses count the apical pulse before giving digoxin and hold the dose if the rate is low

Conclusion Heart rate is set by the SA node and adjusted by the cardiac centre through the vagus (slowing) and sympathetic nerves (speeding), by baroreceptor and other reflexes, hormones, temperature, electrolytes and emotions.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Explain the special features of the coronary and pulmonary circulations.
answer_html:
Introduction Besides the systemic circulation, two special circulations have unique features: the coronary circulation, which supplies the heart muscle, and the pulmonary circulation, which carries blood through the lungs for gas exchange.

A. Coronary circulation

  1. Blood flow – about 250 ml per minute at rest (about 5% of the cardiac output), although the heart is only about 0.5% of body weight
  2. Flow mainly during diastole – during systole the contracting muscle compresses the coronary vessels, especially in the left ventricle; so a fast heart rate (short diastole) reduces coronary flow
  3. High oxygen extraction – the heart removes about 70–75% of the oxygen from coronary blood even at rest; so extra needs can be met only by increasing blood flow
  4. Regulation mainly by local metabolites – adenosine, CO₂, H⁺, K⁺ and low oxygen dilate the coronary vessels
  5. Functional end arteries – sudden blockage causes myocardial infarction
  6. Applied – angina (pain from reduced flow), myocardial infarction; nitrates dilate coronary vessels; tachycardia and anaemia worsen ischaemia

B. Pulmonary circulation

  1. Carries the entire cardiac output through the lungs
  2. Low-pressure system – pulmonary artery pressure about 25/8 mmHg (mean about 15 mmHg), much lower than systemic pressure
  3. Low resistance and high distensibility – vessels are short, wide and thin-walled; extra blood is accommodated easily
  4. Hypoxic vasoconstriction – unlike systemic vessels, pulmonary vessels constrict when oxygen is low, diverting blood to well-ventilated parts of the lung
  5. Blood reservoir – holds about 500 ml of blood
  6. Filter – traps small clots and air bubbles
  7. Gravity effect – more flow to the lower parts of the lungs when upright
  8. Low capillary pressure keeps the alveoli dry
  9. Applied – pulmonary oedema in left heart failure (raised capillary pressure), pulmonary embolism (from leg DVT), pulmonary hypertension (chronic hypoxia, COPD, high altitude)

C. Systemic and pulmonary circulation compared

Point Systemic circulation Pulmonary circulation
Pumped by left ventricle right ventricle
Arterial pressure about 120/80 mmHg about 25/8 mmHg
Resistance high low (about one-tenth)
Vessel walls thick, muscular arteries thin, very distensible
Response to low oxygen vasodilatation vasoconstriction
Blood volume held most of the blood about 500 ml

D. Nursing points

  • Angina – stop activity, rest, give oxygen if needed and the prescribed nitrate under the tongue; report pain lasting more than a few minutes
  • Avoid factors that shorten diastole or raise oxygen demand – tachycardia, fever, anxiety, heavy meals, cold
  • Pulmonary oedema – sit the patient upright with legs down, give oxygen and diuretics as prescribed
  • Early ambulation and leg exercises to prevent pulmonary embolism

Conclusion Coronary flow occurs mainly in diastole, has high oxygen extraction and is controlled by local metabolites, while the pulmonary circulation is a low-pressure, low-resistance system that constricts in hypoxia and carries the whole cardiac output.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Explain the normal electrocardiogram (ECG).
answer_html:
Introduction An electrocardiogram (ECG) is a graphic record of the electrical activity of the heart, picked up by electrodes placed on the skin. It is a simple, painless and very useful investigation.

1. Leads

  • A standard ECG has 12 leads:
    • 3 standard limb leads (I, II, III)
    • 3 augmented limb leads (aVR, aVL, aVF)
    • 6 chest leads (V1–V6)
  • Chest lead positions: V1 – 4th intercostal space at the right sternal border; V2 – 4th space at the left sternal border; V4 – 5th space in the mid-clavicular line; V3 – between V2 and V4; V5 – anterior axillary line and V6 – mid-axillary line at the level of V4

2. ECG paper

  • Runs at 25 mm per second
  • One small square = 0.04 second; one large square (5 small) = 0.2 second
  • Vertically, 10 small squares = 1 mV

3. Waves and intervals

  • P wave – atrial depolarisation; duration less than 0.12 second
  • PR interval – from the start of P to the start of QRS; time for the impulse to pass from the atria through the AV node; normal 0.12–0.20 second
  • QRS complex – ventricular depolarisation; normal 0.06–0.10 second (less than 0.12)
  • ST segment – period when the ventricles are fully depolarised; normally on the baseline
  • T wave – ventricular repolarisation
  • QT interval – total time of ventricular depolarisation and repolarisation; about 0.36–0.44 second (varies with heart rate)
  • Atrial repolarisation is hidden in the QRS complex

4. Calculating heart rate

  • Heart rate = 300 ÷ number of large squares between two R waves (for regular rhythm)

5. Uses

  • Diagnosis of arrhythmias (atrial fibrillation, heart blocks, ventricular tachycardia)
  • Myocardial infarction – ST elevation, Q waves, T inversion
  • Electrolyte disturbances – tall peaked T waves in hyperkalaemia, flat T waves and U waves in hypokalaemia
  • Enlargement of heart chambers; effects of drugs (digoxin)

6. Nursing responsibilities

  • Explain the procedure; ensure privacy; the patient lies relaxed and still
  • Clean the skin; place electrodes correctly; remove metal objects
  • Label the tracing with name, date and time; report abnormal findings promptly
  • On cardiac monitors, recognise dangerous rhythms and act immediately

Conclusion The ECG records the heart's electrical activity as P, QRS and T waves with PR, QRS and QT intervals; it is essential in diagnosing arrhythmias, myocardial infarction and electrolyte disorders.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Explain the properties of cardiac muscle.
answer_html:
Introduction Cardiac muscle is a special type of striated, involuntary muscle found only in the heart. Its properties allow the heart to beat continuously, rhythmically and efficiently throughout life.

1. Automaticity (autorhythmicity)

  • The ability to generate its own impulses without nerve stimulation
  • The SA node has the fastest rate and acts as the pacemaker; the AV node and Purkinje fibres can take over at slower rates
  • A heart removed for transplant continues to beat when supplied with oxygenated fluid

2. Excitability

  • The ability to respond to a stimulus by producing an action potential

3. Conductivity

  • The ability to conduct impulses from cell to cell through intercalated discs (gap junctions), so the whole atria and ventricles contract almost together

4. Contractility

  • The ability to contract in response to a stimulus
  • All-or-none law – because the cells are connected as a functional syncytium, the atria or ventricles contract fully or not at all
  • Starling's law – within limits, the more the muscle fibres are stretched by filling, the stronger the contraction

5. Long refractory period

  • The absolute refractory period lasts almost as long as the contraction (about 0.25–0.3 second)
  • So the heart cannot be tetanised (cannot go into sustained contraction) – it must relax and fill between beats; this protects its pumping action

6. Tonicity

  • Cardiac muscle keeps a slight tone even during rest

7. Applied importance

  • Arrhythmias – disturbances of automaticity and conduction (ectopic beats, fibrillation, heart block)
  • Drugs – digoxin increases contractility; beta blockers reduce rate and contractility; anti-arrhythmics act on excitability
  • Electrolytes – potassium and calcium imbalance disturb excitability and contractility; potassium chloride must never be given as an IV push
  • Pacemakers and defibrillation act through these electrical properties

8. Structural basis of these properties

  • Branched, striated fibres with one central nucleus
  • Intercalated discs containing gap junctions (for spread of impulses) and desmosomes (to hold cells together during contraction)
  • Many mitochondria (about one-quarter to one-third of the cell volume) – cardiac muscle depends on aerobic metabolism and cannot build up an oxygen debt, so it is very sensitive to lack of blood supply
  • Rich capillary network

9. Action potential of ventricular muscle (in brief)

  • Phase 0 – rapid depolarisation (sodium enters)
  • Phase 1 – brief early repolarisation
  • Phase 2 – plateau – slow calcium entry keeps the membrane depolarised for about 0.2 second; this calcium also triggers contraction
  • Phase 3 – repolarisation (potassium leaves)
  • Phase 4 – resting membrane potential (about –90 mV)
  • The plateau is the reason for the long refractory period

Conclusion Cardiac muscle has automaticity, excitability, conductivity, contractility (all-or-none, Starling's law) and a long refractory period that prevents tetanus, enabling the heart to pump rhythmically for life.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Define cardiac output. Explain the factors affecting cardiac output, its regulation and measurement. (2 + 5 + 2 + 1)
answer_html:
(a) Definition (2 marks)

  • Cardiac output (CO) is the volume of blood pumped by each ventricle per minute
  • Cardiac output = stroke volume × heart rate
  • Normal: about 70 ml × 72 beats ≈ 5 litres per minute in a resting adult
  • Cardiac index – cardiac output per square metre of body surface area; about 3.2 litres/min/m² (allows comparison between people of different sizes)
  • Cardiac reserve – the maximum percentage by which CO can increase above resting level (several times in trained athletes)

(b) Factors affecting cardiac output (5 marks) Cardiac output depends on heart rate and stroke volume; stroke volume in turn depends on preload, contractility and afterload.

1. Heart rate

  • Increased by sympathetic stimulation, adrenaline, thyroxine, fever, exercise and emotions; decreased by vagal stimulation
  • A moderate rise in rate increases CO, but very high rates (above about 180) shorten diastole so much that filling and CO fall

2. Preload (venous return and end-diastolic volume)

  • The degree of stretch of the ventricular muscle before contraction, determined by the venous return
  • Frank–Starling law of the heart: "within physiological limits, the force of contraction is directly proportional to the initial length of the muscle fibres" – the more the heart is filled, the more it pumps
  • Venous return is increased by the muscle pump, respiratory pump, venoconstriction, increased blood volume and lying down; decreased by haemorrhage, dehydration and standing still for long

3. Myocardial contractility

  • The strength of contraction at a given fibre length
  • Positive inotropic factors (increase): sympathetic stimulation, adrenaline, calcium, digoxin, dobutamine
  • Negative inotropic factors (decrease): hypoxia, acidosis, myocardial infarction, heart failure, beta blockers, hyperkalaemia

4. Afterload

  • The resistance against which the ventricle pumps – mainly the arterial blood pressure and peripheral resistance
  • High afterload (hypertension, aortic stenosis) reduces stroke volume and makes the heart work harder

5. Physiological variations

  • Exercise – increases CO up to several times
  • Posture – higher when lying down than when standing
  • Emotions and anxiety – increase
  • Pregnancy – increases by about 30–50%
  • After meals, high environmental temperature – increase
  • Sleep – slight decrease
  • Age and sex – slightly lower in women and the elderly

6. Pathological variations

  • Increased – fever, anaemia, hyperthyroidism, arteriovenous fistula
  • Decreased – haemorrhage, shock, myocardial infarction, heart failure, arrhythmias, hypothyroidism, cardiac tamponade

(c) Regulation of cardiac output (2 marks)

  • Intrinsic regulation – the Frank–Starling mechanism matches output to venous return beat by beat
  • Extrinsic regulation – nervous (sympathetic increases rate and force; vagus decreases rate) and hormonal (adrenaline, thyroxine)
  • Reflexes – baroreceptor and Bainbridge reflexes adjust heart rate
  • Peripheral factors – blood volume and vascular resistance, regulated by the kidneys and vasomotor centre

(d) Measurement (1 mark)

  • Fick principle – CO = oxygen consumption per minute ÷ arteriovenous oxygen difference
  • Indicator (dye) dilution and thermodilution methods (using a pulmonary artery catheter in ICUs)
  • Echocardiography and Doppler – non-invasive

Applied importance

  • Low cardiac output (shock, heart failure) shows as low BP, cold clammy skin, fast weak pulse, confusion and reduced urine output – nurses monitor these closely
  • Fluid challenge in hypovolaemia increases preload and CO
  • Vasodilators reduce afterload in heart failure; inotropes increase contractility

Distribution of the resting cardiac output (approximate)

Organ Share of cardiac output
Liver and gut about 25%
Kidneys about 20–25%
Skeletal muscle about 15–20%
Brain about 15%
Skin about 5–10%
Heart (coronary) about 5%

Cardiac output during exercise

  • Sympathetic stimulation raises heart rate (up to about 180–190 per minute) and contractility
  • The muscle pump and respiratory pump increase venous return → greater filling → greater stroke volume (Starling's law)
  • Blood is diverted from the gut and skin to the working muscles
  • CO may rise to about 20–25 litres per minute, and higher in trained athletes
  • Athletes have a larger stroke volume, so their resting heart rate is low (about 50–60)

Starling's law in heart failure

  • When the heart is overstretched beyond its limits, as in heart failure, the force of contraction falls instead of rising; blood backs up into the lungs and veins (congestion, oedema)
  • Diuretics and fluid restriction reduce the excess preload; inotropic drugs such as digoxin improve contractility

Conclusion Cardiac output (stroke volume × heart rate, about 5 litres per minute) depends on heart rate, preload (Frank–Starling law), contractility and afterload, and is regulated by intrinsic, nervous and hormonal mechanisms; it is measured by the Fick principle, dilution methods and echocardiography.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Define erythropoiesis.
answer_html:
Definition Erythropoiesis is the process of formation and development of red blood cells (erythrocytes).

Key points

  1. Site – red bone marrow; in adults mainly in flat bones (sternum, ribs, vertebrae, pelvis, skull) and the ends of long bones; in the foetus – yolk sac, then liver and spleen
  2. Stages – stem cell → proerythroblast → normoblasts (nucleus is lost) → reticulocyte → mature erythrocyte; takes about 7 days
  3. Regulation – the hormone erythropoietin from the kidney, released when tissue oxygen is low (anaemia, high altitude)
  4. Requirements – iron, vitamin B12, folic acid, protein, vitamin C, copper

Applied: kidney failure causes anaemia because erythropoietin falls.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Give the normal values of the main blood constituents.
answer_html:
Introduction Normal blood values help nurses recognise abnormal reports quickly.

Constituent Normal value (adult)
Haemoglobin men 13–17 g/dl; women 12–15 g/dl
RBC count men about 4.5–5.5 million/mm³; women about 4–5 million/mm³
WBC count 4,000–11,000/mm³
Platelet count 1.5–4 lakh/mm³
Blood volume about 5 litres (about 8% of body weight)
Blood pH 7.35–7.45

Note: values are higher in newborns and vary slightly between laboratories.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: What is Rh incompatibility?
answer_html:
Definition Rh incompatibility is a condition in which an Rh-negative mother carries an Rh-positive foetus (father Rh positive), leading to destruction of the baby's red cells by the mother's antibodies.

How it develops

  1. During delivery, abortion or bleeding, foetal Rh-positive red cells enter the mother's blood
  2. The mother forms anti-D antibodies
  3. The first baby is usually not affected
  4. In the next pregnancy, these antibodies cross the placenta and destroy the foetal red cells → haemolytic disease of the newborn: anaemia, severe jaundice, hydrops foetalis

Prevention: inject anti-D immunoglobulin to the Rh-negative mother within 72 hours of delivery or abortion (and antenatally at about 28 weeks).

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Describe the composition and functions of blood.
answer_html:
Introduction Blood is a fluid connective tissue that circulates through the heart and blood vessels. It links every cell of the body with the lungs, gut, kidneys and endocrine glands.

1. Physical properties

  • Volume: about 5 litres in adults (about 8% of body weight)
  • Colour: bright red (arterial) to dark red (venous)
  • pH: slightly alkaline, 7.35–7.45
  • Specific gravity: about 1.055; viscosity: about 4–5 times that of water
  • Temperature: about 38 °C

2. Composition Blood has two parts: plasma (about 55%) and formed elements (about 45%).

A. Plasma – straw-coloured fluid

  • Water – about 91–92%
  • Plasma proteins – about 7 g/dl:
    • Albumin – maintains osmotic pressure; transports drugs and hormones
    • Globulins – antibodies (immunity) and transport proteins
    • Fibrinogen – blood clotting
  • Nutrients – glucose, amino acids, fats, vitamins
  • Electrolytes – sodium, potassium, calcium, chloride, bicarbonate
  • Waste products – urea, uric acid, creatinine
  • Hormones, enzymes and dissolved gases

B. Formed elements (cells)

  • Red blood cells (erythrocytes) – carry oxygen
  • White blood cells (leucocytes) – defence
  • Platelets (thrombocytes) – clotting

3. Functions of blood

  1. Transport
    • Oxygen from the lungs to the tissues; carbon dioxide from the tissues to the lungs
    • Nutrients from the gut to the tissues
    • Waste products to the kidneys
    • Hormones from endocrine glands to their target organs
  2. Protection (defence)
    • WBCs destroy microbes; antibodies give immunity
    • Clotting prevents blood loss
  3. Regulation
    • Body temperature – carries heat from active organs to the skin
    • Acid–base balance – buffers (bicarbonate, plasma proteins, haemoglobin)
    • Water balance – plasma proteins hold water in the vessels
  4. Maintains blood pressure and volume
  5. Reserve of protein for the tissues in starvation

4. Applied / nursing importance

  • Low albumin (malnutrition, liver and kidney disease) → oedema
  • A complete blood count (CBC) reflects many diseases
  • Blood loss reduces oxygen delivery → shock
  • Dehydration increases the concentration of blood (raised haematocrit)

Conclusion Blood consists of plasma and formed elements; it transports, protects and regulates, maintaining the internal environment of the body.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Name the types of white blood cells and give the functions of each.
answer_html:
Introduction White blood cells (leucocytes) are nucleated blood cells that defend the body against infection and foreign substances. They are formed in the bone marrow and lymphoid tissue. The normal total count is 4,000–11,000/mm³.

1. Classification

  • Granulocytes – have granules in the cytoplasm and a lobed nucleus: neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils
  • Agranulocytes – no visible granules: lymphocytes, monocytes

2. Types and functions

A. Neutrophils (polymorphs) – 50–70%

  • Multilobed nucleus (2–5 lobes), fine granules
  • First line of defence – reach infected tissue first
  • Phagocytosis of bacteria; dead neutrophils form pus
  • Increased in acute bacterial infections (pneumonia, appendicitis, abscess)

B. Eosinophils – 1–4%

  • Bilobed nucleus, large red (eosin-staining) granules
  • Fight parasites such as worms
  • Control allergic reactions
  • Increased in allergy, asthma and worm infestation (common in India)

C. Basophils – 0–1%

  • Large blue-staining granules
  • Release histamine (allergic reaction) and heparin (anticoagulant)
  • Increased in some allergic states and blood disorders

D. Lymphocytes – 20–40%

  • Large round nucleus with thin cytoplasm
  • Responsible for specific immunity:
    • B lymphocytes – become plasma cells that make antibodies (humoral immunity)
    • T lymphocytes – kill infected and cancer cells; helper T cells coordinate immunity (cell-mediated immunity)
  • Increased in viral infections, tuberculosis and whooping cough

E. Monocytes – 2–8%

  • The largest WBCs, with a kidney-shaped nucleus
  • Enter tissues and become macrophages
  • Phagocytosis of bacteria and debris; present antigens to lymphocytes
  • Increased in tuberculosis and chronic infections

3. Summary

Type % Main function Increased in
Neutrophils 50–70 phagocytosis, pus bacterial infections
Eosinophils 1–4 parasites, allergy worms, asthma
Basophils 0–1 histamine, heparin allergy
Lymphocytes 20–40 antibodies, cell immunity viral infections, TB
Monocytes 2–8 macrophages TB, chronic infections

Memory aid (most to least common): "Never Let Monkeys Eat Bananas".

4. Applied / nursing importance

  • Leucocytosis (over 11,000/mm³) – infection, inflammation
  • Leucopenia (below 4,000/mm³) – typhoid, dengue, chemotherapy, radiation; such patients need protective isolation, hand hygiene and avoidance of crowds
  • HIV destroys helper T lymphocytes
  • Leukaemia – cancerous increase of abnormal WBCs

Conclusion The five types of WBCs – neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils, lymphocytes and monocytes – each have special defence roles; the differential count helps diagnose infections and blood disorders.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Explain the ABO blood group system and its importance in blood transfusion.
answer_html:
Introduction Blood groups are based on antigens present on the surface of red blood cells. The ABO system was discovered by Karl Landsteiner in 1900. Matching blood groups is essential for safe blood transfusion.

1. ABO system

  • RBCs carry antigens (agglutinogens) A and/or B
  • Plasma contains antibodies (agglutinins) against the antigens that are absent
Blood group Antigen on RBC Antibody in plasma Can receive from
A A anti-B A, O
B B anti-A B, O
AB A and B none all groups – universal recipient
O none anti-A and anti-B O only – universal donor
  • In India, groups O and B are the commonest

2. Rh system

  • Based on the D antigen
  • People with D antigen are Rh positive (the majority); those without it are Rh negative
  • Anti-D antibodies are not naturally present; they form only after exposure to Rh-positive blood (transfusion or pregnancy)

3. Importance in blood transfusion

  • If incompatible blood is given, the recipient's antibodies attack the donor red cells → agglutination (clumping) and haemolysis
  • Haemolytic transfusion reaction: fever, chills, back and chest pain, breathlessness, low BP, red or dark urine (haemoglobinuria), kidney failure, shock
  • Prevented by:
    • Blood grouping (ABO and Rh) of donor and recipient
    • Cross-matching – donor red cells are mixed with recipient serum to check for any reaction

4. Other uses of blood grouping

  • Prevention of Rh disease of the newborn (anti-D for Rh-negative mothers)
  • Organ transplantation
  • Forensic medicine and disputed paternity

5. Nursing responsibilities during transfusion

  • Obtain informed consent; check the doctor's order
  • Two nurses check the patient's identity and the blood bag details (name, number, group, expiry) at the bedside
  • Use the blood within the recommended time after removing it from the refrigerator; do not warm in hot water
  • Record baseline vital signs; start slowly and stay with the patient for the first 15 minutes
  • Monitor vital signs during and after the transfusion
  • If a reaction occurs: stop the transfusion immediately, keep the IV line open with normal saline, inform the doctor, send the blood bag and blood and urine samples to the blood bank, record everything

Conclusion The ABO system depends on A and B antigens and their antibodies; correct grouping and cross-matching, with careful nursing observation, make blood transfusion safe.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Define haemostasis. Describe the intrinsic and extrinsic pathways of blood coagulation. Name any two anticoagulants. (2 + 6 + 2)
answer_html:
(a) Definition and stages of haemostasis (2 marks) Haemostasis is the arrest (stopping) of bleeding from an injured blood vessel. It is the body's emergency response that prevents loss of blood, and it occurs in a series of steps:

  1. Vascular spasm (vasoconstriction)
    • The injured vessel constricts immediately
    • Caused by local muscle response and chemicals (serotonin, thromboxane A₂) released by platelets
    • Reduces blood flow to the injured area
  2. Formation of the platelet plug
    • Adhesion – platelets stick to the exposed collagen of the damaged vessel wall (with the help of von Willebrand factor)
    • Activation – platelets change shape and release ADP and thromboxane A₂
    • Aggregation – more platelets are attracted and clump together to form a temporary plug
    • Enough to seal small injuries (capillaries)
  3. Coagulation (clotting) of blood
    • A network of fibrin threads forms and reinforces the platelet plug, trapping blood cells – a firm clot
  4. Clot retraction
    • Within an hour the clot shrinks, squeezing out serum and pulling the edges of the wound together
  5. Fibrinolysis
    • After healing, the enzyme plasmin dissolves the clot and the vessel is reopened

(b) Coagulation of blood (6 marks)

1. Definition Coagulation is the process by which liquid blood is converted into a semi-solid gel (clot). It takes place through a cascade – a chain of reactions in which inactive clotting factors in plasma are activated one after another, each activating the next, finally converting soluble fibrinogen into insoluble fibrin.

2. Clotting factors

Factor Name
I Fibrinogen
II Prothrombin
III Tissue factor (thromboplastin)
IV Calcium
V Labile factor (proaccelerin)
VII Stable factor (proconvertin)
VIII Antihaemophilic factor A
IX Christmas factor (antihaemophilic factor B)
X Stuart–Prower factor
XI Plasma thromboplastin antecedent
XII Hageman factor
XIII Fibrin-stabilising factor

(There is no factor VI.) Most factors are made in the liver; vitamin K is needed for factors II, VII, IX and X.

3. Extrinsic pathway – fast (takes seconds)

  • Trigger: tissue damage – injured tissues release tissue factor (factor III), which is "extrinsic" (outside) to blood
  • Steps:
    1. Tissue factor combines with factor VII in the presence of calcium
    2. This complex activates factor X
  • Short pathway with few steps, so it produces thrombin quickly
  • Tested by: prothrombin time (PT) / INR – used to monitor warfarin

4. Intrinsic pathway – slower (takes minutes)

  • Trigger: blood coming in contact with damaged vessel wall (exposed collagen) or a foreign surface such as glass; all the factors are present within the blood ("intrinsic")
  • Steps:
    1. Factor XII is activated (XIIa)
    2. XIIa activates factor XI
    3. XIa activates factor IX
    4. IXa, together with factor VIII, calcium and platelet phospholipid, activates factor X
  • Tested by: activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) – used to monitor heparin

5. Common pathway – both pathways meet at factor X

  1. Activated factor X (Xa) combines with factor V, calcium and platelet phospholipid to form prothrombin activator (prothrombinase)
  2. Prothrombin activator converts prothrombin (II) into thrombin
  3. Thrombin converts fibrinogen (I) into fibrin monomers
  4. Fibrin monomers join to form loose fibrin threads
  5. Factor XIII (activated by thrombin) cross-links the threads into a strong, stable fibrin mesh
  6. Blood cells and platelets are trapped in the mesh → clot - Thrombin also has positive feedback – it activates factors V and VIII and platelets, speeding up its own formation

6. Summary

  • Extrinsic: tissue factor + VII → X
  • Intrinsic: XII → XI → IX (+ VIII) → X
  • Common: X (+ V) → prothrombin → thrombin → fibrinogen → fibrin → stable clot (XIII)

7. Normal checks: bleeding time tests platelet function; clotting time, PT and aPTT test the clotting pathways.

(c) Anticoagulants (2 marks) Anticoagulants are substances that prevent or delay clotting of blood.

A. Used in patients (in vivo)

  1. Heparin
    • Acts quickly by activating antithrombin, which inactivates thrombin and factor X
    • Given IV or subcutaneously; monitored by aPTT
    • Antidote: protamine sulphate
  2. Warfarin (oral anticoagulant)
    • A vitamin K antagonist – reduces the formation of factors II, VII, IX and X
    • Takes 2–3 days to act; monitored by PT/INR
    • Antidote: vitamin K
  3. Newer oral anticoagulants – rivaroxaban, apixaban, dabigatran

B. Used in the laboratory (in vitro)

  • EDTA – for blood counts (removes calcium)
  • Sodium citrate – for coagulation tests, ESR and blood bags
  • Oxalate with fluoride – for blood glucose samples

Natural anticoagulants in the body – heparin from mast cells, antithrombin, protein C – keep blood fluid inside normal vessels.

(d) Applied / nursing importance

  • Haemophilia A (lack of factor VIII) and haemophilia B (factor IX) – inherited, X-linked bleeding disorders seen mainly in boys; bleeding into joints and muscles
  • Vitamin K deficiency – every newborn is given vitamin K 1 mg IM at birth to prevent haemorrhagic disease of the newborn; patients with obstructive jaundice get vitamin K before surgery
  • Liver disease reduces clotting factors – bleeding tendency
  • Deep vein thrombosis in immobile patients – early ambulation, leg exercises, compression stockings, prophylactic heparin
  • Patients on anticoagulants – watch for bleeding gums, nosebleeds, blood in urine or stool and bruising; use a soft toothbrush and electric razor; avoid IM injections; check PT/INR or aPTT as ordered
  • Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) – widespread clotting and bleeding in severe sepsis and obstetric emergencies

Conclusion Haemostasis involves vascular spasm, platelet plug, coagulation, clot retraction and fibrinolysis. Coagulation proceeds through the fast extrinsic and slower intrinsic pathways, which meet at factor X to convert prothrombin to thrombin and fibrinogen to fibrin. Heparin and warfarin are the commonly used anticoagulants, and nurses must watch their patients carefully for bleeding.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Define haemoglobin. Give its normal values and functions.
answer_html:
Definition Haemoglobin (Hb) is the iron-containing red pigment of red blood cells that carries oxygen. Each molecule has four globin chains (two alpha and two beta in adult haemoglobin) and four haem groups, each with an atom of iron (Fe²⁺).

Normal values

  • Adult men – about 13–17 g/dl
  • Adult women – about 12–15 g/dl
  • Newborn – about 16–20 g/dl

Functions

  1. Transport of oxygen – each gram of Hb carries about 1.34 ml of oxygen
  2. Transport of carbon dioxide (as carbaminohaemoglobin)
  3. Buffer – helps maintain blood pH
  4. Gives red colour to blood

Applied: low Hb = anaemia; abnormal Hb causes sickle cell disease and thalassaemia.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: What is ESR? Give its normal value and significance.
answer_html:
Definition Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) is the rate at which red blood cells settle at the bottom of a vertical tube of anticoagulated blood in one hour. It is expressed in mm per hour.

Normal values (Westergren method)

  • Men – about 0–15 mm/hour
  • Women – about 0–20 mm/hour

Significance

  1. Raised in tuberculosis, infections, rheumatoid arthritis and other inflammations, anaemia, pregnancy, cancers and multiple myeloma
  2. Lowered in polycythaemia and sickle cell anaemia
  3. It is a non-specific test – it does not diagnose a particular disease but shows that inflammation is present
  4. Useful to monitor the progress of TB and rheumatoid arthritis

subject: Applied Physiology
question: What are plasma proteins? State their functions.
answer_html:
Introduction Plasma proteins are the proteins present in plasma; the total is about 6–8 g/dl.

Types and normal values

  1. Albumin – about 3.5–5 g/dl
  2. Globulins (alpha, beta, gamma) – about 2–3.5 g/dl
  3. Fibrinogen – about 0.2–0.4 g/dl - Albumin, fibrinogen and most globulins are made in the liver; gamma globulins (antibodies) are made by plasma cells

Functions

  1. Oncotic pressure – mainly albumin; holds water in the blood vessels
  2. Transport of hormones, drugs, bilirubin, fatty acids and calcium
  3. Defence – gamma globulins are antibodies
  4. Blood clotting – fibrinogen and prothrombin
  5. Buffering and blood viscosity

Applied: low albumin causes oedema (nephrotic syndrome, cirrhosis, malnutrition).

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Define haemophilia.
answer_html:
Definition Haemophilia is an inherited bleeding disorder caused by the deficiency of a clotting factor, so that blood takes a very long time to clot.

Types

  1. Haemophilia A – deficiency of factor VIII; the commonest type
  2. Haemophilia B (Christmas disease) – deficiency of factor IX

Key features

  • X-linked recessive inheritance – males are affected; females are usually carriers
  • Prolonged clotting time with a normal bleeding time and platelet count
  • Bleeding into joints (haemarthrosis) and muscles, prolonged bleeding after injury, tooth extraction or surgery

Nursing: avoid IM injections; apply firm pressure after venepuncture; soft toothbrush; protect from injury; factor replacement as prescribed.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: What are bleeding time and clotting time? Give their normal values.
answer_html:
Bleeding time (BT)

  • The time taken for bleeding to stop from a small standard skin puncture
  • Normal: about 2–7 minutes (Ivy method); shorter with Duke's method
  • Tests platelet function and the response of small blood vessels
  • Prolonged in thrombocytopenia (e.g. dengue), aspirin use and von Willebrand disease

Clotting time (CT)

  • The time taken for blood to clot after it is removed from the body
  • Normal: about 5–10 minutes (varies with the method used)
  • Tests the clotting factors (coagulation pathway)
  • Prolonged in haemophilia, liver disease, vitamin K deficiency and heparin therapy

Today, platelet count, prothrombin time (INR) and aPTT are more commonly used.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Describe erythropoiesis and the factors affecting it.
answer_html:
Introduction Erythropoiesis is the process of formation of red blood cells (erythrocytes). The body produces about 2–3 million red cells every second to replace those destroyed after their life span of about 120 days.

1. Sites

  • Fetus – yolk sac (early weeks), then liver and spleen, and finally bone marrow in the last months
  • Children – red marrow of almost all bones
  • Adults – red marrow of flat bones (sternum, ribs, vertebrae, pelvis, skull) and the ends of long bones (humerus, femur)

2. Stages

  1. Haemocytoblast – pluripotent stem cell
  2. Proerythroblast
  3. Early (basophilic) normoblast
  4. Intermediate (polychromatic) normoblast – haemoglobin begins to appear
  5. Late (orthochromatic) normoblast – nucleus is pushed out
  6. Reticulocyte – no nucleus; a network of remaining RNA; enters the blood; normal count 0.5–2%
  7. Mature erythrocyte – biconcave, non-nucleated - The whole process takes about 7 days - During maturation the cell becomes smaller, haemoglobin increases and the nucleus disappears

3. Factors affecting erythropoiesis

  • Erythropoietin – hormone produced mainly by the kidneys in response to hypoxia; the main stimulus
  • Hypoxia – high altitude, lung disease and anaemia increase erythropoietin
  • Nutrients:
    • proteins – for globin
    • iron – for haem (deficiency causes microcytic anaemia)
    • vitamin B₁₂ and folic acid – the maturation factors, needed for DNA synthesis (deficiency causes megaloblastic anaemia); vitamin B₁₂ absorption needs intrinsic factor from the stomach
    • vitamin C (iron absorption), vitamin B₆, copper and cobalt
  • Hormones – thyroxine, androgens (one reason men have higher Hb), growth hormone, cortisol
  • Healthy bone marrow

4. Applied importance

  • Anaemia of chronic kidney disease – lack of erythropoietin; treated with erythropoietin injections
  • Polycythaemia at high altitude
  • Bone marrow suppression by cancer chemotherapy, radiation and some drugs
  • Pernicious anaemia – lack of intrinsic factor
  • Reticulocyte count rises after blood loss or effective treatment of anaemia

5. Feedback regulation by erythropoietin

  • Low oxygen delivery to the kidneys (anaemia, haemorrhage, high altitude, lung disease) → more erythropoietin
  • Erythropoietin stimulates the marrow → more red cells → oxygen delivery improves → erythropoietin secretion falls again
  • This negative feedback keeps the red cell count steady

6. Nursing assessment

  • Tests – haemoglobin, RBC count, packed cell volume (haematocrit), reticulocyte count, peripheral smear and red cell indices
  • Look for pallor, tiredness and breathlessness; dietary counselling on iron, protein, folate and vitamin B₁₂ (for strict vegetarians); give iron and folic acid supplements as prescribed

Conclusion Erythropoiesis takes place in the red bone marrow through stages from stem cell to mature red cell over about 7 days; it is stimulated by erythropoietin and needs protein, iron, vitamin B₁₂, folic acid and hormones.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Explain the functions of platelets.
answer_html:
Introduction Platelets (thrombocytes) are small, non-nucleated, disc-shaped fragments of megakaryocytes in the bone marrow. The normal count is about 1.5–4 lakh per cubic millimetre, and they live for about 7–10 days. Their production is stimulated by thrombopoietin.

Structure in brief

  • Contain granules with ADP, serotonin, calcium, clotting factors and growth factors, and contractile proteins

Functions of platelets

1. Vasoconstriction

  • Release serotonin and thromboxane A₂, which constrict the injured vessel and reduce bleeding

2. Formation of the platelet plug (primary haemostasis)

  • Adhesion – platelets stick to exposed collagen at the injured site (with von Willebrand factor)
  • Activation – they change shape and release ADP and thromboxane A₂
  • Aggregation – more platelets are attracted and stick together to form a temporary plug that seals small injuries

3. Role in blood coagulation

  • Provide a phospholipid surface (platelet factor 3) on which clotting factors act to form fibrin

4. Clot retraction

  • Their contractile proteins pull the fibrin threads together, making the clot firm and squeezing out serum

5. Repair of blood vessels

  • Platelet-derived growth factor stimulates repair of the vessel wall

6. Maintenance of the integrity of capillaries

  • They plug tiny gaps in the endothelium daily; in their absence small bleeds (petechiae) appear

Applied importance

  • Thrombocytopenia (low platelets) – in dengue, ITP, leukaemia, chemotherapy; causes petechiae, bruising, gum and nose bleeding; platelet transfusion when very low
  • Aspirin and clopidogrel inhibit platelet aggregation – used to prevent heart attacks and strokes; they increase bleeding risk before surgery
  • Nursing: in low platelets – avoid IM injections and razors, use a soft toothbrush, apply prolonged pressure after venepuncture, watch for bleeding

Platelet disorders and nursing care

  • Thrombocytopenia – count below about 1.5 lakh/mm³; spontaneous bleeding becomes likely when it falls to around 20,000 or less
  • Thrombocytosis – count above about 4.5 lakh/mm³ (after splenectomy, iron deficiency, inflammation); increases the risk of thrombosis
  • Tests – platelet count, bleeding time, peripheral smear
  • Dengue – daily platelet count and haematocrit; watch for warning signs (bleeding, abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, restlessness); platelet transfusion is usually given only for very low counts or active bleeding, as ordered
  • Storage of platelet concentrate – at 20–24 °C (room temperature) with continuous gentle agitation, for up to 5 days; never refrigerate

Conclusion Platelets cause vasoconstriction, form the platelet plug, help coagulation and clot retraction, and repair vessels; their deficiency, as in dengue, causes bleeding.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Define anaemia. Explain its types and causes.
answer_html:
Introduction Anaemia is a reduction in the haemoglobin concentration (or the number of red blood cells) below the normal level for age and sex, which reduces the oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood. It is very common in India, especially among women, children and adolescent girls.

WHO levels for anaemia: Hb below 13 g/dl in men, below 12 g/dl in non-pregnant women, and below 11 g/dl in pregnant women and children aged 6–59 months.

A. Types according to cause

1. Anaemia due to blood loss

  • Acute – haemorrhage from injury, surgery, childbirth
  • Chronic – hookworm infestation, heavy menstrual bleeding, bleeding piles, peptic ulcer

2. Anaemia due to impaired production

  • Nutritional deficiency:
    • iron deficiency – the commonest type; poor diet, increased needs in pregnancy and growth, chronic blood loss
    • vitamin B₁₂ and folic acid deficiency – megaloblastic anaemia; strict vegetarian diets, pregnancy, lack of intrinsic factor
  • Aplastic anaemia – failure of the bone marrow (drugs, radiation, infections)
  • Anaemia of chronic disease and kidney disease (lack of erythropoietin)

3. Haemolytic anaemia (increased destruction)

  • Inherited – sickle cell anaemia (common in some tribal and central Indian populations), thalassaemia, G6PD deficiency, hereditary spherocytosis
  • Acquired – malaria, mismatched blood transfusion, Rh incompatibility, drugs, snake bite

B. Types according to red cell appearance

  • Microcytic hypochromic – small, pale cells: iron deficiency, thalassaemia
  • Macrocytic – large cells: vitamin B₁₂ and folate deficiency
  • Normocytic normochromic – normal-looking cells: acute blood loss, chronic disease, aplastic anaemia

C. Common features

  • Tiredness, weakness, pallor (conjunctiva, nails, tongue), breathlessness on exertion, palpitations, dizziness, headache, poor concentration
  • Koilonychia (spoon nails) and glossitis in iron deficiency

D. Prevention and nursing role

  • Iron-rich diet (green leafy vegetables, jaggery, pulses, meat), vitamin C with meals, avoid tea with meals
  • Iron and folic acid supplementation and deworming under Anaemia Mukt Bharat
