  • Antenatal screening; sickle cell screening in high-risk communities
  • Give oral iron after meals (explain black stools); watch for transfusion reactions

E. Grading of anaemia (WHO, haemoglobin in g/dl)

Group Mild Moderate Severe
Non-pregnant women 11–11.9 8–10.9 below 8
Pregnant women 10–10.9 7–9.9 below 7
Men 11–12.9 8–10.9 below 8
  • Severe anaemia in pregnancy is dangerous – it increases the risk of heart failure, postpartum haemorrhage, low birth weight and maternal death; such women need urgent referral

Conclusion Anaemia is a fall in haemoglobin below normal, caused by blood loss, impaired production (especially iron deficiency) or increased destruction (haemolysis); it is largely preventable through nutrition, supplementation and deworming.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Explain the reticuloendothelial (mononuclear phagocyte) system.
answer_html:
Introduction The reticuloendothelial system (RES), now called the mononuclear phagocyte system, is a widespread system of phagocytic cells – monocytes in the blood and macrophages in the tissues – that defend the body and remove worn-out cells.

1. Components

  • Monocytes in the blood (which become macrophages in tissues)
  • Kupffer cells – liver
  • Alveolar macrophages (dust cells) – lungs
  • Microglia – brain and spinal cord
  • Histiocytes – connective tissue
  • Macrophages of the spleen, lymph nodes and bone marrow
  • Osteoclasts – bone
  • Langerhans cells – skin
  • Mesangial cells – kidney

2. Functions

  • Phagocytosis – engulf and destroy bacteria, viruses, dead cells, dust and debris
  • Destruction of old red blood cells (mainly in the spleen) → formation of bilirubin; iron is saved and reused
  • Immunity – antigen presentation to lymphocytes, starting specific immune responses
  • Storage of iron (ferritin, haemosiderin)
  • Secretion of cytokines (interleukin-1, tumour necrosis factor) that cause fever and inflammation
  • Removal of cholesterol and other substances
  • Wound healing – clean the wound and stimulate repair

3. Applied importance

  • Hepatosplenomegaly (enlarged liver and spleen) in malaria, kala-azar, typhoid and infectious mononucleosis – due to RES hyperactivity
  • Splenectomy – increased risk of serious infections; vaccination against pneumococcus and other organisms is needed
  • Tuberculosis – the bacilli survive inside macrophages
  • Silicosis and anthracosis – dust-laden macrophages in the lungs of miners
  • Haemolytic anaemias – increased red cell destruction by the RES

4. Origin of the cells

  • All are derived from monocytes formed in the bone marrow
  • Monocytes circulate for about 1–3 days, then enter the tissues and enlarge into macrophages, which may live for months
  • Some macrophages stay fixed in organs (Kupffer cells, microglia); others wander through tissues

5. Steps of phagocytosis

  1. Chemotaxis – the cell moves towards chemicals released by microbes and damaged tissue
  2. Recognition and attachment – helped by opsonins (antibodies and complement coating the microbe)
  3. Engulfment – the cell surrounds the particle to form a phagosome
  4. Killing and digestion – the phagosome fuses with a lysosome; enzymes and oxygen radicals destroy the microbe
  5. Removal of the undigested remains

6. Nursing points

  • After splenectomy, vaccines (pneumococcal, Hib, meningococcal) are given as advised, and any fever is reported and treated promptly

Conclusion The reticuloendothelial system consists of monocytes and tissue macrophages throughout the body; it removes microbes and old red cells, forms bilirubin, stores iron and starts immune responses.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Define immunity. Describe innate and acquired immunity, with the types of acquired immunity. (2 + 3 + 3 + 2)
answer_html:
(a) Definition (2 marks)

  • Immunity is the ability of the body to resist and fight infections and other foreign substances (antigens), and to recognise and remove abnormal cells
  • An antigen is any substance that the body recognises as foreign and that stimulates an immune response
  • An antibody (immunoglobulin) is a protein produced by plasma cells that combines specifically with an antigen

(b) Innate (natural, non-specific) immunity (3 marks) Present from birth; acts immediately; the same response to all microbes; no memory.

1. First line – physical and chemical barriers

  • Intact skin; mucous membranes with mucus and cilia
  • Secretions – lysozyme in tears and saliva, hydrochloric acid in the stomach, acidic vaginal secretions, sebum
  • Reflexes – coughing, sneezing, vomiting; flushing by urine and tears
  • Normal flora – compete with harmful microbes

2. Second line – internal defences

  • Phagocytes – neutrophils and macrophages engulf microbes
  • Natural killer (NK) cells – destroy virus-infected and cancer cells
  • Inflammation – redness, heat, swelling, pain; brings defence cells to the site
  • Fever – inhibits microbial growth
  • Complement system and interferons (protect neighbouring cells from viruses)

(c) Acquired (adaptive, specific) immunity (3 marks) Develops after exposure to an antigen; specific to that antigen; has memory, so a second exposure gives a faster, stronger response.

1. Humoral (antibody-mediated) immunity – B lymphocytes

  • B cells mature in the bone marrow; on meeting an antigen they become plasma cells that produce antibodies, and memory B cells
  • Classes of antibodies:
    • IgG – the most abundant; the only one that crosses the placenta; long-term protection
    • IgM – the first antibody produced in an infection; the largest
    • IgA – in secretions – breast milk (colostrum), saliva, tears, gut mucus
    • IgE – allergy and worm infections
    • IgD – on B-cell surfaces
  • Antibodies neutralise toxins, coat microbes for phagocytosis, activate complement and clump bacteria
  • Protects mainly against bacteria, toxins and extracellular viruses

2. Cell-mediated immunity – T lymphocytes

  • T cells mature in the thymus
  • Helper T cells (CD4) – coordinate the immune response; destroyed in HIV infection
  • Cytotoxic T cells (CD8) – kill virus-infected and cancer cells
  • Regulatory T cells – control the response; memory T cells
  • Protects against viruses, intracellular bacteria (TB), fungi and cancer cells; responsible for graft rejection

Primary and secondary response

  • First exposure – slow, weak response (mainly IgM)
  • Second exposure – rapid, strong, long-lasting response (mainly IgG) – the basis of booster doses

(d) Types of acquired immunity (2 marks)

Type How acquired Example Duration
Active natural after an infection recovery from measles or chickenpox long-lasting, often lifelong
Active artificial vaccination BCG, measles, polio, hepatitis B, tetanus toxoid long-lasting; boosters may be needed
Passive natural antibodies from the mother IgG across the placenta, IgA in breast milk a few months
Passive artificial ready-made antibodies injected anti-rabies immunoglobulin, anti-tetanus immunoglobulin, anti-snake venom immediate but short (weeks)
  • Active immunity develops slowly but lasts long and has memory; passive immunity acts immediately but is short-lived, with no memory

Applied importance

  • Immunisation programme (Universal Immunisation Programme) – vaccines given on schedule protect children; tetanus toxoid in pregnancy protects the newborn
  • Breastfeeding and colostrum give passive protection to infants
  • Immunodeficiency – HIV/AIDS, cancer chemotherapy, steroids → opportunistic infections
  • Hypersensitivity (allergy, anaphylaxis) and autoimmune diseases (type 1 diabetes, rheumatoid arthritis)
  • Cold chain maintenance keeps vaccines effective

Organs of the immune system

  • Primary lymphoid organs – bone marrow (B cells mature) and thymus (T cells mature)
  • Secondary lymphoid organs – lymph nodes, spleen, tonsils and mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue such as Peyer's patches, where lymphocytes meet antigens

Innate and acquired immunity compared

Point Innate immunity Acquired immunity
Present from birth develops after exposure or vaccination
Specificity non-specific specific to one antigen
Memory none present
Speed immediate (minutes to hours) slower at first (days)
Components barriers, phagocytes, NK cells, complement, fever B and T lymphocytes, antibodies

Factors that lower immunity

  • Extremes of age (newborns, elderly), malnutrition, stress and lack of sleep
  • Chronic diseases – diabetes, kidney and liver disease, cancer
  • Drugs – steroids, anticancer drugs, transplant drugs
  • HIV infection, splenectomy

Conclusion Immunity is the body's ability to resist infection. Innate immunity – barriers, phagocytes, NK cells, inflammation, fever and complement – acts immediately and non-specifically, while acquired immunity – humoral (B cells, antibodies) and cell-mediated (T cells) – is specific with memory, and may be active or passive, natural or artificial.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Define gigantism.
answer_html:
Definition Gigantism is a condition of excessive growth in height caused by too much growth hormone (GH) before the epiphyses of long bones have fused, i.e. in childhood or adolescence.

Key points

  1. Cause – usually a tumour (adenoma) of the anterior pituitary producing excess GH
  2. Features – very tall stature (often above 2 metres), long limbs, large hands and feet, muscle weakness, raised blood sugar
  3. Acromegaly – if GH excess begins after the epiphyses have fused (in adults), bones cannot grow longer; instead the hands, feet, jaw, nose and soft tissues enlarge and the face becomes coarse
  4. Treatment – surgery or drugs to reduce GH

subject: Applied Physiology
question: List the functions of insulin.
answer_html:
Introduction Insulin is a hormone secreted by the β (beta) cells of the islets of Langerhans in the pancreas. It is the only hormone that lowers blood glucose.

Functions

  1. Increases glucose uptake into muscle and fat cells
  2. Increases glycogen formation (glycogenesis) in liver and muscle
  3. Reduces glucose production – inhibits glycogen breakdown and gluconeogenesis
  4. Promotes fat storage and prevents fat breakdown and ketone formation
  5. Increases protein synthesis – an anabolic (building) hormone
  6. Moves potassium into cells – insulin with glucose is used to treat high potassium

subject: Applied Physiology
question: State the functions of oxytocin.
answer_html:
Introduction Oxytocin is made in the hypothalamus and released from the posterior pituitary.

Functions

  1. Contraction of the uterus during labour – a positive-feedback loop that strengthens contractions until delivery (Ferguson reflex)
  2. Milk ejection (let-down reflex) – when the baby sucks, oxytocin contracts the cells around the breast alveoli and milk flows
  3. Contraction of the uterus after delivery – helps involution and reduces bleeding
  4. Promotes mother–baby bonding

Applied: synthetic oxytocin is used to induce or augment labour and to prevent postpartum haemorrhage (active management of the third stage of labour); early breastfeeding also releases oxytocin and helps the uterus contract.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Explain the functions of thyroid hormones.
answer_html:
Introduction The thyroid gland secretes thyroxine (T4) and triiodothyronine (T3). They are made from the amino acid tyrosine and iodine. T3 is the more active form; most T4 is converted to T3 in the tissues. Thyroid hormones act on almost every cell of the body.

1. Regulation of secretion

  • Hypothalamus → TRH → anterior pituitary → TSH → thyroid → T3, T4
  • High T3/T4 levels suppress TRH and TSH (negative feedback)
  • An adult needs about 150 micrograms of iodine a day

2. Functions

  1. Metabolism
    • Increase the basal metabolic rate (BMR) and oxygen consumption of most tissues
    • Increase heat production (calorigenic effect)
  2. Carbohydrate metabolism – increase absorption of glucose from the gut and its use by cells; increase glycogen breakdown
  3. Fat metabolism – increase fat breakdown; lower blood cholesterol
  4. Protein metabolism – needed for normal protein synthesis; in excess they cause protein breakdown and muscle wasting
  5. Growth and development
    • Work with growth hormone for normal growth of the body and bones
    • Essential for development of the brain in the foetus and early infancy
  6. Cardiovascular system – increase heart rate, force of contraction and cardiac output
  7. Nervous system – maintain alertness, quick thinking and reflexes
  8. Gastrointestinal tract – increase appetite and gut motility
  9. Reproduction – needed for normal menstrual cycles and fertility
  10. Increase the effects of adrenaline (more receptors)

3. Disorders

Hypothyroidism Hyperthyroidism
low BMR, weight gain high BMR, weight loss in spite of good appetite
cold intolerance heat intolerance, sweating
slow pulse, constipation fast pulse, palpitations, diarrhoea
dry skin, hair loss, puffy face warm moist skin, tremor
lethargy, slow thinking, depression anxiety, irritability, insomnia
cretinism in infants (mental and physical retardation) exophthalmos in Graves' disease

4. Applied / nursing importance

  • Newborn screening (heel-prick TSH) detects congenital hypothyroidism early, so cretinism can be prevented
  • Iodised salt prevents iodine-deficiency goitre and cretinism
  • Thyroid hormone tablets are taken on an empty stomach every morning; patients on antithyroid drugs are watched for sore throat (low WBC)

Conclusion Thyroid hormones control the body's metabolic rate, growth and brain development and influence almost every organ; both their deficiency and excess produce well-defined disorders.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Explain the regulation of blood calcium level.
answer_html:
Introduction Calcium is essential for bones and teeth, nerve and muscle excitability, heart contraction, blood clotting and the action of many enzymes and hormones. About 99% of body calcium is stored in bones and teeth. The normal serum calcium is about 9–11 mg/dl, and this narrow range is maintained by three hormones.

1. Parathormone (PTH) – from the parathyroid glands; raises blood calcium

  • Bone – stimulates osteoclasts to release calcium and phosphate from bone
  • Kidney – increases reabsorption of calcium and increases loss of phosphate in urine
  • Intestine (indirectly) – stimulates the kidney to form active vitamin D (calcitriol), which increases calcium absorption from food
  • Stimulus: fall in blood calcium

2. Calcitonin – from the parafollicular (C) cells of the thyroid; lowers blood calcium

  • Bone – inhibits osteoclasts, so less calcium is released
  • Kidney – increases excretion of calcium
  • Stimulus: rise in blood calcium
  • Its role in adults is relatively small; more important in children and pregnancy

3. Vitamin D (calcitriol – active form)

  • Formation: made in the skin by sunlight (or taken in food), converted in the liver and activated in the kidney (with the help of PTH)
  • Actions:
    • Increases absorption of calcium and phosphate from the intestine – its main action
    • Helps mineralisation of bone
    • Increases calcium reabsorption in the kidney

4. Feedback control

  • Low calcium → more PTH → calcium rises
  • High calcium → less PTH and more calcitonin → calcium falls

5. Summary

Hormone Source Effect on blood calcium Main sites of action
Parathormone parathyroids raises bone, kidney, (gut via vitamin D)
Calcitonin thyroid C cells lowers bone, kidney
Calcitriol skin → liver → kidney raises intestine, bone, kidney

6. Applied / nursing importance

  • Hypocalcaemia – after thyroid or parathyroid surgery, vitamin D deficiency, chronic kidney disease
    • Signs: tingling around the lips and fingers, muscle cramps, carpopedal spasm, Chvostek's sign (tapping the facial nerve twitches the face), Trousseau's sign (BP cuff inflation causes hand spasm), laryngospasm, convulsions → tetany
    • Treatment: IV calcium gluconate 10%, given slowly with cardiac monitoring
  • Hypercalcaemia – overactive parathyroid, cancer; causes kidney stones, bone pain, constipation and confusion ("stones, bones, groans and moans")
  • Rickets (children) and osteomalacia (adults) – vitamin D deficiency; prevented by sunlight and diet
  • Osteoporosis – calcium and vitamin D supplements, exercise
  • Monitor serum calcium in kidney disease

Conclusion Blood calcium is kept constant by parathormone and vitamin D, which raise it, and calcitonin, which lowers it, acting on bone, kidney and intestine.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Describe the hormones of the anterior pituitary and their functions.
answer_html:
Introduction The anterior pituitary (adenohypophysis) secretes six major hormones that control growth, metabolism, the stress response, reproduction and lactation. Most of them stimulate other endocrine glands, so they are called tropic hormones. The anterior pituitary itself is controlled by the hypothalamus.

1. Growth hormone (GH, somatotropin)

  • Stimulates growth of bones and tissues, mainly through IGF-1 (somatomedin) made in the liver
  • Increases protein synthesis
  • Increases fat breakdown for energy
  • Raises blood glucose (anti-insulin effect)
  • Disorders: gigantism (children) and acromegaly (adults) from excess; dwarfism from deficiency in childhood

2. Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH)

  • Stimulates the growth of the thyroid gland and the secretion of T3 and T4
  • Disorders: hypo- or hyperthyroidism

3. Adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH)

  • Stimulates the adrenal cortex to secrete cortisol
  • Released in stress; shows a daily rhythm (highest in the early morning)
  • Disorder: Cushing's disease (excess)

4. Follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) – a gonadotropin

  • Women: growth of ovarian follicles and secretion of oestrogen
  • Men: spermatogenesis (acts on Sertoli cells)

5. Luteinising hormone (LH) – a gonadotropin

  • Women: causes ovulation (LH surge) and formation of the corpus luteum, which secretes progesterone
  • Men: stimulates the Leydig cells to secrete testosterone

6. Prolactin

  • Stimulates milk production by the breasts after delivery
  • Suppresses ovulation during breastfeeding
  • Excess (pituitary tumour, some drugs) causes milk discharge, absence of periods and infertility

(The small intermediate part secretes MSH, which affects skin pigmentation.)

7. Control by the hypothalamus

  • Releasing hormones – GHRH, TRH, CRH, GnRH
  • Inhibiting hormones – somatostatin (inhibits GH) and dopamine (inhibits prolactin)
  • They reach the anterior pituitary through the hypophyseal portal vessels
  • Hormones of the target glands give negative feedback to the hypothalamus and pituitary

8. Summary

Hormone Target Main action
GH bones, tissues, liver growth, protein synthesis
TSH thyroid T3, T4 secretion
ACTH adrenal cortex cortisol secretion
FSH ovary / testis follicle growth / sperm
LH ovary / testis ovulation, progesterone / testosterone
Prolactin breast milk production

9. Applied / nursing importance

  • Sheehan's syndrome – necrosis of the pituitary after severe postpartum haemorrhage; failure of lactation is the first sign, followed by lack of periods and other hormones
  • Pituitary tumours – headache, visual field loss, hormone excess
  • Hormone replacement in pituitary failure must be continued lifelong

Conclusion The anterior pituitary secretes GH, TSH, ACTH, FSH, LH and prolactin under hypothalamic control; through these hormones it regulates growth, metabolism, stress responses, reproduction and lactation.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Explain the regulation of blood glucose level. Add a note on its disorders. (2 + 3 + 3 + 2)

diagram.caption: Regulation of blood glucose
labels: glucose into cells and glycogen formed

answer_html:
Introduction Glucose is the main fuel of the body. The brain depends almost entirely on glucose and cannot store it, so even a short fall in blood glucose can cause confusion, fits and coma, while a long-standing rise damages blood vessels, nerves, kidneys and eyes. The body therefore keeps blood glucose within a narrow range through the balance of several hormones.

(a) Normal values, sources and uses (2 marks) 1. Normal values

  • Fasting blood glucose: about 70–100 mg/dl
  • 2 hours after a meal: below 140 mg/dl
  • Renal threshold: about 180 mg/dl – above this level glucose appears in urine

2. Sources of blood glucose

  • Diet – digestion of carbohydrates
  • Glycogenolysis – breakdown of glycogen stored in the liver
  • Gluconeogenesis – formation of new glucose in the liver (and kidney) from amino acids, lactate and glycerol

3. Uses of glucose

  • Oxidation to release energy in all cells
  • Storage as glycogen in liver and muscle (glycogenesis)
  • Conversion to fat (lipogenesis) when in excess

(b) Hormones that lower blood glucose – insulin (3 marks) Insulin is secreted by the β cells of the islets of Langerhans. It is the only hormone that lowers blood glucose.

1. Actions

  • Increases glucose uptake into skeletal muscle and fat cells (by bringing GLUT4 carriers to the cell membrane)
  • Increases glycogenesis in liver and muscle
  • Inhibits glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis in the liver
  • Promotes fat storage and prevents fat breakdown and ketone body formation
  • Increases protein synthesis and prevents protein breakdown
  • Moves potassium into cells

2. Regulation of insulin secretion

  • Increased by: rise in blood glucose (the main stimulus), amino acids, gut hormones released after a meal (incretins such as GLP-1 and GIP), vagal stimulation
  • Decreased by: low blood glucose, fasting, adrenaline (sympathetic stimulation in stress), somatostatin

(c) Hormones that raise blood glucose (3 marks) These are called counter-regulatory or "anti-insulin" hormones. They prevent hypoglycaemia.

1. Glucagon – from the α cells of the islets

  • Stimulates glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis in the liver
  • Promotes fat breakdown and ketone formation
  • Released when blood glucose falls, during fasting and exercise

2. Adrenaline – from the adrenal medulla

  • Rapid glycogenolysis in liver and muscle
  • Released in stress, fear and hypoglycaemia (causes the sweating and palpitations of hypoglycaemia)

3. Cortisol (glucocorticoid) – from the adrenal cortex

  • Increases gluconeogenesis from proteins
  • Reduces glucose uptake by tissues
  • Long-term steroid therapy can cause steroid-induced diabetes

4. Growth hormone – reduces glucose uptake by tissues; raises blood sugar

5. Thyroxine – increases glucose absorption from the gut and glycogen breakdown

6. How these hormones work together

  • After a meal: blood glucose rises → insulin rises, glucagon falls → glucose enters cells and is stored as glycogen and fat → glucose returns to normal within about 2 hours
  • During fasting (overnight): glucose falls → insulin falls, glucagon rises → liver glycogen is broken down (lasts about 12–24 hours) → then gluconeogenesis supplies glucose
  • In prolonged starvation: fat is broken down and ketone bodies are formed; the brain gradually uses ketones for part of its energy
  • In exercise and stress: adrenaline and glucagon raise glucose for the working muscles

Summary

Lowers blood glucose Raises blood glucose
insulin glucagon, adrenaline, cortisol, growth hormone, thyroxine

(d) Disorders (2 marks)

1. Diabetes mellitus – a chronic state of high blood glucose due to lack of insulin, resistance to its action, or both

  • Type 1 – destruction of β cells (autoimmune); usually children and young adults; total insulin deficiency; prone to diabetic ketoacidosis; needs insulin for life
  • Type 2 – insulin resistance with relative deficiency; adults, often obese and inactive; the commonest type and very common in India; treated with diet, exercise, oral drugs and sometimes insulin
  • Gestational diabetes – first appears in pregnancy; screened in all pregnant women
  • Features: polyuria, polydipsia, polyphagia, weight loss, tiredness, blurred vision, frequent infections, slow wound healing
  • Diagnosis: fasting glucose ≥126 mg/dl, 2-hour glucose ≥200 mg/dl, HbA1c ≥6.5%, or random glucose ≥200 mg/dl with symptoms
  • Complications: ketoacidosis, heart attack, stroke, kidney failure, retinopathy, neuropathy, diabetic foot

2. Hypoglycaemia – blood glucose below 70 mg/dl

  • Causes: excess insulin or oral drugs, missed meals, heavy exercise, alcohol
  • Features: sweating, tremor, palpitations, hunger, anxiety, confusion, abnormal behaviour, fits, coma
  • Treatment:
    • Conscious patient – 15–20 g of quick-acting sugar (glucose powder, sugar in water, fruit juice); recheck after 15 minutes
    • Unconscious patient – IV dextrose (25–50%) or IM glucagon; never put food or fluid in the mouth

3. Nursing points

  • Monitor capillary blood glucose as ordered and record
  • Correct insulin injection technique, with rotation of sites (abdomen, thigh, arm)
  • Teach diet, exercise, foot care and recognition of both high and low sugar
  • Patients on insulin should carry sugar and an identity card

Conclusion Blood glucose is kept between about 70 and 140 mg/dl by insulin, which lowers it, and glucagon, adrenaline, cortisol, growth hormone and thyroxine, which raise it. Failure of this balance causes diabetes mellitus or hypoglycaemia – conditions that nurses meet daily in every ward.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: State the functions of antidiuretic hormone (ADH).
answer_html:
Introduction Antidiuretic hormone (ADH, vasopressin) is made in the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei of the hypothalamus and released from the posterior pituitary.

Stimuli for release

  • Rise in plasma osmolality (dehydration), fall in blood volume or BP, pain, stress, nausea; inhibited by alcohol and cold

Functions

  1. Increases water reabsorption in the collecting ducts and distal tubules of the kidney (by inserting water channels – aquaporins)
  2. Produces a small volume of concentrated urine
  3. Maintains plasma osmolality and blood volume
  4. In large doses causes vasoconstriction and raises BP (hence "vasopressin")

Applied: deficiency causes diabetes insipidus; excess causes SIADH with water retention and low sodium.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: What is tetany? State its causes.
answer_html:
Definition Tetany is a condition of increased excitability of nerves and muscles causing painful muscle spasms, due to a low level of ionised calcium in the blood.

Causes

  1. Hypoparathyroidism – especially after accidental removal of the parathyroids during thyroid surgery
  2. Vitamin D deficiency (rickets, osteomalacia)
  3. Alkalosis – hyperventilation, prolonged vomiting (calcium becomes less ionised)
  4. Chronic kidney disease, low magnesium

Signs

  • Tingling around the mouth and in the fingers, carpopedal spasm, laryngeal spasm
  • Trousseau's sign (spasm of the hand when a BP cuff is inflated) and Chvostek's sign (twitching of the face on tapping the facial nerve)

Treatment: IV calcium gluconate as prescribed.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Differentiate between cretinism and myxoedema.
answer_html:
Introduction Both are due to deficiency of thyroid hormones (hypothyroidism), but at different ages.

Point Cretinism Myxoedema
Age congenital or childhood hypothyroidism adult hypothyroidism
Main effects stunted growth, intellectual disability, delayed milestones slowing of body functions; mental slowness, not permanent disability
Features large protruding tongue, coarse face, umbilical hernia, dry skin, constipation, delayed teething weight gain, cold intolerance, dry skin, hair loss, puffy face, hoarse voice, slow pulse, non-pitting oedema
Prevention / treatment newborn screening (TSH), iodised salt, early thyroxine – damage may be permanent if late thyroxine replacement – features reverse

subject: Applied Physiology
question: What is Cushing's syndrome?
answer_html:
Definition Cushing's syndrome is a condition caused by prolonged excess of cortisol (glucocorticoids) in the body.

Causes

  1. Long-term steroid therapy – the commonest cause
  2. Pituitary tumour producing excess ACTH (Cushing's disease)
  3. Adrenal tumour producing cortisol

Features

  • Moon face, buffalo hump, central (trunk) obesity with thin limbs
  • Purple stretch marks (striae), thin skin, easy bruising
  • High blood pressure, high blood sugar, osteoporosis, muscle weakness
  • Poor wound healing, frequent infections, mood changes

Nursing: never stop long-term steroids suddenly (risk of adrenal crisis); monitor BP, blood sugar and weight.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: What is diabetes insipidus?
answer_html:
Definition Diabetes insipidus (DI) is a condition in which the body passes large volumes of very dilute urine because of lack of ADH or the kidneys' failure to respond to ADH.

Types

  1. Central (cranial) DI – deficient ADH from the hypothalamus or posterior pituitary: head injury, pituitary surgery, tumours
  2. Nephrogenic DI – kidneys do not respond to ADH (drugs such as lithium, kidney disease)

Features

  • Polyuria (more than 3 litres of urine a day), low specific gravity (below about 1.005), excessive thirst (polydipsia), dehydration
  • Blood sugar is normal (unlike diabetes mellitus)

Treatment and nursing: desmopressin for central DI; accurate intake–output chart, daily weight and urine specific gravity.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Explain the functions of the hormones of the adrenal cortex.
answer_html:
Introduction The adrenal cortex produces steroid hormones from cholesterol, collectively called corticosteroids. They are essential for life. They are secreted by three zones: zona glomerulosa (mineralocorticoids), zona fasciculata (glucocorticoids) and zona reticularis (sex hormones).

A. Mineralocorticoids – aldosterone

  • Increases sodium reabsorption and potassium (and H⁺) excretion in the distal tubules and collecting ducts of the kidney
  • Water follows sodium → increases blood volume and BP
  • Regulated mainly by the renin–angiotensin system and the plasma potassium level (ACTH has a minor role)

B. Glucocorticoids – cortisol

  1. Carbohydrate metabolism – increases gluconeogenesis, raises blood glucose (anti-insulin effect)
  2. Protein metabolism – breaks down proteins in muscle, skin and bone (catabolic)
  3. Fat metabolism – mobilises fat; in excess, redistributes fat to the face and trunk
  4. Anti-inflammatory and immunosuppressive – reduces inflammation, allergy and immune responses (used as drugs)
  5. Resistance to stress – essential for coping with injury, surgery, infection and emotional stress
  6. Permissive action – helps adrenaline and noradrenaline maintain BP
  7. Other effects – reduces bone formation, affects mood, increases gastric acid - Secreted in a daily rhythm – highest in the early morning - Regulated by ACTH from the anterior pituitary (CRH → ACTH → cortisol) with negative feedback

C. Sex hormones – adrenal androgens

  • Mainly dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA); responsible for pubic and axillary hair and libido in females; small effect in males

D. Disorders

  • Addison's disease (deficiency) – weakness, weight loss, low BP, low blood sugar, low sodium and high potassium, darkening of skin; adrenal crisis is life-threatening
  • Cushing's syndrome (excess cortisol) – moon face, obesity, hypertension, diabetes
  • Conn's syndrome (excess aldosterone) – hypertension with low potassium
  • Congenital adrenal hyperplasia – excess androgens; ambiguous genitalia in girls

E. Nursing importance

  • Patients on long-term steroids need gradual tapering, monitoring of blood sugar, BP, weight and infection, and protection of the stomach and bones
  • Extra steroid doses may be needed during surgery or severe illness

F. Regulation in brief

  • Cortisol – HPA axis: stress → hypothalamus (CRH) → anterior pituitary (ACTH) → adrenal cortex (cortisol); high cortisol inhibits CRH and ACTH (negative feedback)
  • Aldosterone – renin–angiotensin system: low BP or low sodium → kidneys release renin → angiotensinogen → angiotensin I → (ACE, mainly in the lungs) → angiotensin II → vasoconstriction and aldosterone secretion → sodium and water retained → BP rises
  • High plasma potassium directly stimulates aldosterone

Conclusion The adrenal cortex secretes aldosterone (sodium and water retention, BP), cortisol (glucose, stress, anti-inflammation) and androgens; their deficiency causes Addison's disease and excess causes Cushing's or Conn's syndrome.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Explain the functions of the hormones of the adrenal medulla.
answer_html:
Introduction The adrenal medulla is the inner part of the adrenal gland. It is a modified sympathetic ganglion made of chromaffin cells. When stimulated by sympathetic nerves (with acetylcholine) during stress, it releases catecholamines – about 80% adrenaline (epinephrine) and 20% noradrenaline (norepinephrine) – into the blood. Their actions resemble and prolong those of the sympathetic system – the "fight or flight" response.

Functions

1. Heart

  • Increase heart rate, force of contraction and cardiac output (beta-1 receptors)

2. Blood vessels and BP

  • Noradrenaline causes widespread vasoconstriction → raises both systolic and diastolic BP
  • Adrenaline constricts vessels of the skin and gut but dilates vessels of skeletal muscle (beta-2) → blood goes to muscles

3. Lungs

  • Bronchodilation (adrenaline, beta-2) – more air to the lungs

4. Metabolism

  • Raises blood glucose – glycogen breakdown in the liver and muscle
  • Lipolysis – releases fatty acids for energy
  • Increases metabolic rate and oxygen consumption

5. Eyes

  • Dilatation of pupils

6. Gastrointestinal tract and bladder

  • Reduces gut movements and secretion; contracts sphincters; relaxes the bladder wall

7. Skin

  • Sweating, goose flesh, pallor

8. Nervous system

  • Increased alertness and quicker reactions

Regulation: stress, exercise, fear, cold, low blood sugar and haemorrhage stimulate secretion through the hypothalamus and sympathetic nerves.

Applied importance

  • Phaeochromocytoma – tumour of the medulla; attacks of very high BP, headache, palpitations and sweating
  • Adrenaline is the drug of choice in anaphylaxis and is used in cardiac arrest
  • Noradrenaline infusion is used in septic shock to raise BP (given through a central line; watch the infusion site)
  • Stress response – explains the fast pulse, pallor, sweating and high blood sugar seen in injured and anxious patients

Receptors through which they act

  • Alpha-1 – vasoconstriction, dilatation of pupil
  • Beta-1 – increased heart rate and force
  • Beta-2 – bronchodilation, vasodilatation in muscle, glycogen breakdown

Adrenaline and noradrenaline compared

Point Adrenaline Noradrenaline
Heart rate increased may fall reflexly (due to high BP)
Systolic BP raised raised
Diastolic BP little change or falls raised
Peripheral resistance decreased (muscle vessels dilate) increased
Blood glucose markedly raised slightly raised
Bronchi dilated little effect
Main clinical use anaphylaxis, cardiac arrest septic shock

Conclusion The adrenal medulla releases adrenaline and noradrenaline, which raise heart rate, BP, blood glucose and alertness, dilate the bronchi and pupils and divert blood to muscles – preparing the body for fight or flight.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Describe hyperthyroidism and hypothyroidism.
answer_html:
Introduction The thyroid hormones (T3 and T4) control the body's metabolic rate, growth and brain development. Too much hormone causes hyperthyroidism, and too little causes hypothyroidism. Both are common, especially in women.

A. Hyperthyroidism (thyrotoxicosis)

1. Causes

  • Graves' disease – autoimmune; antibodies stimulate the thyroid (the commonest cause)
  • Toxic nodular goitre; thyroiditis; excess thyroxine tablets

2. Features – everything "speeds up"

  • Weight loss despite good appetite, heat intolerance, excessive sweating
  • Fast pulse, palpitations, atrial fibrillation
  • Tremor, nervousness, irritability, insomnia
  • Diarrhoea, scanty periods
  • Goitre; in Graves' disease – exophthalmos (protruding eyes)

3. Tests: low TSH, high T3 and T4

4. Treatment: antithyroid drugs (carbimazole), beta blockers for symptoms, radioactive iodine, thyroidectomy

B. Hypothyroidism

1. Causes

  • Hashimoto's (autoimmune) thyroiditis, iodine deficiency, after thyroid surgery or radioactive iodine, congenital

2. Features – everything "slows down"

  • Tiredness, weight gain, cold intolerance
  • Dry rough skin, hair loss, puffy face, hoarse voice
  • Slow pulse, constipation, slow reflexes, depression, poor memory
  • Heavy periods, infertility
  • Myxoedema in adults; cretinism in infants (stunted growth and intellectual disability)

3. Tests: high TSH, low T4

4. Treatment: levothyroxine daily for life, taken on an empty stomach in the morning

C. Comparison

Point Hyperthyroidism Hypothyroidism
Metabolic rate increased decreased
Weight loss gain
Temperature tolerance heat intolerance cold intolerance
Pulse fast slow
Bowels diarrhoea constipation
Skin warm, moist dry, rough
TSH low high

D. Nursing points

  • Hyperthyroidism – cool, quiet environment; high-calorie diet; eye care (lubricants, dark glasses); watch for thyroid storm (very high fever, fast pulse); after thyroidectomy watch for bleeding, airway obstruction, tetany and voice changes
  • Hypothyroidism – warm clothing, high-fibre diet, regular thyroxine, check pulse; start doses slowly in elderly and heart patients
  • Iodised salt prevents iodine-deficiency disorders

E. Goitre

  • Enlargement of the thyroid gland; it may occur with normal, high or low hormone levels
  • Simple (endemic) goitre – due to iodine deficiency: low hormone → more TSH → gland enlarges
  • Prevented by iodised salt under the National Iodine Deficiency Disorders Control Programme – salt must contain at least 15 ppm iodine at the consumer level

F. Investigations

  • Serum TSH – the best first test
  • Free T4 and T3, thyroid antibodies
  • Ultrasound of the neck, radioactive iodine uptake scan, fine-needle aspiration of nodules

Conclusion Hyperthyroidism speeds up metabolism (weight loss, heat intolerance, tachycardia, tremor), while hypothyroidism slows it down (weight gain, cold intolerance, bradycardia, myxoedema or cretinism); TSH testing guides diagnosis and treatment.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Explain the mechanism of hormone action and the feedback control of hormone secretion.

diagram.caption: Negative feedback in the hypothalamic–pituitary–thyroid axis

answer_html:
Introduction A hormone is a chemical messenger secreted by an endocrine gland into the blood, which acts on target cells having specific receptors. Hormones are of three chemical types:

  • Proteins and peptides – insulin, growth hormone, ADH
  • Steroids – cortisol, aldosterone, oestrogen, testosterone
  • Amines – adrenaline, thyroxine

A. Mechanism of hormone action

1. Water-soluble hormones (peptides, proteins, catecholamines) – membrane receptors

  • Cannot cross the cell membrane; bind to receptors on the cell surface
  • The hormone (first messenger) activates a second messenger inside the cell – e.g. cyclic AMP, calcium, IP₃
  • The second messenger activates enzymes that produce the effect
  • Action is rapid but short-lived
  • Example: adrenaline raising blood glucose; glucagon acting on the liver; insulin acts through a receptor enzyme (tyrosine kinase)

2. Lipid-soluble hormones (steroids, thyroid hormones) – intracellular receptors

  • Cross the cell membrane and bind to receptors in the cytoplasm or nucleus
  • The hormone–receptor complex acts on DNA → switches genes on or off → new proteins are made
  • Action is slower but longer lasting
  • Example: aldosterone forming sodium channels; cortisol; thyroxine increasing metabolic enzymes

B. Control of hormone secretion

1. Negative feedback – the commonest mechanism

  • A rise in the hormone (or its effect) inhibits further secretion, keeping levels steady
  • Example – thyroid: hypothalamus (TRH) → anterior pituitary (TSH) → thyroid (T3, T4); high T3/T4 inhibit TRH and TSH
  • Example – blood glucose: high glucose → insulin → glucose falls → insulin secretion falls
  • Example – calcium: low calcium → parathyroid hormone → calcium rises → PTH falls

2. Positive feedback – less common

  • The response increases the stimulus until an event is completed
  • Oxytocin during labour – contractions push the head on the cervix → more oxytocin → stronger contractions until delivery
  • LH surge before ovulation (stimulated by rising oestrogen)

3. Nervous control

  • Sympathetic nerves stimulate the adrenal medulla; the hypothalamus controls the pituitary

4. Biological rhythms

  • Cortisol highest in the early morning; melatonin at night; growth hormone during deep sleep

C. Applied importance

  • TSH testing uses feedback – high TSH means the thyroid is underactive
  • Long-term steroid drugs suppress ACTH by negative feedback, causing adrenal atrophy – so steroids must be tapered, not stopped suddenly
  • Oral contraceptive pills suppress FSH and LH by negative feedback, preventing ovulation
  • Oxytocin infusion for induction of labour must be closely monitored (risk of over-stimulation)

Conclusion Water-soluble hormones act through surface receptors and second messengers (fast), and lipid-soluble hormones act on genes through intracellular receptors (slow, lasting); hormone levels are mainly kept steady by negative feedback, with positive feedback in labour and ovulation.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: List the functions of the skin.
answer_html:
Introduction The skin is the largest organ of the body and has many functions besides covering it.

Functions of the skin

  1. Protection – a barrier against microbes, injury, chemicals, ultraviolet rays (melanin) and water loss
  2. Temperature regulation – sweating and changes in skin blood flow
  3. Sensation – touch, pressure, pain, heat and cold
  4. Synthesis of vitamin D in sunlight
  5. Excretion – water, salts and small amounts of urea in sweat
  6. Absorption – of some drugs (ointments, skin patches)
  7. Storage – fat in the subcutaneous tissue
  8. Immunity – Langerhans cells
  9. Expression – blushing, pallor

subject: Applied Physiology
question: How is body temperature regulated?
answer_html:
Introduction Normal body temperature is about 37 °C (98.6 °F). It stays constant because heat production equals heat loss, controlled by the hypothalamus (the body's "thermostat").

1. Heat production – metabolism (liver, muscles), muscular activity, shivering, thyroxine and adrenaline

2. Heat loss – mainly through the skin by radiation, conduction, convection and evaporation of sweat

3. Responses

  • When hot – sweating, dilation of skin vessels (skin becomes warm and flushed), less activity
  • When cold – constriction of skin vessels, shivering, "goose flesh", curling up, seeking warmth

Applied: fever occurs when the hypothalamic set point is raised by pyrogens.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Define accommodation of the eye.
answer_html:
Definition Accommodation is the ability of the eye to adjust its focus so that near objects are seen clearly on the retina.

Mechanism (near response)

  1. Ciliary muscle contracts
  2. The suspensory ligaments slacken
  3. The elastic lens becomes more convex (rounder) – its focusing power increases
  4. The pupils constrict – sharper image
  5. The eyes converge (turn inwards) towards the object

Applied: the lens hardens with age, so near vision fails after about 40 years (presbyopia) – corrected with convex (reading) glasses.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Name the errors of refraction and their correction.
answer_html:
Introduction Errors of refraction occur when light is not focused exactly on the retina, so the image is blurred.

Types and correction

  1. Myopia (short-sightedness) – distant objects blurred; image forms in front of the retina (long eyeball); corrected by concave lens
  2. Hypermetropia (long-sightedness) – near objects blurred; image forms behind the retina (short eyeball); corrected by convex lens
  3. Presbyopia – loss of accommodation with age; difficulty in reading; corrected by convex lens for near work
  4. Astigmatism – unequal curvature of the cornea; blurred, distorted vision; corrected by cylindrical lens

Applied: school eye screening detects refractive errors early (National Programme for Control of Blindness).

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Explain the physiology of hearing.
answer_html:
Introduction Hearing is the ability to perceive sound. Sound is a wave of vibrations in the air. The ear collects these waves, amplifies them and converts them into nerve impulses that the brain interprets as sound. The normal human ear hears frequencies of about 20 to 20,000 Hz.

1. Collection of sound – external ear

  • The auricle (pinna) collects sound waves and directs them into the external acoustic meatus
  • The waves strike the tympanic membrane, which vibrates at the same frequency

2. Transmission and amplification – middle ear

  • Vibrations pass through the chain of ossicles: malleus → incus → stapes
  • The footplate of the stapes pushes in and out of the oval window
  • The sound is amplified about 20 times because the eardrum is much larger than the oval window and the ossicles act as levers
  • The Eustachian tube keeps air pressure equal on both sides of the eardrum so it can vibrate freely
  • The tiny muscles (stapedius, tensor tympani) contract with very loud sounds and protect the inner ear

3. Conversion into nerve impulses – inner ear (cochlea)

  • Movements of the stapes set up pressure waves in the perilymph of the cochlea
  • The waves pass to the endolymph and make the basilar membrane vibrate
  • The hair cells of the organ of Corti on the basilar membrane bend against the overlying tectorial membrane
  • Bending of the hairs produces receptor potentials → nerve impulses in the cochlear nerve
  • High-pitched sounds stimulate hair cells near the base of the cochlea, low-pitched sounds near the apex (place theory)
  • The pressure waves are released through the round window

4. Auditory pathway Cochlear nerve (8th cranial nerve) → cochlear nuclei in the brainstem → superior olivary nucleus → inferior colliculus (midbrain) → medial geniculate body (thalamus) → primary auditory cortex in the superior temporal gyrus (areas 41, 42) → Wernicke's area for understanding speech

5. Loudness and pitch

  • Pitch depends on the frequency of the sound
  • Loudness depends on the amplitude of vibration; measured in decibels (dB); sounds above about 85 dB for long periods damage hearing

6. Types of deafness

  • Conductive deafness – problem in the external or middle ear (wax, otitis media, perforated drum, otosclerosis)
  • Sensorineural deafness – damage to the cochlea or nerve (noise, ageing – presbycusis, ototoxic drugs, meningitis, congenital)

7. Nursing importance

  • Simple tests: Rinne's and Weber's tests with a tuning fork; audiometry
  • Speak clearly, face the patient and avoid shouting with hearing-impaired patients
  • Monitor hearing in patients on streptomycin or gentamicin
  • Newborn hearing screening; ear protection for industrial workers

Conclusion Sound waves are collected by the external ear, amplified by the ossicles of the middle ear and converted into nerve impulses by the organ of Corti; the impulses are interpreted in the auditory cortex of the temporal lobe.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Explain the physiology of taste and smell.
answer_html:
Introduction Taste (gustation) and smell (olfaction) are chemical senses – their receptors respond to chemicals dissolved in saliva or in the mucus of the nose. Together they create the flavour of food and also warn us of spoiled food and dangers like gas leaks.

A. Taste 1. Receptors – taste buds

  • About 10,000 taste buds, mainly on the fungiform and circumvallate papillae of the tongue; a few on the palate, pharynx and epiglottis
  • Each taste bud contains gustatory (taste) cells with tiny taste hairs that project through a taste pore
  • Taste cells are replaced every 1–2 weeks

2. Mechanism

  • Food chemicals dissolve in saliva, enter the taste pore and bind to receptors on the taste hairs
  • This produces a receptor potential and nerve impulses

3. Primary tastes

  • Sweet, salty, sour, bitter and umami (savoury taste of glutamate)
  • All areas of the tongue can sense all tastes

4. Taste pathway

  • Anterior two-thirds of the tongue – facial nerve (chorda tympani)
  • Posterior one-third – glossopharyngeal nerve
  • Epiglottis – vagus nerve
  • → nucleus of the tractus solitarius (medulla) → thalamus → gustatory cortex (insula and lower postcentral gyrus)

B. Smell 1. Receptors

  • In the olfactory epithelium in the roof of the nasal cavity
  • Olfactory receptor cells are bipolar neurons with cilia; they are the only neurons that are regularly replaced
  • A layer of mucus covers the epithelium

2. Mechanism

  • Odour molecules dissolve in the mucus and bind to receptors on the cilia → nerve impulses
  • Sniffing brings more air to the olfactory area
  • The sense of smell adapts quickly – we stop noticing a smell after a short time

3. Olfactory pathway

  • Olfactory nerve fibres pass through the cribriform plate → olfactory bulb → olfactory tract → olfactory cortex in the temporal lobe (uncus)
  • Close links with the limbic system explain why smells bring back memories and emotions

C. Relationship of taste and smell

  • Much of what we call "taste" is really smell – food tastes dull when the nose is blocked by a cold
  • Both stimulate salivary and gastric secretion

D. Applied / nursing importance

  • Loss of smell (anosmia) – common cold, COVID-19, head injury with fracture of the cribriform plate
  • Elderly people lose taste and smell – poor appetite and risk of eating spoiled food or missing gas leaks
  • Taste changes during chemotherapy and with some drugs
  • Serve attractive, aromatic food to stimulate appetite in sick patients; maintain oral hygiene

Conclusion Taste buds on the tongue and olfactory cells in the roof of the nose detect dissolved chemicals; their impulses travel to the gustatory and olfactory cortex, and together they produce the flavour of food.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Explain the physiology of vision, including the visual pathway. (3 + 3 + 4)

diagram.caption: Visual pathway
labels: effects of lesions at optic nerve

answer_html:
Introduction Vision is the most important special sense; a large part of the information we receive about the world comes through the eyes. Seeing involves three steps: the eye focuses light to form an image on the retina, the photoreceptors convert light into nerve impulses, and the brain interprets these impulses.

(a) Formation of the image (3 marks) 1. Refraction of light

  • Light rays pass through the cornea → aqueous humour → pupil → lens → vitreous body and are bent (refracted) so that they meet exactly on the retina
  • The cornea does most of the bending (it has the greatest curvature)
  • The lens makes the fine adjustment for distance

2. Accommodation

  • For near vision, the ciliary muscle contracts, the suspensory ligaments slacken and the lens becomes more convex
  • For distant vision, the ciliary muscle relaxes and the lens becomes flatter

3. Control of light by the pupil

  • Bright light → pupil constricts (parasympathetic, 3rd nerve)
  • Dim light → pupil dilates (sympathetic)

4. The image

  • The image formed on the retina is real, inverted (upside down) and reversed left to right, and smaller than the object
  • The brain interprets it the right way up
  • The sharpest image is formed on the fovea centralis

(b) Photoreceptors and conversion of light into impulses (3 marks) 1. Rods – about 120 million, mostly in the periphery of the retina

  • Very sensitive; work in dim light (night vision)
  • Give black-and-white vision, poor detail
  • Contain the pigment rhodopsin (visual purple), made of opsin + retinal (a form of vitamin A)
  • Light breaks down rhodopsin → changes in the rod's membrane potential → signal
  • Rhodopsin is re-formed in the dark; this needs vitamin A – deficiency causes night blindness

2. Cones – about 6 million, concentrated at the fovea

  • Work in bright light
  • Give colour vision and sharp detail
  • Three types, sensitive to red, green and blue light; other colours are seen by mixing their signals (trichromatic theory)
  • Lack of one type causes colour blindness – usually red–green, inherited, more common in men

3. Adaptation

  • Dark adaptation – on entering a dark room vision slowly improves over 20–30 minutes as rhodopsin builds up
  • Light adaptation – on coming into bright light, the eyes adjust within a few minutes

4. Signal processing in the retina

  • Rods and cones → bipolar cells → ganglion cells
  • Axons of the ganglion cells come together at the optic disc to form the optic nerve

(c) Visual pathway (4 marks)

  1. Retina – each retina has a nasal (inner) half and a temporal (outer) half
  2. Optic nerve (2nd cranial nerve) – carries all fibres from one eye; passes back through the optic canal
  3. Optic chiasma – above the pituitary gland
    • Fibres from the nasal half of each retina cross to the opposite side
    • Fibres from the temporal half do not cross
  4. Optic tract – each tract now carries fibres from the temporal half of the same eye and the nasal half of the opposite eye, i.e. it carries information from the opposite half of the visual field
  5. Lateral geniculate body of the thalamus – relay station
  6. Optic radiation – fibres fan out through the temporal and parietal lobes
  7. Primary visual cortex (area 17) – around the calcarine sulcus in the occipital lobe; here we "see"
  8. Visual association areas (18, 19) – recognise and interpret what is seen

Reflex pathway: some fibres of the optic tract go to the midbrain (pretectal nucleus and superior colliculus) for the pupillary light reflex and reflex eye movements.

Effects of lesions in the pathway

Site of lesion Effect on vision
Optic nerve blindness of that eye
Optic chiasma (pituitary tumour) loss of outer (temporal) half of the field in both eyes – bitemporal hemianopia
Optic tract or radiation (stroke) loss of the same half of the field in both eyes – homonymous hemianopia
Visual cortex cortical blindness of the opposite field

(d) Reflexes of the eye

  • Pupillary light reflex – light in one eye constricts both pupils (direct and consensual)
  • Accommodation reflex – near vision: lens thickens, pupils constrict, eyes converge
  • Corneal reflex – touching the cornea causes blinking (5th and 7th nerves)

(e) Applied / nursing importance

  • Night blindness and xerophthalmia due to vitamin A deficiency – prevented by vitamin A prophylaxis for children (9 months to 5 years)
  • Refractive errors – screening and spectacles
  • Cataract and glaucoma – common causes of visual loss in the elderly
  • Colour blindness – tested with Ishihara charts
  • Pupil examination in head injury: size, equality and reaction to light (PERRLA); a fixed dilated pupil is a danger sign
  • Field defects after stroke – approach and place objects on the patient's seeing side

Conclusion Light is focused on the retina by the cornea and lens, converted into nerve impulses by rods and cones, and carried by the optic nerve, chiasma, tract and radiation to the visual cortex in the occipital lobe; damage at different points in this pathway produces characteristic patterns of visual loss.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Define visual acuity. How is it tested?
answer_html:
Definition Visual acuity is the sharpness of vision – the ability of the eye to see fine details and to distinguish two points close together as separate. It is highest at the fovea centralis, where cones are packed most densely.

Testing

  1. Distant vision – Snellen's chart read at 6 metres, one eye at a time with the other covered
    • Recorded as d/D – normal is 6/6; 6/60 means the person reads at 6 m what a normal eye reads at 60 m
  2. Near vision – Jaeger's or N-series reading chart at about 30–35 cm
  3. Children and people who cannot read – "E" chart, Landolt C or picture charts
  4. Pinhole test – vision that improves with a pinhole indicates a refractive error

Applied: reduced in refractive errors, cataract, glaucoma and retinal disease; blindness is defined as visual acuity below 3/60 in the better eye.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: What is dark adaptation?
answer_html:
Definition Dark adaptation is the gradual increase in the sensitivity of the eyes when a person moves from bright light into darkness, so that objects slowly become visible.

Mechanism

  1. Rhodopsin in the rods, bleached in bright light, is resynthesised in the dark – this needs vitamin A
  2. The pupils dilate, letting in more light
  3. Vision shifts from cones to rods - Maximum sensitivity is reached in about 20–30 minutes; light adaptation (the reverse) is much quicker

Applied

  • Delayed in vitamin A deficiency → night blindness, its earliest symptom; prevented by the vitamin A supplementation given to children up to 5 years
  • Slower in the elderly – night lights in wards prevent falls

subject: Applied Physiology
question: What is colour blindness?
answer_html:
Definition Colour blindness is the inability to distinguish certain colours, due to the absence or defect of one type of cone (red, green or blue).

Types

  1. Red–green colour blindness – the commonest; protanopia (red) or deuteranopia (green)
  2. Blue–yellow (tritanopia) – rare
  3. Total colour blindness (monochromatism) – very rare; sees only shades of grey

Key facts

  • Usually inherited as X-linked recessive – far more common in males
  • May also be acquired in retinal or optic nerve disease and with some drugs
  • Test: Ishihara's pseudo-isochromatic plates

Importance: may limit certain occupations – drivers, pilots and work that depends on colour codes (reading urine dipsticks, coloured signals).

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Name the cutaneous receptors and their functions.
answer_html:
Introduction Cutaneous receptors are sensory nerve endings in the skin that detect touch, pressure, temperature and pain.

Receptors and functions

  1. Free nerve endings – pain, temperature, itch and crude touch
  2. Meissner's corpuscles – fine (light) touch; plentiful in fingertips and lips
  3. Merkel's discs – sustained touch and pressure; recognising texture
  4. Pacinian corpuscles – deep pressure and vibration
  5. Ruffini endings – stretch of the skin and sustained pressure
  6. Hair follicle receptors – movement of hairs
  7. Thermoreceptors – separate warm and cold receptors

Applied: loss of skin sensation in diabetic neuropathy and leprosy leads to unnoticed injuries, burns and ulcers – daily foot inspection and footwear care are important.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: What is the field of vision? Name its common defects.
answer_html:
Definition The field of vision (visual field) is the entire area that can be seen by one eye while it looks fixedly at a point straight ahead.

Normal extent (approximately)

  • About 90–100° temporally (outwards), 60° nasally, 60° upwards and 70° downwards
  • The blind spot (optic disc, which has no rods or cones) lies about 15° to the temporal side

Testing: confrontation test at the bedside; perimetry for accurate charting.

Common defects

  1. Tunnel vision – loss of peripheral field in glaucoma, retinitis pigmentosa
  2. Bitemporal hemianopia – loss of both outer halves; pituitary tumour pressing the optic chiasma
  3. Homonymous hemianopia – loss of the same half in both eyes; stroke affecting the optic tract or visual cortex
  4. Scotoma – a blind patch, e.g. in macular disease

subject: Applied Physiology
question: What is aqueous humour? Give its functions and the normal intraocular pressure.
answer_html:
Definition Aqueous humour is the clear, watery fluid filling the anterior and posterior chambers of the eye.

Formation and drainage

  • Formed by the ciliary processes → flows from the posterior chamber through the pupil into the anterior chamber → drained through the trabecular meshwork into the canal of Schlemm → veins

Functions

  1. Maintains the shape of the eyeball and the intraocular pressure
  2. Nourishes the lens and cornea, which have no blood vessels, and removes their wastes
  3. Forms part of the refractive media

Normal intraocular pressure: about 10–21 mmHg.

Applied: blocked drainage raises the pressure → glaucoma, which damages the optic nerve and can cause permanent blindness; acute angle-closure glaucoma is an emergency.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Describe the age-related changes in the special senses and skin, with their nursing implications.
answer_html:
Introduction Ageing gradually reduces the sharpness of all the senses. These changes affect the elderly person's safety (falls, burns), communication, nutrition and quality of life. Knowing them helps the nurse plan care that keeps older people safe and independent.

1. Vision

  • Presbyopia – after about 40 years the lens loses its elasticity → difficulty with near vision
  • Cataract – clouding of the lens
  • Smaller pupils and slower dark adaptation → poor vision in dim light; more sensitivity to glare
  • Yellowing of the lens → difficulty distinguishing blue and green
  • Less tear production → dry eyes
  • Higher risk of glaucoma, macular degeneration and diabetic retinopathy
  • Nursing: bright light without glare, night lights, large print, keep spectacles clean and within reach, contrasting colours on steps, regular eye check-ups

2. Hearing

  • Presbycusis – gradual, bilateral sensorineural hearing loss, high-pitched sounds first; difficulty following speech in noisy places
  • Tinnitus; hard, accumulated ear wax
  • Nursing: face the person, speak clearly and slowly in a lower pitch (do not shout), reduce background noise, check hearing aids and batteries, arrange wax removal

3. Taste and smell

  • Fewer taste buds and smell receptors; dentures, drugs and smoking reduce taste further
  • Leads to poor appetite, weight loss and excess use of salt and sugar
  • Danger – may not smell smoke, gas leaks or spoiled food
  • Nursing: attractive meals flavoured with herbs and lemon, good oral hygiene, check food freshness, smoke and gas alarms

4. Touch, pain, temperature and position sense

  • Reduced sensitivity → unnoticed injuries and burns from hot water bottles
  • Reduced proprioception and vestibular function → poor balance, dizziness and falls
  • Nursing: check bath water temperature, avoid hot packs, inspect skin and feet, provide walking aids, handrails and non-slip floors

5. Skin

  • Thin, dry, less elastic skin (less collagen and elastin) – wrinkles
  • Fewer sweat and oil glands → poor heat tolerance and dryness
  • Less subcutaneous fat → feels cold easily
  • Fragile blood vessels → easy bruising; slow wound healing; less vitamin D production
  • High risk of pressure ulcers and skin tears
  • Nursing: mild soap and moisturisers, lift rather than drag the patient, reposition at least every 2 hours, adequate fluids and nutrition, protect from heat and cold

Conclusion Ageing dulls vision, hearing, taste, smell and touch and makes the skin thin and fragile; simple nursing measures – good lighting, clear speech, tasty food, safe temperatures, fall prevention and skin care – keep the elderly safe and independent.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Explain the pupillary reflexes.

diagram.caption: Pathway of the pupillary light reflex

answer_html:
Introduction The pupil is the opening in the centre of the iris. Its size is controlled by two muscles:

  • Sphincter pupillae – circular; supplied by parasympathetic fibres of the oculomotor nerve; constricts the pupil (miosis)
  • Dilator pupillae – radial; supplied by sympathetic fibres; dilates the pupil (mydriasis)

Normal pupils are round, equal, about 2–4 mm in bright light and larger in dim light. Pupillary reflexes control the amount of light entering the eye and help in focusing.

1. Light reflex

  • Direct light reflex – light shone into one eye → that pupil constricts
  • Consensual (indirect) light reflex – the other pupil also constricts, because fibres cross to both sides in the midbrain
  • Pathway: retina → optic nerve → optic chiasma → optic tract → pretectal nucleus (midbrain) → Edinger–Westphal nuclei of both sides → oculomotor nerve → ciliary ganglion → short ciliary nerves → sphincter pupillae → constriction
  • Purpose – protects the retina from excess light and sharpens the image

2. Accommodation (near) reflex When looking at a near object, three changes occur together – the near triad:

  • Convergence of the eyes
  • Constriction of the pupils
  • Increased convexity of the lens (ciliary muscle contracts)

3. Ciliospinal reflex

  • Pinching the skin of the neck → pupil dilates (sympathetic); used in assessing unconscious patients

4. Other influences

  • Pupils dilate in darkness, pain, fear and excitement (sympathetic); constrict in sleep

5. Applied importance

  • Neurological observation – pupils are checked for size, equality and reaction (PERRLA – pupils equal, round, reactive to light and accommodation)
  • One dilated, non-reacting pupil after head injury → raised intracranial pressure compressing the oculomotor nerve – an emergency
  • Pinpoint pupils – opioid (morphine) overdose, organophosphorus poisoning, pontine haemorrhage
  • Dilated fixed pupils – severe brain damage; atropine or datura poisoning
  • Argyll Robertson pupil – reacts to accommodation but not to light (neurosyphilis, diabetes)
  • Drugs – mydriatics (tropicamide) for eye examination; miotics (pilocarpine) in glaucoma

6. Nursing points

  • Use a pen torch in a dim room; bring the light from the side
  • Record pupil size in mm with a pupil gauge; compare both eyes
  • Report any change immediately

Conclusion The light reflex (direct and consensual) and the accommodation reflex adjust pupil size through the oculomotor nerve; pupil checks are a vital part of neurological observation, especially in head injury and poisoning.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Explain the physiology of equilibrium (vestibular apparatus).

diagram.caption: Vestibular apparatus of the internal ear

answer_html:
Introduction Equilibrium (balance) is the ability to maintain the posture of the body and the position of the head in space. It depends on three inputs – the vestibular apparatus of the internal ear, the eyes and proprioceptors in muscles and joints – which are integrated by the cerebellum and brainstem.

1. Vestibular apparatus It is part of the membranous labyrinth, filled with endolymph.

A. Utricle and saccule (otolith organs)

  • Each has a macula with hair cells covered by a jelly-like membrane containing otoliths (calcium carbonate crystals)
  • Detect static equilibrium – position of the head in relation to gravity (tilting)
  • Detect linear acceleration – utricle for forward-backward movement (car starting), saccule for up-down movement (lift)

B. Three semicircular canals

  • Anterior, posterior and lateral, at right angles to each other
  • Each has a swelling – the ampulla – containing the crista ampullaris, with hair cells embedded in a jelly-like cupula
  • Detect dynamic equilibrium – rotation (angular acceleration) of the head

2. Mechanism

  • Movement of the head → endolymph moves or the otoliths shift → hair cells bend → change in the rate of impulses in the vestibular nerve (part of the 8th cranial nerve)
  • Impulses reach the vestibular nuclei in the brainstem, which connect with:
    • the cerebellum – coordination
    • the spinal cord (vestibulospinal tract) – posture and anti-gravity muscles
    • the nuclei of eye muscles – the vestibulo-ocular reflex keeps the eyes fixed on an object while the head moves
    • the cerebral cortex – awareness of position and movement

3. Other inputs

  • Eyes – visual cues about position
  • Proprioceptors in joints, muscles and neck; pressure receptors in the soles of the feet

4. Applied importance

  • Motion sickness – conflicting signals from the eyes and vestibular apparatus → nausea, vomiting, pallor; prevented by antihistamines and by looking at the horizon
  • Vertigo – a false sense of spinning:
    • BPPV (benign paroxysmal positional vertigo) – displaced otoliths
    • Ménière's disease – excess endolymph; vertigo, tinnitus and deafness
    • Labyrinthitis; ototoxic drugs such as streptomycin and gentamicin
  • Nystagmus – involuntary rhythmic eye movements in vestibular or cerebellar disease
  • Tests – Romberg's test (standing with feet together and eyes closed), caloric test

5. Nursing points

  • Prevent falls – assist walking, ask the patient to rise slowly, keep the bed low and rails up, good lighting
  • Give antiemetics and vestibular sedatives as prescribed; avoid sudden head movements
  • Monitor hearing and balance in patients on aminoglycosides

Conclusion The utricle and saccule sense head position and linear movement, and the semicircular canals sense rotation; together with the eyes and proprioceptors, and through the cerebellum, they keep the body balanced.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: What is a lever? Give its types with examples from the body.
answer_html:
Definition A lever is a rigid bar that moves around a fixed point (fulcrum) when a force (effort) is applied to overcome a resistance (load). In the body, bones act as levers, joints as fulcrums and muscles provide the effort.

Types of levers

  1. First-class lever – fulcrum lies between effort and load
    • Example: nodding the head at the atlanto-occipital joint
  2. Second-class lever – load lies between fulcrum and effort; gives power
    • Example: standing on tiptoe (fulcrum at the toes, load = body weight, effort by calf muscles)
  3. Third-class lever – effort lies between fulcrum and load; gives speed and range; the commonest in the body
    • Example: bending the elbow by the biceps

Applied: in body mechanics, keep the load close to the body to reduce strain on the back.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Write the functions of the axial skeleton.
answer_html:
Introduction The axial skeleton (80 bones) forms the central axis of the body – skull, hyoid, ear ossicles, vertebral column, ribs and sternum.

Functions

  1. Support – supports the head, neck and trunk and keeps the body upright
  2. Protection
    • Skull protects the brain
    • Vertebral column protects the spinal cord
    • Rib cage protects the heart and lungs
  3. Breathing – movements of the ribs help ventilation
  4. Attachment – gives attachment to muscles of the back, neck, chest and limbs
  5. Blood formation – red marrow in the sternum, ribs, vertebrae and skull
  6. Transmission of body weight to the lower limbs through the pelvis

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Define muscle tone.
answer_html:
Definition Muscle tone is the state of slight, continuous partial contraction of a skeletal muscle at rest.

Key points

  1. Maintained by the stretch reflex – muscle spindles sense stretch and the spinal cord sends a steady flow of impulses to the muscle
  2. Controlled by the cerebellum and higher brain centres
  3. Importance – maintains posture, keeps muscles ready for quick action, helps venous return and produces some body heat
  4. Hypotonia (low tone) – cerebellar disease, lower motor neuron lesion, spinal shock, sleep
  5. Hypertonia (high tone) – spasticity in upper motor neuron lesions (stroke); rigidity in Parkinsonism

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Describe the pelvic girdle and explain the functions of the pelvis.
answer_html:
Introduction The pelvic girdle connects the lower limbs with the vertebral column. Together with the sacrum and coccyx it forms the bony pelvis, a strong basin that carries the weight of the upper body and protects the pelvic organs.

1. Bones of the pelvis

  • Two hip bones (innominate bones) – each formed by three bones fused at the acetabulum (the socket of the hip joint):
    • Ilium – the upper, wide, flat part; its upper border is the iliac crest
    • Ischium – the lower back part; its ischial tuberosity bears weight when we sit
    • Pubis – the front part
  • Sacrum – five fused vertebrae at the back
  • Coccyx – the tail bone

2. Joints

  • Sacroiliac joints – between the sacrum and each ilium
  • Pubic symphysis – between the two pubic bones in front (fibrocartilage)
  • Sacrococcygeal joint
  • In pregnancy, the hormone relaxin loosens these joints slightly for childbirth

3. Parts of the pelvis

  • Pelvic brim – a ring formed by the sacral promontory, arcuate lines and pubic crest
  • False (greater) pelvis – above the brim; part of the abdominal cavity; supports the intestines
  • True (lesser) pelvis – below the brim; has an inlet, cavity and outlet; forms the birth canal

4. Differences between male and female pelvis

Feature Female pelvis Male pelvis
General build light, smooth, wide and shallow heavy, rough, narrow and deep
Inlet round or oval heart-shaped
Subpubic angle wide (about 90° or more) narrow (about 50–60°)
Sacrum short and wide long and narrow
Greater sciatic notch wide narrow
Ischial spines less projecting more projecting

5. Functions of the pelvis

  1. Transmits body weight from the vertebral column to the lower limbs when standing, and to the ischial tuberosities when sitting
  2. Protects the pelvic organs – urinary bladder, rectum, uterus and ovaries
  3. Supports the abdominal organs
  4. Attachment for muscles of the trunk, lower limbs and pelvic floor
  5. Forms the birth canal in women
  6. Blood formation – red marrow in the iliac crests

6. Applied / nursing importance

  • Pelvic measurements in pregnancy – a small pelvis may cause cephalopelvic disproportion and obstructed labour
  • Pelvic fractures in road accidents – severe internal bleeding and bladder or urethral injury; do not catheterise if there is blood at the meatus
  • Bone marrow aspiration and biopsy from the posterior iliac crest
  • The iliac crests are landmarks for lumbar puncture (L4) and for the ventrogluteal IM site

Conclusion The pelvis, formed by the two hip bones, sacrum and coccyx, transmits body weight, protects pelvic organs and, in women, forms the birth canal; the female pelvis is wider and shallower to allow childbirth.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Explain the stages of bone (fracture) healing.
answer_html:
Introduction A fracture is a break in the continuity of a bone. Bone has an excellent power of repair – it heals by forming new bone, not a fibrous scar. Healing passes through overlapping stages and takes weeks to months.

1. Stage of haematoma formation (first few days)

  • Blood vessels in the bone and periosteum tear and bleed
  • A blood clot (haematoma) forms between the broken ends
  • Inflammation follows – swelling, pain, warmth
  • Bone cells at the fracture ends die for lack of blood

2. Stage of fibrocartilaginous (soft) callus (about 1–3 weeks)

  • New capillaries grow into the haematoma
  • Fibroblasts and chondroblasts form granulation tissue, then fibrous tissue and cartilage
  • This soft callus bridges the gap and holds the fragments loosely

3. Stage of bony (hard) callus (about 3–12 weeks)

  • Osteoblasts lay down woven bone, converting the soft callus into hard bony callus
  • The fracture becomes firm – clinical union (no movement or pain at the site)
  • X-ray shows the callus

4. Stage of remodelling (months to years)

  • Osteoclasts remove extra bone; osteoblasts lay down compact bone along lines of stress
  • The bone regains its normal shape and strength; the marrow cavity is restored
  • In children remodelling can even correct some deformity

5. Factors that help healing

  • Proper reduction and immobilisation (plaster, splint, internal fixation)
  • Good blood supply
  • Good nutrition – protein, calcium, vitamin D, vitamin C
  • Young age – children heal faster

6. Factors that delay healing

  • Movement at the fracture site
  • Infection (open fractures)
  • Poor blood supply – neck of femur, scaphoid, lower third of tibia
  • Old age, diabetes, smoking, steroids, malnutrition
  • Soft tissue trapped between the fragments

7. Complications: delayed union, non-union, malunion (healing in a wrong position), avascular necrosis.

8. Nursing importance

  • Plaster care – keep it dry and clean, elevate the limb
  • Neurovascular checks – watch for pain, pallor, pulselessness, paraesthesia and paralysis (signs of compartment syndrome)
  • Adequate diet and early mobilisation of the other joints
  • Prevent falls in the elderly (osteoporosis)

Conclusion Fracture healing passes through haematoma, soft callus, hard callus and remodelling stages; immobilisation, blood supply and nutrition decide how quickly and how well a bone unites.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Explain the types of muscle contraction and muscle fatigue.
answer_html:
Introduction When a skeletal muscle is stimulated it contracts – it develops tension and may shorten. Contractions are classified by whether the muscle length or tension changes, and by the pattern of stimulation.

1. Isotonic contraction

  • Tension stays the same but the muscle length changes and movement occurs
  • Concentric – the muscle shortens while contracting (lifting a glass, climbing stairs)
  • Eccentric – the muscle lengthens while contracting (lowering a weight slowly, walking downstairs)

2. Isometric contraction

  • The length stays the same but tension increases; no movement
  • Examples: pushing against a wall, holding a bag steady, maintaining posture
  • Isometric (static) exercises such as quadriceps setting are taught to bedridden or plastered patients to keep muscles strong without moving the joint

3. Twitch, summation and tetanus

  • Simple twitch – a single brief contraction to a single stimulus
  • Summation – stimuli in quick succession make contractions add up
  • Tetanus (tetanic contraction) – very rapid stimuli produce a smooth, sustained contraction; normal voluntary movements are of this type
  • (This is different from the disease tetanus, caused by a toxin)

4. Muscle tone – slight continuous contraction at rest, maintaining posture.

5. Muscle fatigue

  • Definition: a gradual decrease in the force of contraction after prolonged or repeated activity, even though the muscle is still being stimulated
  • Causes:
    • Depletion of ATP, creatine phosphate and glycogen
    • Accumulation of lactic acid and fall in pH (anaerobic metabolism)
    • Lack of oxygen
    • Changes in ion balance
  • Recovery – rest, oxygen supply and nutrition
  • Oxygen debt – after heavy exercise we keep breathing hard to repay the oxygen used to remove lactic acid and rebuild energy stores

6. Other terms

  • Cramp – a sudden painful involuntary contraction (dehydration, low calcium or sodium)
  • Rigor mortis – stiffness of muscles after death because ATP runs out and the cross-bridges stay locked; begins a few hours after death

7. Nursing importance

  • Isometric and isotonic exercises in rehabilitation
  • Prevent muscle wasting in immobile patients
  • Plan nursing activities with rest periods for weak patients (e.g. heart failure, anaemia)
