Conclusion Muscles contract isotonically (with movement) or isometrically (without movement); continued activity leads to fatigue due to energy depletion and lactic acid build-up.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Explain the mechanism of contraction of skeletal muscle. (2 + 2 + 4 + 2)

diagram.caption: Sarcomere and sliding filaments
labels: thin filament (actin with troponin and tropomyosin)

answer_html:
Introduction Skeletal muscle contraction is the basis of all voluntary movement, posture and breathing. It is explained by the sliding filament theory (Huxley and Huxley, 1954): during contraction the thin actin filaments slide over the thick myosin filaments, so each sarcomere shortens – the filaments themselves do not change length.

(a) Structure of a skeletal muscle fibre (2 marks)

  • A muscle is made of bundles of muscle fibres (cells); each fibre contains many myofibrils
  • Each myofibril is a chain of repeating units called sarcomeres – the functional unit of contraction, extending from one Z line to the next
  • Thick filaments – made of myosin; each myosin molecule has a head that can bind actin and split ATP
  • Thin filaments – made of actin, with the regulatory proteins tropomyosin (covers the binding sites on actin) and troponin (binds calcium)
  • Bands: the dark A band (length of the thick filaments), the light I band (thin filaments only), the H zone (thick filaments only) and the M line
  • Sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR) – stores calcium ions
  • T-tubules – inward extensions of the cell membrane that carry the impulse deep into the fibre

(b) Excitation of the muscle fibre (2 marks)

  1. A nerve impulse travels down the motor neuron to the neuromuscular junction
  2. Acetylcholine (ACh) is released and binds to receptors on the motor end plate
  3. An end-plate potential generates a muscle action potential
  4. The action potential spreads along the muscle membrane (sarcolemma) and down the T-tubules into the fibre

(c) Excitation–contraction coupling and the cross-bridge cycle (4 marks) 1. Release of calcium

  • The action potential in the T-tubules causes the sarcoplasmic reticulum to release calcium ions into the cytoplasm

2. Exposure of the binding sites

  • Calcium binds to troponin
  • Troponin changes shape and pulls tropomyosin away from the myosin-binding sites on actin

3. Cross-bridge cycling (the "power stroke")

  1. Attachment – the energised myosin head (which has already split ATP into ADP and phosphate) binds to actin, forming a cross-bridge
  2. Power stroke – the myosin head tilts, pulling the actin filament towards the centre (M line) of the sarcomere; ADP and phosphate are released
  3. Detachment – a new ATP molecule binds to the myosin head, which then lets go of actin
  4. Re-cocking – myosin splits the ATP and the head returns to its high-energy position, ready to bind again further along the actin - The cycle repeats many times a second as long as calcium and ATP are present – like a team pulling a rope hand over hand

4. Result – shortening of the sarcomere

  • The thin filaments slide towards the centre
  • Z lines come closer together
  • I band and H zone become shorter
  • A band stays the same length (the thick filaments do not change)
  • All sarcomeres shorten together, so the whole muscle shortens and pulls on the bone

5. Relaxation

  • When nerve impulses stop, acetylcholinesterase destroys the ACh
  • Calcium is pumped back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum (this needs ATP)
  • Tropomyosin again covers the binding sites; cross-bridges cannot form
  • The filaments slide back and the muscle relaxes

6. Energy for contraction

  • ATP is needed for the power stroke, for detachment of myosin and for pumping calcium back
  • ATP is renewed from:
    • Creatine phosphate – a quick store for the first few seconds
    • Anaerobic glycolysis – fast, but produces lactic acid
    • Aerobic respiration in mitochondria – slow, but gives a large amount of ATP for prolonged activity

(d) Applied / nursing importance (2 marks)

  • Hypocalcaemia increases nerve excitability → tetany (muscle spasms)
  • Rigor mortis – after death ATP runs out, so myosin cannot detach from actin and muscles become stiff
  • Myasthenia gravis and organophosphorus poisoning affect the neuromuscular junction, the first step of contraction
  • Muscle relaxant drugs in anaesthesia block transmission – ventilation is needed
  • Muscle cramps – dehydration and electrolyte imbalance
  • Exercise and physiotherapy strengthen muscles; disuse causes wasting – encourage active and passive exercises in bedridden patients
  • Malignant hyperthermia – a rare reaction to some anaesthetic drugs with uncontrolled calcium release; high fever and rigidity

Conclusion Skeletal muscle contracts when a nerve impulse releases calcium from the sarcoplasmic reticulum; calcium binds troponin, exposing actin, and myosin heads use ATP to pull the actin filaments inward, shortening every sarcomere. Removal of calcium allows relaxation, and both contraction and relaxation depend on a constant supply of ATP.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Define a motor unit.
answer_html:
Definition A motor unit is a single motor neuron together with all the skeletal muscle fibres it supplies. When the neuron fires, all its fibres contract together.

Key facts

  1. Small motor units – a few muscle fibres per neuron (about 10 or fewer in eye muscles) → fine, precise movements (eyes, fingers)
  2. Large motor units – up to about 2,000 fibres per neuron (e.g. gastrocnemius) → powerful, gross movements
  3. The force of contraction is increased by:
    • recruiting more motor units
    • increasing the frequency of impulses

Applied: diseases of motor neurons – poliomyelitis, motor neuron disease – cause paralysis and wasting of the muscle fibres of those units; electromyography (EMG) studies motor units.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: What is rigor mortis?
answer_html:
Definition Rigor mortis is the stiffening of muscles after death.

Cause

  • After death ATP is no longer produced
  • ATP is needed to detach myosin heads from actin, so the cross-bridges stay locked and the muscles become rigid

Time course (approximate; faster in hot weather)

  • Begins about 2–6 hours after death, first in small muscles (eyelids, jaw, face)
  • Complete in about 12 hours
  • Passes off in about 24–48 hours, as the muscle proteins break down

Importance

  1. Helps in estimating the time since death (forensic medicine)
  2. Last offices – close the eyes and mouth, straighten the limbs and position the body before rigor mortis sets in

subject: Applied Physiology
question: State the all-or-none law.
answer_html:
Statement A single muscle fibre (or nerve fibre) either responds fully to a stimulus or does not respond at all.

Explanation

  1. A subthreshold stimulus produces no response
  2. A threshold stimulus produces a maximal response of that fibre
  3. Increasing the stimulus above threshold does not increase the response of that fibre

Applies to

  • A single skeletal muscle fibre
  • A single nerve fibre
  • The heart as a whole – because it acts as a functional syncytium

Does not apply to a whole skeletal muscle, which contains many motor units; stronger stimuli recruit more units and give graded contractions.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: What is myasthenia gravis?
answer_html:
Definition Myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune disease in which antibodies destroy or block acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction, causing muscle weakness that increases with activity and improves with rest.

Features

  • Drooping eyelids (ptosis), double vision
  • Difficulty in chewing, swallowing and speaking; limb weakness
  • Often associated with an abnormal thymus
  • Myasthenic crisis – weakness of breathing muscles; may need a ventilator

Treatment: anticholinesterases (pyridostigmine, neostigmine), steroids and other immunosuppressants, thymectomy.

Nursing: give pyridostigmine on time, about 30–60 minutes before meals; watch swallowing and breathing closely.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: What is osteoporosis?
answer_html:
Definition Osteoporosis is a condition in which bone mass and density decrease and the bone becomes porous and fragile, so that it fractures easily.

Risk factors

  • Postmenopausal women (lack of oestrogen), old age
  • Long-term steroid therapy, immobility
  • Low calcium and vitamin D, smoking, alcohol, thin body build

Common fracture sites

  • Vertebrae – loss of height, stooped back (kyphosis)
  • Neck of femur (hip) and wrist

Diagnosis: DEXA scan (bone mineral density).

Prevention: weight-bearing exercise, calcium and vitamin D (sunlight), avoiding smoking and alcohol, and fall prevention.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Describe the types of movements at synovial joints with examples.

diagram.caption: Types of movements at synovial joints

answer_html:
Introduction Synovial joints are freely movable joints. Muscles acting across them produce movements, and the shape of the articular surfaces decides which movements are possible – for example, a hinge joint such as the elbow allows only bending and straightening, while a ball-and-socket joint such as the shoulder allows movement in all directions. Movements are described from the anatomical position.

1. Gliding (sliding) movements

  • Flat surfaces slide over each other – intercarpal and intertarsal joints

2. Angular movements

  • Flexion – decreases the angle between two bones; bending the elbow or knee
  • Extension – increases the angle; straightening; hyperextension goes beyond the anatomical position (bending the neck backwards)
  • Abduction – movement away from the midline; raising the arm sideways
  • Adduction – movement towards the midline
  • Lateral flexion – bending the trunk or neck to the side

3. Circumduction

  • A circular movement combining flexion, abduction, extension and adduction, so the limb draws a cone – shoulder, hip, thumb

4. Rotation

  • Turning a bone around its long axis
  • Medial (internal) and lateral (external) rotation – shoulder and hip
  • Shaking the head "no" – atlanto-axial joint

5. Special movements

  • Supination and pronation – turning the palm up and down (radio-ulnar joints)
  • Inversion and eversion – turning the sole inwards and outwards (subtalar joint)
  • Dorsiflexion and plantar flexion – lifting the foot upwards; pointing the toes / standing on tiptoe (ankle)
  • Protraction and retraction – moving forwards and backwards (jaw, shoulder blades)
  • Elevation and depression – raising and lowering (shrugging the shoulders, closing and opening the jaw)
  • Opposition – touching the tip of each finger with the thumb; essential for grasping

6. Nursing importance

  • Range-of-motion (ROM) exercises – active (by the patient) and passive (by the nurse) – prevent stiffness and contractures in bedridden patients; each joint is moved through its full range several times a day
  • Positioning:
    • a footboard or pillow keeps the feet in dorsiflexion and prevents foot drop
    • a trochanter roll prevents external rotation of the hip
    • a hand roll keeps the fingers in a functional position
  • Assessment – record the range of each joint; report pain or restricted movement
  • Teach correct body mechanics while lifting

Conclusion Synovial joints allow gliding, angular (flexion, extension, abduction, adduction), circumduction, rotation and special movements such as supination, inversion, dorsiflexion and opposition; maintaining these movements through ROM exercises and positioning prevents contractures.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Explain the properties of smooth muscle.
answer_html:
Introduction Smooth muscle (involuntary, non-striated muscle) is found in the walls of hollow organs – the gut, blood vessels, bronchi, urinary bladder, ureters and uterus – and in the iris, ciliary body and arrector pili. Its fibres are spindle-shaped with a single central nucleus and no striations, because actin and myosin are not arranged in sarcomeres.

Types

  • Single-unit (visceral) smooth muscle – fibres joined by gap junctions contract together as one unit and show spontaneous activity – gut, uterus, ureters, small blood vessels
  • Multi-unit smooth muscle – each fibre is supplied separately, allowing fine control – iris, ciliary muscle, large arteries, arrector pili

Properties

1. Slow, sustained contraction

  • Contracts and relaxes slowly but can maintain contraction for long periods using very little energy (the "latch" state)
  • Suits the steady tone of blood vessels and sphincters; it rarely fatigues

2. Automaticity (rhythmicity)

  • Visceral smooth muscle produces slow waves and action potentials on its own; pacemaker cells in the gut wall (interstitial cells of Cajal) drive peristalsis

3. Plasticity (stress relaxation)

  • When stretched slowly, the tension first rises and then falls back as the muscle adapts to its new length
  • Allows the bladder, stomach and uterus to fill without a large rise in pressure

4. Response to stretch

  • Sudden stretch causes contraction (myogenic response) – seen in arterioles (autoregulation of blood flow) and in the gut (peristalsis)

5. Calcium and contraction

  • Calcium comes mainly from the extracellular fluid
  • It binds to calmodulin (not troponin), which activates myosin light-chain kinase and starts cross-bridge cycling

6. Control

  • Involuntary – by autonomic nerves (sympathetic and parasympathetic)
  • Hormones – oxytocin, adrenaline
  • Local factors – stretch, CO₂, H⁺, temperature
  • Can contract even without a nerve supply

7. Tone

  • Continuous partial contraction maintains blood pressure and the closure of sphincters

Applied importance

  • Asthma – spasm of bronchial smooth muscle; relieved by bronchodilators (salbutamol)
  • Hypertension – increased arteriolar tone; calcium-channel blockers (amlodipine) relax it
  • Colic – painful spasm in renal, biliary or intestinal colic; antispasmodics (hyoscine, dicyclomine)
  • Labour – oxytocin stimulates uterine muscle; tocolytics relax it
  • Postoperative urinary retention and paralytic ileus – reduced smooth muscle activity

Conclusion Smooth muscle contracts slowly and for long periods with little energy, shows automaticity, plasticity and response to stretch, uses calmodulin for contraction and is controlled involuntarily by autonomic nerves, hormones and local factors.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Explain the factors affecting bone growth and remodelling.
answer_html:
Introduction Bone is living tissue. It grows during childhood and adolescence and is continuously remodelled throughout life. Three types of bone cells take part:

  • Osteoblasts – bone-forming cells
  • Osteocytes – mature bone cells that maintain the bone
  • Osteoclasts – large, multinucleated bone-resorbing cells

A. Bone growth

  1. Growth in length – at the epiphyseal (growth) plate of cartilage between the epiphysis and the shaft; cartilage cells multiply and are replaced by bone; growth stops when the plate fuses after puberty, usually in the late teens or early twenties
  2. Growth in thickness (appositional growth) – osteoblasts under the periosteum add new bone on the outer surface, while osteoclasts remove bone from the inside, enlarging the medullary cavity

B. Bone remodelling

  • A continuous cycle of resorption by osteoclasts and formation by osteoblasts; roughly 10% of the adult skeleton is replaced each year
  • Purposes – repairs tiny cracks, reshapes bone according to the stresses placed on it (bone is laid down where it is needed – Wolff's law), and keeps the blood calcium level normal
  • Balance – in childhood formation is greater than resorption; in young adults they are equal; after about 35–40 years, and especially after menopause, resorption exceeds formation → bone loss

C. Factors affecting bone growth and remodelling

1. Nutrition

  • Calcium and phosphorus – minerals of bone
  • Vitamin D – absorption of calcium from the gut
  • Vitamin C – collagen formation (deficiency – scurvy)
  • Vitamin A, vitamin K and proteins

2. Hormones

  • Growth hormone (through IGF-1) – stimulates the growth plates
  • Thyroid hormones – growth and maturation of bone
  • Sex hormones – cause the pubertal growth spurt and later closure of the epiphyses; oestrogen protects bone by restraining osteoclasts
  • Parathyroid hormone – increases bone resorption to raise blood calcium
  • Calcitonin – inhibits osteoclasts
  • Excess cortisol – causes bone loss

3. Physical activity

  • Weight-bearing and exercise stimulate bone formation
  • Immobility and bed rest cause rapid bone loss

4. Other factors

  • Age, sex and heredity; sunlight exposure
  • Smoking, alcohol; drugs such as steroids, heparin and some anticonvulsants

D. Applied importance

  • Rickets in children and osteomalacia in adults – vitamin D deficiency
  • Osteoporosis – postmenopausal women, elderly, long-term steroids
  • Gigantism and acromegaly (excess growth hormone); dwarfism (deficiency)
  • Immobilised patients – active exercises, early ambulation, adequate calcium and vitamin D
  • Fractures through the growth plate in children may affect limb length

Conclusion Bone grows in length at the epiphyseal plate and in thickness under the periosteum, and is constantly remodelled by osteoblasts and osteoclasts; nutrition (calcium, vitamin D), hormones and physical activity are the main factors controlling it.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Explain the sources of energy for muscle contraction.
answer_html:
Introduction Muscle contraction needs energy in the form of ATP (adenosine triphosphate). ATP is used for:

  • Cross-bridge cycling – the power stroke and the detachment of myosin from actin
  • Pumping calcium back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum – needed for relaxation
  • The sodium–potassium pump, which restores ion gradients after each action potential

Muscle stores only enough ATP for a few seconds of strong contraction, so it must be regenerated continuously from three sources.

1. Creatine phosphate (phosphocreatine) system

  • Creatine phosphate + ADP → ATP + creatine (enzyme: creatine kinase)
  • The fastest source; needs no oxygen
  • With stored ATP, lasts about 10–15 seconds of maximal effort – a sprint, lifting a heavy weight
  • Applied – creatine kinase (CK) rises in the blood after muscle injury and myocardial infarction (CK-MB)

2. Anaerobic glycolysis (glycogen–lactic acid system)

  • Muscle glycogen → glucose → pyruvic acid → lactic acid when oxygen is insufficient
  • Gives only 2 ATP per glucose molecule, but quickly
  • Supports intense activity for about 1–2 minutes
  • Lactic acid accumulation contributes to fatigue and a burning pain in the muscles

3. Aerobic (oxidative) metabolism

  • In the mitochondria, with oxygen, glucose and fatty acids are completely oxidised to CO₂ and water (Krebs cycle and electron transport chain)
  • Gives about 30–38 ATP per glucose (figures vary between textbooks)
  • Slow but long-lasting – the main source at rest and in prolonged activity such as walking or long-distance running; fatty acids become the main fuel in prolonged exercise
  • Needs a good blood supply; myoglobin stores oxygen in muscle

4. Oxygen debt

  • After strenuous exercise, breathing stays deep and fast for some time
  • The extra oxygen is used to convert lactic acid back to glucose (in the liver), rebuild creatine phosphate and ATP, and reload myoglobin with oxygen

5. Types of muscle fibres

  • Red (slow-twitch) fibres – rich in myoglobin and mitochondria; aerobic; resist fatigue – postural muscles such as the soleus and back muscles
  • White (fast-twitch) fibres – fewer mitochondria; depend on glycolysis; strong, quick contractions but fatigue quickly

6. Applied and nursing importance

  • Heat production – only about 20–25% of the energy becomes work; the rest is heat (so shivering warms the body and exercise raises body temperature)
  • Patients with anaemia, heart or lung disease tire early because oxygen delivery is poor – graded activity and rest periods
  • Diabetic patients – exercise uses glucose; watch for hypoglycaemia
  • Bed rest and malnutrition cause muscle wasting – early ambulation and good nutrition

Conclusion ATP for muscle contraction is regenerated from creatine phosphate (immediate), anaerobic glycolysis (short bursts) and aerobic metabolism (prolonged activity); the oxygen debt is repaid after exercise.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: List the steps of urine formation.
answer_html:
Introduction Urine is formed by the nephrons of the kidneys from blood plasma. About 180 litres of filtrate is formed daily, but only about 1–1.5 litres of urine is passed.

Steps of urine formation

  1. Glomerular filtration – plasma (without cells and most proteins) is filtered from the glomerulus into Bowman's capsule
  2. Tubular reabsorption – useful substances (water, glucose, amino acids, sodium, bicarbonate) are taken back into the blood – about 99% of the filtrate
  3. Tubular secretion – unwanted substances (H⁺, K⁺, creatinine, drugs) are added from the blood into the tubule
  4. Concentration of urine – water is reabsorbed in the collecting ducts under the control of ADH

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Enlist any four abnormal constituents of urine.
answer_html:
Introduction Normal urine contains water, urea, creatinine, uric acid and salts. The presence of the following is abnormal:

  1. Glucose (glycosuria) – diabetes mellitus (blood glucose above the renal threshold)
  2. Protein/albumin (proteinuria) – kidney disease (nephrotic syndrome), pre-eclampsia
  3. Ketone bodies (ketonuria) – uncontrolled diabetes (ketoacidosis), starvation, severe vomiting
  4. Blood (haematuria) – stones, injury, infection, tumours, glomerulonephritis
  5. Bile pigments and bile salts – obstructive jaundice (dark yellow urine)
  6. Pus cells (pyuria) – urinary tract infection
  7. Haemoglobin – haemolysis (mismatched transfusion)
  8. Casts and crystals – kidney disease, stones

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Define glomerular filtration rate (GFR) and give its normal value.
answer_html:
Definition Glomerular filtration rate (GFR) is the volume of filtrate formed by all the glomeruli of both kidneys per minute.

Normal value

  • About 125 ml per minute, i.e. about 180 litres per day
  • About 99% of this is reabsorbed

Factors affecting GFR

  1. Blood pressure in the glomerular capillaries
  2. Renal blood flow
  3. Plasma protein (oncotic) pressure
  4. Pressure in Bowman's capsule (raised in urinary obstruction)
  5. Constriction or dilation of the afferent and efferent arterioles

Applied: GFR is estimated from serum creatinine (eGFR) to stage chronic kidney disease; a fall in GFR raises urea and creatinine.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Explain the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system.
answer_html:
Introduction The renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system (RAAS) is a chain of hormones that raises blood pressure and blood volume when they fall. It links the kidneys, liver, lungs and adrenal glands, and is the target of many antihypertensive drugs.

1. Stimuli for renin release

  • Fall in blood pressure or reduced blood flow to the kidneys (haemorrhage, dehydration, shock)
  • Fall in sodium reaching the macula densa of the distal tubule
  • Sympathetic stimulation of the kidneys

2. Steps of the system

  1. Renin is released by the juxtaglomerular (JG) cells in the wall of the afferent arteriole
  2. Renin acts on angiotensinogen (a plasma protein made by the liver) and converts it into angiotensin I (inactive)
  3. Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE), present mainly in the lungs, converts angiotensin I into angiotensin II – the active hormone

3. Actions of angiotensin II

  • Powerful vasoconstriction of arterioles → BP rises quickly
  • Stimulates the adrenal cortex (zona glomerulosa) to secrete aldosterone
  • Stimulates release of ADH from the posterior pituitary → water retention
  • Stimulates thirst → more water intake
  • Increases sympathetic activity
  • Constricts the efferent arteriole, helping maintain GFR

4. Actions of aldosterone

  • Acts on the distal tubule and collecting duct
  • Increases reabsorption of sodium (and water follows)
  • Increases excretion of potassium
  • Result: blood volume and BP rise

5. Negative feedback

  • When BP and sodium return to normal, renin secretion falls and the system switches off

6. Applied / nursing importance

  • ACE inhibitors (enalapril, ramipril) block the formation of angiotensin II – used in hypertension and heart failure; side effects: dry cough, high potassium
  • Angiotensin receptor blockers (losartan, telmisartan)
  • Aldosterone antagonists (spironolactone) – potassium-sparing diuretics
  • Renal artery stenosis activates RAAS and causes hypertension
  • In heart failure and cirrhosis, an overactive RAAS causes salt and water retention and oedema
  • Monitor BP and serum potassium in patients on these drugs

Conclusion When BP or sodium falls, renin from the kidney starts a chain – angiotensinogen → angiotensin I → angiotensin II → aldosterone – that constricts vessels and retains salt and water, restoring blood pressure.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Explain the physiology of micturition.
answer_html:
Introduction Micturition is the act of emptying the urinary bladder. It is basically a spinal reflex that is controlled voluntarily by higher centres in the brain after early childhood.

1. Filling of the bladder

  • Urine enters the bladder from the ureters by peristalsis
  • During filling the detrusor muscle relaxes (sympathetic action) and the internal sphincter stays closed, so pressure in the bladder rises very little at first
  • The external sphincter is kept closed voluntarily

2. Sensation of filling

  • First desire to pass urine at about 150–200 ml
  • Strong desire at about 300–400 ml
  • Discomfort and pain when the bladder is over-distended
  • Normal capacity about 500 ml

3. Micturition reflex

  1. Stretch receptors in the bladder wall are stimulated as it fills
  2. Impulses travel through the pelvic nerves to the sacral segments S2–S4 of the spinal cord
  3. Parasympathetic impulses return through the pelvic nerves → the detrusor contracts and the internal sphincter relaxes
  4. The reflex strengthens itself (positive feedback) once it starts

4. Voluntary control

  • The pontine micturition centre coordinates the reflex
  • The cerebral cortex can inhibit the reflex until a suitable time and place, by keeping the external sphincter contracted (pudendal nerve)
  • When convenient, the cortex removes inhibition, the external sphincter relaxes and the abdominal muscles contract to help emptying
  • The bladder empties almost completely (residual urine less than about 50 ml)

5. Development

  • Infants pass urine by pure reflex
  • Voluntary control develops by about 2–3 years (toilet training)

6. Disorders

  • Retention of urine – after surgery and anaesthesia, enlarged prostate, urethral stricture, spinal cord injury
  • Incontinence – stress incontinence (weak pelvic floor), urge incontinence, overflow incontinence
  • Automatic (reflex) bladder – spinal cord injury above the sacral segments; the bladder empties by reflex without control
  • Atonic bladder – damage to the sacral segments or nerves; the bladder overfills and dribbles
  • Nocturnal enuresis – bed-wetting in children

7. Nursing importance

  • Encourage voiding with privacy, an upright position, running tap water, a warm bedpan and pouring warm water over the perineum
  • Catheterise if retention persists
  • Bladder training – regular voiding schedule; pelvic floor exercises
  • Record intake and output

Conclusion Micturition is a sacral spinal reflex – stretch of the bladder causes detrusor contraction – controlled voluntarily by the brain through the external sphincter; disorders of this pathway cause retention or incontinence.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Explain the role of the kidneys in maintaining homeostasis.
answer_html:
Introduction The kidneys are the main organs that keep the internal environment constant. They do far more than form urine – they regulate water, salts, acids and blood pressure and produce important hormones.

1. Excretion of waste products

  • Remove urea (from proteins), creatinine (from muscle), uric acid (from nucleic acids), bile pigments, drugs and toxins

2. Regulation of water balance

  • Under the control of ADH, the kidneys produce concentrated urine when the body needs water and dilute urine when there is excess water
  • Urine volume can vary from about 0.5 to several litres a day

3. Regulation of electrolytes

  • Control the levels of sodium (aldosterone), potassium, calcium (parathormone), phosphate and magnesium

4. Regulation of acid–base balance

  • Secrete hydrogen ions into urine
  • Reabsorb and generate bicarbonate
  • Excrete acid as ammonium
  • Keep blood pH at 7.35–7.45

5. Regulation of blood pressure

  • Through the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system
  • By controlling blood volume through salt and water excretion

6. Endocrine functions

  • Erythropoietin – stimulates red blood cell formation
  • Calcitriol (active vitamin D) – calcium absorption and bone health
  • Renin – blood pressure control
  • Prostaglandins

7. Metabolic function

  • Gluconeogenesis during prolonged fasting

8. Applied / nursing importance – chronic kidney disease Loss of these functions explains the features of kidney failure:

  • Raised urea and creatinine (uraemia) – nausea, itching, confusion
  • Oedema and fluid overload
  • Hypertension
  • Hyperkalaemia – dangerous heart rhythms
  • Metabolic acidosis – deep breathing
  • Anaemia – lack of erythropoietin
  • Bone disease – lack of active vitamin D
  • Nursing: fluid and salt restriction, daily weight, intake–output chart, BP monitoring, care of dialysis access

Conclusion The kidneys maintain homeostasis by excreting wastes and regulating water, electrolytes, acid–base balance and blood pressure, and by producing erythropoietin, renin and active vitamin D.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Describe the mechanism of urine formation. (2 + 3 + 3 + 2)
answer_html:
Introduction Urine is formed by the nephrons – about one million in each kidney. The kidneys receive about 1.2 litres of blood per minute (20–25% of cardiac output). From this, about 180 litres of filtrate is formed every day, but 99% of it is taken back, so only about 1–1.5 litres of urine is passed. Urine formation takes place in three main steps, plus concentration of urine.

(a) Glomerular filtration (2 marks) 1. Definition – the filtration of plasma from the glomerular capillaries into Bowman's capsule.

2. Filtration membrane – three layers:

  • Endothelium of the glomerular capillaries (with pores)
  • Basement membrane
  • Podocytes of Bowman's capsule (with filtration slits)
  • It allows water and small solutes (glucose, amino acids, salts, urea) to pass, but holds back blood cells and most plasma proteins

3. Forces

  • Glomerular capillary pressure (about 55–60 mm Hg) pushes fluid out – high because the efferent arteriole is narrower than the afferent
  • Opposed by plasma oncotic pressure (about 25–30 mm Hg) and Bowman's capsule pressure (about 15 mm Hg)
  • Net filtration pressure is about 10–15 mm Hg

4. GFR – about 125 ml/min (180 L/day)

5. Autoregulation – GFR stays nearly constant over a wide range of blood pressure (about 80–180 mm Hg mean pressure); below this range, filtration falls (shock → low urine output)

6. Glomerular filtrate – similar to plasma but almost free of proteins.

(b) Tubular reabsorption (3 marks) Definition – the return of useful substances from the tubules into the blood of the peritubular capillaries. About 99% of the filtrate is reabsorbed.

1. Proximal convoluted tubule (PCT) – the main site

  • Reabsorbs about 65–70% of water and sodium
  • 100% of glucose and amino acids (with sodium – secondary active transport)
  • Most bicarbonate, potassium, chloride, phosphate and some urea
  • Glucose is reabsorbed completely only up to a limit; when blood glucose exceeds about 180 mg/dl (renal threshold), glucose appears in urine (glycosuria)

2. Loop of Henle

  • Descending limb – permeable to water; water leaves into the salty medulla
  • Thick ascending limb – actively pumps out sodium, potassium and chloride but is impermeable to water
  • This creates a high salt concentration in the medulla (countercurrent mechanism) and makes the tubular fluid dilute

3. Distal convoluted tubule (DCT) and collecting duct

  • Aldosterone increases sodium reabsorption (water follows)
  • Parathormone increases calcium reabsorption
  • ADH makes the collecting duct permeable to water

Types of water reabsorption

  • Obligatory (about 85–87%) – in the PCT and loop; not under hormonal control
  • Facultative (about 13%) – in the DCT and collecting duct; controlled by ADH according to the body's needs

(c) Tubular secretion (3 marks) Definition – the transfer of substances from the blood into the tubular fluid. It removes substances that were not filtered enough and helps regulate blood composition.

Substances secreted

  • Hydrogen ions (H⁺) – to keep blood pH normal
  • Potassium (K⁺) – in the DCT and collecting duct, under aldosterone
  • Ammonia – buffers acid in urine
  • Creatinine
  • Drugs and toxins – penicillin, para-aminohippuric acid, many others

Concentration of urine

  • The salty medulla (created by the loop of Henle) and the action of ADH on the collecting ducts allow water to be reabsorbed
  • Dehydration → more ADH → small volume of concentrated urine
  • Excess water intake → less ADH → large volume of dilute urine
  • Urine can range from very dilute to about four times as concentrated as plasma

(d) Normal urine and applied aspects (2 marks) Normal urine

  • Volume: about 1–1.5 litres a day
  • Colour: pale yellow (urochrome); clear
  • Reaction: slightly acidic (pH about 6)
  • Specific gravity: about 1.010–1.025
  • Constituents: water (about 95%), urea, creatinine, uric acid, sodium, potassium, chloride, phosphate
  • Volume terms: oliguria – less than 400 ml/day; anuria – less than 100 ml/day; polyuria – more than 3 litres/day

Applied / nursing importance

  • Diuretics act at different sites – furosemide on the loop of Henle (powerful), thiazides on the DCT, spironolactone on the collecting duct (potassium-sparing)
  • Low urine output in shock reflects poor kidney perfusion – measure hourly urine output (at least 0.5 ml/kg/hour in adults)
  • Glycosuria in diabetes; proteinuria in glomerular damage and pre-eclampsia
  • Acute kidney injury after dehydration, sepsis, nephrotoxic drugs
  • Maintain intake–output charts and test urine as ordered

Conclusion Urine is formed by glomerular filtration of plasma, reabsorption of about 99% of the filtrate (mostly in the PCT) and secretion of unwanted substances, and it is finally concentrated in the collecting ducts under ADH; by adjusting these steps the kidneys keep the body's fluids constant.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: What are the characteristics of normal urine?
answer_html:
Introduction Urine is the fluid excreted by the kidneys. Its normal characteristics are:

  1. Volume – about 1–1.5 litres per day (at least 0.5 ml/kg/hour in adults)
  2. Colour – pale yellow to amber (due to urochrome); clear when fresh
  3. Odour – faintly aromatic; ammoniacal on standing (bacteria break down urea)
  4. Reaction (pH) – slightly acidic, about 6 (range 4.5–8); more alkaline on a vegetarian diet
  5. Specific gravity – about 1.010–1.025
  6. Composition – about 95% water; the main solute is urea, with creatinine, uric acid, sodium, potassium, chloride, phosphates and sulphates
  7. Normally absent – glucose, protein (only traces), ketone bodies, blood, pus cells and bile pigments

subject: Applied Physiology
question: What is the renal threshold for glucose?
answer_html:
Definition The renal threshold for glucose is the blood glucose level above which glucose begins to appear in the urine (glycosuria). It is about 180 mg/dl.

Mechanism

  • Glucose is freely filtered and normally completely reabsorbed in the proximal convoluted tubule by carrier proteins
  • These carriers have a limit – the tubular maximum for glucose (about 375 mg/min)
  • When the filtered glucose exceeds this, the excess spills into the urine

Applied

  1. Diabetes mellitus – glycosuria when blood glucose is above about 180 mg/dl
  2. Renal glycosuria – glucose in urine with normal blood glucose (low threshold); may occur in pregnancy
  3. SGLT2 inhibitors (dapagliflozin, empagliflozin) lower blood sugar by causing glycosuria

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Define polyuria, oliguria, anuria and nocturia.
answer_html:
1. Polyuria – urine output more than about 3 litres per day
    • Causes: diabetes mellitus, diabetes insipidus, diuretics, excess fluid intake, recovery phase of acute kidney injury
  2. Oliguria – urine output less than 400 ml per day (or below 0.5 ml/kg/hour)
    • Causes: dehydration, shock, acute kidney injury, heart failure
  3. Anuria – urine output less than 100 ml per day or complete absence
    • Causes: bilateral urinary obstruction, severe acute kidney injury, mismatched blood transfusion
  4. Nocturia – waking at night to pass urine more than once
    • Causes: old age, enlarged prostate, heart failure, diabetes, urinary infection, evening diuretics or fluids

Nursing: maintain an accurate intake–output chart; report an hourly urine output below 30 ml.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Define renal clearance.
answer_html:
Definition Renal clearance of a substance is the volume of plasma completely cleared of that substance by the kidneys per minute.

Formula

  • C = (U × V) ÷ P
  • U = concentration in urine, V = urine flow (ml/min), P = concentration in plasma

Important clearances

  1. Inulin clearance = GFR (about 125 ml/min) – inulin is filtered but neither reabsorbed nor secreted
  2. Creatinine clearance – used clinically to estimate GFR; normal about 100–125 ml/min; needs a 24-hour urine collection
  3. PAH (para-aminohippuric acid) clearance = renal plasma flow (about 600–650 ml/min)

Applied: doses of many drugs are reduced when clearance is low; estimated GFR is used to stage chronic kidney disease.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: What is diuresis? Name the types of diuretics.
answer_html:
Definition Diuresis is an increased formation and flow of urine.

Types of diuresis

  1. Water diuresis – after drinking a large amount of water, ADH is suppressed → large volume of dilute urine
  2. Osmotic diuresis – unabsorbed solutes hold water in the tubules – glucose in uncontrolled diabetes, mannitol

Diuretic drugs

  1. Loop diuretics – furosemide (most powerful)
  2. Thiazides – hydrochlorothiazide, chlorthalidone
  3. Potassium-sparing – spironolactone, amiloride
  4. Osmotic – mannitol (raised intracranial pressure)
  5. Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors – acetazolamide (glaucoma) - Alcohol causes diuresis by inhibiting ADH

Nursing: give diuretics in the morning; daily weight, intake–output chart and serum potassium.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Explain the factors affecting glomerular filtration rate (GFR).
answer_html:
Introduction The glomerular filtration rate (GFR) is the volume of filtrate formed by both kidneys per minute – normally about 125 ml/min (about 180 litres per day), of which about 99% is reabsorbed. GFR depends on the net filtration pressure, the renal blood flow and the filtration membrane.

1. Net filtration pressure

  • Glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure (about 55–60 mmHg) – favours filtration
  • Plasma colloid osmotic pressure (about 25–30 mmHg) – opposes filtration
  • Bowman's capsule pressure (about 15 mmHg) – opposes filtration
  • Net filtration pressure = about 10–20 mmHg; any factor that changes these forces changes GFR

2. Factors affecting GFR

a. Renal blood flow

  • About 1.2–1.3 litres per minute (about one-fifth to one-quarter of the cardiac output); more flow → higher GFR

b. Glomerular capillary pressure

  • Falls with a severe fall in systemic BP (shock, haemorrhage)
  • Afferent arteriole constriction → GFR falls (sympathetic stimulation; NSAIDs, which block the dilating prostaglandins)
  • Efferent arteriole constriction (angiotensin II) → GFR is maintained or rises; ACE inhibitors relax it and may lower GFR in dehydration

c. Plasma colloid osmotic pressure

  • Low plasma proteins (malnutrition, liver disease) → GFR rises
  • Dehydration (concentrated plasma proteins) → GFR falls

d. Bowman's capsule pressure

  • Raised in urinary obstruction – stones, enlarged prostate → GFR falls (hydronephrosis)

e. Filtration membrane

  • Reduced surface area or permeability – glomerulonephritis, diabetic nephropathy, loss of nephrons in chronic kidney disease and ageing → GFR falls

f. Nervous and hormonal factors

  • Strong sympathetic stimulation (haemorrhage, shock, severe exercise) → GFR falls
  • Atrial natriuretic peptide increases GFR; angiotensin II and prostaglandins also influence it

3. Autoregulation

  • GFR and renal blood flow stay nearly constant while mean arterial pressure varies between about 80 and 180 mmHg
  • Myogenic mechanism – the afferent arteriole contracts when stretched by high pressure
  • Tubuloglomerular feedback – the macula densa senses the salt in the distal tubule and adjusts the afferent arteriole
  • Below about 80 mmHg (shock), GFR falls sharply → oliguria

4. Applied and nursing importance

  • Shock and hypotension → prerenal acute kidney injury; hourly urine output must stay at least 0.5 ml/kg/hour
  • NSAIDs and ACE inhibitors in dehydrated elderly patients increase the risk of kidney injury
  • Estimated GFR (from serum creatinine) is used to stage chronic kidney disease; very low GFR needs dialysis

Conclusion GFR depends on the net filtration pressure (glomerular capillary pressure, plasma oncotic pressure, capsular pressure), renal blood flow, afferent and efferent arteriolar tone and the filtration membrane; autoregulation keeps it steady over a wide range of BP.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Explain the renal function tests.
answer_html:
Introduction Renal function tests (kidney function tests) assess how well the kidneys filter blood, excrete wastes, concentrate urine and maintain the internal environment. They help in diagnosis, in monitoring kidney disease and in adjusting drug doses.

A. Urine examination

  1. Physical – volume (24-hour), colour, appearance, specific gravity (1.010–1.025), pH
  2. Chemical – protein (albuminuria; microalbuminuria is an early sign of diabetic kidney disease), glucose, ketones, blood, bile salts and pigments
  3. Microscopic – red cells, pus cells, casts (red cell casts suggest glomerulonephritis), crystals
  4. Culture and sensitivity – for urinary tract infection

B. Blood tests

  1. Blood urea – about 15–40 mg/dl; raised in kidney failure, dehydration, gastrointestinal bleeding and high-protein diet
  2. Serum creatinine – about 0.6–1.2 mg/dl (lower in women); a better indicator of kidney function than urea, as it is less affected by diet
  3. Serum electrolytes – sodium (135–145 mEq/L), potassium (3.5–5 mEq/L) – hyperkalaemia is dangerous in kidney failure – and bicarbonate
  4. Uric acid, calcium, phosphate; haemoglobin (anaemia in chronic kidney disease)

C. Tests of glomerular filtration

  1. Creatinine clearance – 24-hour urine creatinine with blood creatinine; normal about 100–125 ml/min
  2. Estimated GFR (eGFR) – calculated from serum creatinine, age and sex; used to stage chronic kidney disease

D. Tests of tubular function

  1. Urine concentration test (water deprivation test) – normal kidneys concentrate urine to a specific gravity above about 1.025
  2. Urine dilution test and urine osmolality - In advanced kidney disease the specific gravity stays fixed at about 1.010

E. Imaging and other tests

  • Ultrasound of kidneys, ureters and bladder (size, stones, obstruction), X-ray KUB, CT scan
  • Intravenous pyelography, isotope renogram, renal biopsy

F. Nursing responsibilities

  • Explain the test; collect the correct sample:
    • early morning sample for routine examination
    • midstream clean-catch sample in a sterile container for culture; send within an hour or refrigerate
    • 24-hour collection – discard the first morning urine, then collect all urine for 24 hours including the final specimen; keep it cool; add preservative if required; label correctly
  • Before contrast studies – check allergy and serum creatinine, ensure hydration; metformin may be withheld as ordered
  • After renal biopsy – bed rest, monitor vital signs and watch the urine for blood

Conclusion Renal function is assessed by urine examination, blood urea, serum creatinine and electrolytes, creatinine clearance and eGFR, tests of concentrating ability and imaging; correct sample collection by the nurse is essential for reliable results.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Describe the changes in renal function in old age and their nursing implications.
answer_html:
Introduction The kidneys age gradually like other organs. In health, function remains adequate, but the reserve falls, so elderly people easily develop dehydration, electrolyte imbalance, drug toxicity and kidney injury during illness.

A. Structural changes

  • Kidney mass decreases, mainly the cortex
  • The number of functioning glomeruli falls; many become scarred (glomerulosclerosis)
  • Tubules shorten; renal arteries become thickened and narrowed

B. Functional changes

  1. GFR falls steadily with age (roughly 1 ml/min each year after about 40, varying widely)
    • Serum creatinine may look normal because muscle mass also falls – so creatinine clearance or eGFR is a better guide
  2. Renal blood flow falls
  3. Poor concentrating ability – less response to ADH and a reduced thirst sensation → nocturia and easy dehydration
  4. Poor sodium conservation and poor diluting ability – risk of both low and high sodium
  5. Reduced excretion of acid and potassium – risk of acidosis and hyperkalaemia, especially with ACE inhibitors or spironolactone
  6. Less activation of vitamin D – contributes to osteoporosis
  7. Slower drug excretion – drugs such as digoxin, aminoglycosides, metformin and lithium accumulate and cause toxicity

C. Changes in the bladder and urinary tract

  • Smaller bladder capacity, overactive bladder muscle → urgency and frequency
  • Incomplete emptying (residual urine) → urinary tract infections
  • Weak pelvic floor in women → stress incontinence
  • Enlarged prostate in men → hesitancy, poor stream, retention

D. Nursing implications

  • Encourage adequate fluids (about 1.5–2 litres a day unless restricted); offer drinks regularly, as thirst is weak; reduce fluids in the late evening to limit nocturia
  • Monitor intake–output, weight and signs of dehydration (dry tongue, confusion, low urine output)
  • Drug safety – doses adjusted to kidney function; avoid NSAIDs; extra care with contrast media
  • Continence care – toileting schedule, bladder training, pelvic floor exercises, easy access to the toilet and a night light to prevent falls
  • Watch for urinary infection, which in the elderly may show only as confusion; good perineal hygiene; avoid unnecessary catheterisation

Conclusion Ageing reduces kidney mass, GFR, concentrating ability and drug excretion, and the bladder becomes smaller and less efficient; careful fluid management, drug dosing and continence care protect the elderly patient.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Explain the mechanism of concentration of urine. Describe the counter-current mechanism and the role of ADH. (2 + 5 + 2 + 1)
answer_html:
(a) Introduction (2 marks)

  • Plasma osmolality is about 290–300 mOsm/L
  • The kidneys can excrete urine as dilute as about 50–100 mOsm/L (when the body has excess water) or as concentrated as about 1200–1400 mOsm/L (when water must be saved)
  • This ability to concentrate urine conserves water during dehydration and keeps plasma osmolality constant
  • To excrete the daily solute load (about 600 mOsm), at least about 500 ml of urine per day must be passed – the obligatory urine volume
  • Two things are needed to concentrate urine:
    1. a highly concentrated (hyperosmotic) medullary interstitium, built up by the counter-current mechanism
    2. ADH, which makes the collecting ducts permeable to water

(b) Counter-current mechanism (5 marks) "Counter-current" means that fluid flows in opposite directions in two limbs lying close and parallel to each other – the descending and ascending limbs of the loop of Henle, and the descending and ascending vasa recta. The juxtamedullary nephrons, whose long loops dip deep into the medulla, are mainly responsible.

1. Counter-current multiplier – the loop of Henle

  • Thick ascending limb:
    • actively pumps sodium, potassium and chloride (Na⁺–K⁺–2Cl⁻ co-transporter) out into the interstitium
    • is impermeable to water
    • so the interstitium becomes concentrated, while the tubular fluid becomes dilute (about 100 mOsm/L) by the time it reaches the distal tubule – hence it is called the "diluting segment"
  • Descending limb:
    • is permeable to water but relatively impermeable to salt
    • water moves out into the concentrated interstitium, so the tubular fluid becomes more and more concentrated, reaching about 1200 mOsm/L at the tip of the loop
  • This process is repeated continuously as fluid flows round the loop – it is "multiplied" – building an osmotic gradient from about 300 mOsm/L at the corticomedullary junction to about 1200 mOsm/L in the inner medulla
  • The longer the loop, the greater the gradient (desert animals have very long loops)

2. Role of urea (urea recycling)

  • Under the influence of ADH, urea passes out of the inner medullary collecting duct into the interstitium
  • It provides nearly half of the osmolality of the inner medulla; part of it re-enters the loop and recirculates
  • A very low-protein diet reduces urea and so reduces the ability to concentrate urine

3. Counter-current exchanger – the vasa recta

  • The vasa recta are hairpin-shaped capillaries arising from the efferent arterioles of juxtamedullary nephrons, running beside the loops
  • As blood flows down, it gains salt and loses water; as it flows up, it gives back salt and regains water
  • So the vasa recta supply the medulla with blood without washing away the solutes – the gradient is preserved
  • Blood flow in the vasa recta is slow (only a small fraction of renal blood flow), which helps

4. Final concentration in the collecting duct

  • The collecting duct passes down through this concentrated medulla
  • With ADH, water leaves the duct by osmosis → small volume of concentrated urine (up to about 1200–1400 mOsm/L)
  • Without ADH, the duct stays impermeable → large volume of dilute urine

(c) Role of ADH (2 marks)

  • Antidiuretic hormone (vasopressin) is made in the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei of the hypothalamus and released from the posterior pituitary
  • Stimuli – rise in plasma osmolality (sensed by hypothalamic osmoreceptors), fall in blood volume or BP, pain, nausea, stress, morphine
  • Inhibited by – excess water intake, alcohol, cold
  • Action:
    • binds to receptors on the cells of the late distal tubule and collecting duct
    • causes water channels (aquaporin-2) to be inserted into the luminal membrane
    • water is reabsorbed into the concentrated interstitium → urine becomes concentrated and its volume falls
    • increases the permeability of the inner medullary collecting duct to urea, strengthening the gradient
  • This ADH-dependent reabsorption is called facultative water reabsorption (it varies with the body's needs), unlike the obligatory reabsorption in the proximal tubule and descending limb

(d) Applied importance (1 mark)

  • Diabetes insipidus – lack of ADH or kidney unresponsiveness → large volumes of dilute urine (specific gravity below about 1.005), thirst
  • SIADH – excess ADH → water retention and low serum sodium
  • Loop diuretics (furosemide) block the pump in the thick ascending limb, destroying the medullary gradient → heavy diuresis
  • Chronic kidney disease and old age – poor concentrating ability → nocturia; specific gravity fixed at about 1.010
  • Alcohol suppresses ADH → diuresis
  • Tests – urine specific gravity and osmolality, water deprivation test
  • Nursing – accurate intake–output, daily weight and urine specific gravity in patients with polyuria or after pituitary surgery and head injury

Conclusion Urine is concentrated by the counter-current multiplier of the loop of Henle, which builds a medullary gradient of about 300 to 1200 mOsm/L, aided by urea recycling and preserved by the counter-current exchange in the vasa recta; ADH then makes the collecting ducts permeable so that water is reabsorbed and a small volume of concentrated urine is passed.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Write the functions of the placenta.
answer_html:
Introduction The placenta is a temporary organ formed in pregnancy that connects the foetus with the mother's uterus through the umbilical cord.

Functions

  1. Respiratory – supplies oxygen to the foetus and removes carbon dioxide
  2. Nutritive – transfers glucose, amino acids, fats, vitamins and minerals
  3. Excretory – removes foetal waste such as urea
  4. Endocrine – secretes hCG, human placental lactogen, oestrogen and progesterone
  5. Protective (barrier) – blocks many microbes; passes maternal IgG antibodies (passive immunity); but some drugs, alcohol and viruses can cross
  6. Storage – glycogen and iron

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Define ovulation and list its signs.
answer_html:
Definition Ovulation is the release of a mature ovum (secondary oocyte) from the Graafian follicle of the ovary. In a 28-day cycle it occurs about the 14th day (about 14 days before the next period), triggered by the LH surge.

Signs of ovulation

  1. Rise in basal body temperature by about 0.3–0.5 °C after ovulation (effect of progesterone)
  2. Cervical mucus becomes clear, thin and stretchy (like raw egg white)
  3. Mid-cycle pain (mittelschmerz) on one side of the lower abdomen
  4. Slight spotting, breast tenderness

Applied: the ovum lives for about 12–24 hours; the days around ovulation are the fertile period – used in natural family planning and infertility care.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: State the functions of testosterone.
answer_html:
Introduction Testosterone is the main male sex hormone, secreted by the Leydig (interstitial) cells of the testes under the control of LH.

Functions

  1. Before birth – development of the male genital organs and descent of the testes into the scrotum
  2. At puberty – growth of the penis and testes; secondary sexual characters: beard and body hair, deep voice, broad shoulders, muscular build
  3. Spermatogenesis – together with FSH
  4. Sex drive (libido)
  5. Anabolic – increases protein synthesis, muscle mass and bone growth; finally closes the epiphyses
  6. Increases red blood cell production
  7. Increases sebaceous secretion (acne at puberty)

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Explain the functions of oestrogen and progesterone.
answer_html:
Introduction Oestrogen and progesterone are the female sex hormones. They are secreted by the ovary – oestrogen by the growing follicles, progesterone mainly by the corpus luteum – and in pregnancy in large amounts by the placenta. They control the menstrual cycle, pregnancy and female body characteristics.

A. Functions of oestrogen ("hormone of femininity")

  1. Puberty – growth of the uterus, tubes and vagina; development of the breasts (ducts and fat); female fat distribution (hips and thighs); broadening of the pelvis
  2. Menstrual cycle – causes the proliferative phase: rebuilds and thickens the endometrium after menstruation
  3. Cervical mucus – makes it thin, watery and stretchy, so sperm can pass easily at ovulation
  4. Vagina – thickens and strengthens the vaginal lining
  5. Uterus – increases muscle excitability and sensitivity to oxytocin
  6. Bones – maintains bone density; closes the epiphyses (loss after menopause → osteoporosis)
  7. Blood vessels – raises "good" cholesterol (HDL), protects against heart disease before menopause
  8. Feedback – a high level just before ovulation triggers the LH surge (positive feedback)
  9. Causes some salt and water retention

B. Functions of progesterone ("hormone of pregnancy")

  1. Menstrual cycle – converts the endometrium into the secretory phase: glands secrete nutrients, lining becomes soft and ready for implantation
  2. Maintenance of pregnancy – keeps the endometrium (decidua) intact
  3. Relaxes uterine muscle – reduces contractions, preventing early expulsion of the foetus
  4. Cervical mucus – makes it thick and sticky, blocking sperm and infection
  5. Breasts – development of the milk-secreting alveoli
  6. Raises body temperature by about 0.3–0.5 °C after ovulation
  7. Feedback – inhibits LH and FSH (prevents further ovulation) – the basis of oral contraceptive pills
  8. Relaxes smooth muscle elsewhere – constipation and heartburn in pregnancy

C. Comparison

Oestrogen Progesterone
from growing follicles from corpus luteum (and placenta)
proliferative phase secretory phase
thin cervical mucus thick cervical mucus
increases uterine activity relaxes the uterus
breast ducts breast alveoli

D. Applied / nursing importance

  • Oral contraceptive pills (combined oestrogen + progestin; progestin-only pills)
  • Menopause – fall in oestrogen → hot flushes, vaginal dryness, osteoporosis, higher heart risk
  • Hormone therapy in some menstrual disorders and infertility
  • Progesterone support in threatened abortion (as prescribed)

Conclusion Oestrogen builds and feminises – it develops female characters and the proliferative endometrium – while progesterone prepares and protects – it makes the endometrium secretory and maintains pregnancy.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Describe spermatogenesis and the composition of semen.

diagram.caption: Stages of spermatogenesis
labels: Sertoli cell; structure of sperm - head with acrosome

answer_html:
Introduction Spermatogenesis is the process of formation of mature sperm (spermatozoa) from the germ cells in the seminiferous tubules of the testes. It begins at puberty and continues throughout life. One complete cycle takes about 64–74 days.

1. Stages of spermatogenesis

  1. Spermatogonia (46 chromosomes) – stem cells near the basement membrane; divide by mitosis to keep a supply
  2. Primary spermatocytes (46) – grow and enter the first meiotic division
  3. Secondary spermatocytes (23) – formed by meiosis I; quickly undergo the second meiotic division
  4. Spermatids (23) – formed by meiosis II
  5. Spermiogenesis – spermatids change into spermatozoa: the nucleus condenses into the head, an acrosome (enzyme cap) forms, mitochondria gather in the middle piece and a tail grows - One primary spermatocyte gives four sperm

2. Structure of a sperm

  • Head – nucleus with 23 chromosomes (X or Y) and the acrosome containing enzymes to penetrate the ovum
  • Middle piece – mitochondria for energy
  • Tail – for movement (swimming)

3. Factors controlling spermatogenesis

  • FSH – acts on Sertoli cells, which nourish developing sperm
  • LH → testosterone (Leydig cells) – essential for sperm production
  • Inhibin from Sertoli cells – negative feedback on FSH
  • Temperature – about 2–3 °C below body temperature (scrotum)
  • Growth hormone, thyroid hormones, good nutrition

4. Maturation

  • Sperm become mature and motile in the epididymis (about 2 weeks)
  • They gain full ability to fertilise (capacitation) in the female tract

5. Semen

  • Volume: about 2–5 ml per ejaculation
  • Reaction: slightly alkaline (pH about 7.2–8) – protects sperm from vaginal acidity
  • Sperm count: normally 15 million or more per ml
  • Composition:
    • Sperm – a small part of the volume
    • Seminal vesicle fluid (about 60%) – fructose (energy for sperm), prostaglandins, clotting proteins
    • Prostatic fluid (about 30%) – thin, milky, alkaline; citrate, enzymes (acid phosphatase)
    • Bulbourethral gland mucus – lubrication
  • Semen clots after ejaculation and liquefies within about 20–30 minutes

6. Applied / nursing importance

  • Oligospermia (low count) and azoospermia (no sperm) – causes of male infertility; semen analysis after 3–5 days of abstinence
  • Heat (tight clothing, hot baths), varicocele, smoking, alcohol and mumps orchitis reduce sperm production
  • Vasectomy – sperm no longer reach the semen; semen volume barely changes; contraception is used until a test shows no sperm
  • Undescended testes in childhood should be corrected early

Conclusion Spermatogenesis converts spermatogonia through spermatocytes and spermatids into sperm in the seminiferous tubules under FSH and testosterone; sperm mixed with fluid from the seminal vesicles, prostate and bulbourethral glands form semen.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Explain fertilisation and implantation.
answer_html:
Introduction Fertilisation is the fusion of a sperm with an ovum to form a zygote. Implantation is the embedding of the developing embryo (blastocyst) in the endometrium of the uterus. Together they mark the beginning of pregnancy.

A. Fertilisation 1. Site and time

  • Usually in the ampulla of the fallopian tube
  • Within about 12–24 hours of ovulation (the ovum's lifespan); sperm survive about 2–3 days in the female tract

2. Steps

  1. Transport of sperm – millions of sperm deposited in the vagina; only a few hundred reach the ampulla
  2. Capacitation – changes in the sperm in the female tract that make them able to fertilise
  3. Acrosome reaction – enzymes released from the acrosome (hyaluronidase, acrosin) digest a path through the corona radiata and zona pellucida
  4. Fusion – one sperm fuses with the ovum's membrane and its nucleus enters
  5. Block to polyspermy – the zona pellucida changes immediately so that no other sperm can enter
  6. Completion of meiosis – the ovum completes its second meiotic division
  7. Fusion of nuclei – male and female pronuclei unite → zygote with 46 chromosomes

3. Results

  • Restores the diploid number (46)
  • Sex is determined – an X-bearing sperm gives a girl (XX), a Y-bearing sperm a boy (XY)
  • Starts cleavage (cell division)

B. From zygote to blastocyst

  • The zygote divides repeatedly as it moves along the tube
  • About day 3–4: a ball of 16 cells (morula) enters the uterus
  • About day 5: a hollow blastocyst forms – an inner cell mass (future embryo) and an outer layer, the trophoblast (future placenta)

C. Implantation 1. Time – about 6–7 days after fertilisation (around day 20–21 of a 28-day cycle); completed by about day 10–11

2. Site – usually the upper part of the posterior wall of the uterine body

3. Process

  • The blastocyst attaches to the endometrium (now called decidua)
  • The trophoblast invades the endometrium and the embryo becomes completely buried in it (interstitial implantation)
  • The trophoblast secretes hCG, which keeps the corpus luteum alive, so progesterone continues and menstruation does not occur
  • hCG is the basis of the urine pregnancy test
  • Slight spotting (implantation bleeding) may occur

D. Applied / nursing importance

  • Ectopic pregnancy – implantation outside the uterus, commonest in the fallopian tube (ampulla); rupture causes severe pain and internal bleeding – an emergency
  • IVF – fertilisation outside the body and transfer of the embryo
  • Contraception acts at these steps – barrier methods prevent sperm meeting the ovum; IUCDs prevent fertilisation and implantation; emergency pills delay ovulation
  • Twins – two ova (non-identical) or division of one embryo (identical)

Conclusion Fertilisation in the ampulla unites sperm and ovum to form a zygote that develops into a blastocyst; about a week later the blastocyst implants in the endometrium and its hCG maintains the pregnancy.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Describe the menstrual cycle with its phases and hormonal control. (2 + 3 + 3 + 2)

diagram.caption: Menstrual cycle - hormones, ovary and endometrium
labels: FSH and LH curves (LH surge day 14)

answer_html:
(a) Definition and key facts (2 marks)

  • The menstrual cycle is the series of cyclical changes in the ovaries and the endometrium that occur about every 28 days (normal range 21–35 days) in a woman of reproductive age, preparing the body for pregnancy
  • It is counted from the first day of menstrual bleeding
  • Menarche – the first period, usually at about 12–13 years
  • Menopause – the permanent stop of periods, usually at about 45–50 years
  • The cycle includes the ovarian cycle (changes in the follicles) and the uterine (endometrial) cycle (changes in the lining), both controlled by hormones

(b) Hormonal control (3 marks) 1. Hypothalamus – secretes GnRH in pulses

2. Anterior pituitary – in response to GnRH secretes:

  • FSH – stimulates growth of ovarian follicles and oestrogen secretion
  • LH – causes ovulation and formation of the corpus luteum

3. Ovary

  • Growing follicles secrete oestrogen
  • The corpus luteum secretes progesterone (and oestrogen)

4. Feedback

  • Most of the cycle – oestrogen and progesterone inhibit GnRH, FSH and LH (negative feedback)
  • Just before ovulation – a high, sustained level of oestrogen stimulates a sudden LH surge (positive feedback) → ovulation

(c) Phases of the cycle (3 marks)

A. Ovarian cycle

  1. Follicular phase (days 1–14)
    • Under FSH, several follicles begin to grow; one becomes dominant and matures into a Graafian follicle
    • Oestrogen levels rise steadily
  2. Ovulation (about day 14)
    • The LH surge makes the Graafian follicle rupture and release the ovum
  3. Luteal phase (days 15–28)
    • The ruptured follicle becomes the corpus luteum, which secretes progesterone and oestrogen
    • The luteal phase is fairly constant at about 14 days
    • No pregnancy → corpus luteum degenerates into the corpus albicans → hormones fall → menstruation
    • Pregnancy → hCG from the embryo keeps the corpus luteum active

B. Uterine (endometrial) cycle

  1. Menstrual phase (days 1–5)
    • Fall of progesterone and oestrogen → the spiral arteries constrict → the functional layer of the endometrium dies and is shed with blood
    • Blood loss about 30–80 ml; it does not clot because of fibrinolysins
  2. Proliferative (pre-ovulatory) phase (days 6–14)
    • Under oestrogen the endometrium regenerates from the basal layer
    • Glands and blood vessels grow; the lining thickens
    • Cervical mucus becomes thin and stretchy
  3. Secretory (post-ovulatory) phase (days 15–28)
    • Under progesterone the glands become coiled and secrete glycogen-rich fluid
    • The stroma becomes swollen and the spiral arteries coil
    • The endometrium is soft, thick and ready for implantation
    • Cervical mucus becomes thick

C. Summary table

Days Ovary Endometrium Main hormone
1–5 new follicles start menstrual (shedding) low oestrogen, progesterone
6–14 follicular growth proliferative oestrogen
~14 ovulation – LH surge
15–28 corpus luteum secretory progesterone

D. Other cyclical changes

  • Basal body temperature rises by about 0.3–0.5 °C after ovulation
  • Breast fullness and tenderness before periods
  • Mood changes (premenstrual syndrome)

(d) Applied / nursing importance (2 marks)

  • Amenorrhoea – pregnancy is the commonest cause; others: PCOS, anaemia, stress, extreme weight loss, thyroid disease
  • Dysmenorrhoea (painful periods), menorrhagia (heavy bleeding), irregular cycles
  • Fertile period (days around ovulation) – used in natural family planning and infertility treatment
  • Contraceptive pills prevent ovulation by suppressing FSH and LH
  • Menstrual hygiene – sanitary pads, privacy, safe disposal (Menstrual Hygiene Scheme for adolescent girls)
  • Anaemia in adolescent girls due to menstrual loss – weekly iron and folic acid supplementation (WIFS)
  • Teach girls about normal menstruation before menarche

Conclusion The menstrual cycle is a monthly rhythm controlled by GnRH, FSH, LH, oestrogen and progesterone; the ovary passes through follicular, ovulatory and luteal phases while the endometrium passes through menstrual, proliferative and secretory phases, preparing each month for a possible pregnancy.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Define menarche. Give its normal age and the factors affecting it.
answer_html:
Definition Menarche is the first menstrual period in a girl's life. It marks the beginning of reproductive life, although the first few cycles are often anovulatory and irregular.

Normal age

  • Usually between 10 and 16 years; in India commonly about 12–13 years
  • It occurs about 2–3 years after breast budding begins

Factors affecting the age of menarche

  1. Nutrition and body fat – well-nourished and overweight girls reach menarche earlier; undernutrition delays it
  2. Heredity – age of the mother's menarche
  3. Socio-economic status and urban living – earlier
  4. Chronic illness and heavy athletic training – later
  5. Hormonal disorders – early or delayed puberty

Nursing: prepare girls beforehand with information on menstrual hygiene, nutrition and when to seek help.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: What is capacitation of sperm?
answer_html:
Definition Capacitation is the process by which ejaculated sperm become capable of fertilising the ovum. It takes place in the female genital tract – the uterus and fallopian tubes – over about 5–7 hours.

Changes during capacitation

  1. Removal of the glycoprotein coat and seminal plasma proteins from the surface of the sperm head
  2. The membrane over the acrosome becomes thinner and more permeable to calcium
  3. Sperm develop hyperactivated motility – strong whip-like tail movements

Importance

  • Only capacitated sperm can undergo the acrosome reaction, releasing enzymes that help them penetrate the corona radiata and zona pellucida
  • In IVF, sperm are capacitated artificially in a culture medium

subject: Applied Physiology
question: What is the corpus luteum? State its functions.
answer_html:
Definition The corpus luteum ("yellow body") is a temporary endocrine gland formed from the ruptured Graafian follicle after ovulation, under the influence of LH. Its cells contain a yellow pigment, lutein.

Functions

  1. Secretes progesterone (mainly) and oestrogen
  2. Converts the endometrium into the secretory phase, preparing it for implantation
  3. Maintains early pregnancy – stimulated by hCG, it keeps secreting hormones until the placenta takes over at about 8–12 weeks
  4. Inhibits FSH and LH by negative feedback

Fate: if pregnancy does not occur, it degenerates after about 10–14 days into a white scar, the corpus albicans; the fall in hormones causes menstruation.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: What is the fertile period?
answer_html:
Definition The fertile period is the part of the menstrual cycle during which intercourse can result in pregnancy.

Basis

  • Ovulation occurs about 14 days before the next period (around day 14 in a 28-day cycle)
  • The ovum survives about 12–24 hours; sperm survive up to about 5 days in the female tract
  • So the fertile period covers about 6 days – the 5 days before ovulation and the day of ovulation; in a regular 28-day cycle, roughly days 10–17

Calendar method: first fertile day = shortest cycle minus 18; last fertile day = longest cycle minus 11.

Signs of ovulation: clear, stretchy cervical mucus; a rise in basal body temperature of about 0.3–0.5 °C after ovulation.

Use: natural family planning, and timing intercourse for couples wishing to conceive.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: What is amenorrhoea? Give its types.
answer_html:
Definition Amenorrhoea is the absence of menstruation in a woman of reproductive age.

Types

  1. Physiological amenorrhoea – before puberty, during pregnancy and lactation, and after menopause
  2. Primary amenorrhoea – menstruation has never started by about 15 years of age (or by 13 years when there are no secondary sexual characters)
    • Causes: Turner syndrome, absent uterus, imperforate hymen (blood collects behind it – cryptomenorrhoea), hormonal disorders
  3. Secondary amenorrhoea – menses stop for 3 months or more in a woman who was menstruating regularly
    • Causes: pregnancy (the commonest), polycystic ovary syndrome, thyroid disorders, high prolactin, severe weight loss, stress, excessive exercise, premature ovarian failure

Nursing: always rule out pregnancy first.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Describe oogenesis.

diagram.caption: Stages of oogenesis
labels: primary oocyte arrested in prophase I
secondary oocyte arrested in metaphase II

answer_html:
Introduction Oogenesis is the process of formation of the mature ovum (female gamete) from the primordial germ cells in the ovary. Unlike spermatogenesis, it begins before birth, pauses for years and is completed only at fertilisation.

Stages

1. Multiplication phase (fetal life)

  • Primordial germ cells reach the ovary and divide by mitosis to form oogonia (46 chromosomes – diploid)
  • The number peaks at about 6–7 million around the fifth month of fetal life

2. Growth phase

  • Oogonia enlarge to form primary oocytes
  • They begin the first meiotic division but stop (are arrested) in prophase I before birth
  • Each primary oocyte is surrounded by a single layer of flat follicular cells – a primordial follicle
  • Numbers: about 1–2 million at birth and about 3–4 lakh at puberty; the rest degenerate (atresia)

3. Maturation phase (from puberty, each month)

  • Under FSH, several follicles develop (primary → secondary → Graafian follicle); usually only one becomes dominant
  • Just before ovulation, the LH surge makes the primary oocyte complete meiosis I:
    • one large secondary oocyte (23 chromosomes – haploid)
    • one small first polar body
  • The secondary oocyte starts meiosis II but is arrested in metaphase II; it is released in this state at ovulation

4. Completion at fertilisation

  • Meiosis II is completed only when a sperm penetrates the secondary oocyte → mature ovum + second polar body
  • The female pronucleus fuses with the male pronucleus → zygote (46 chromosomes)
  • If fertilisation does not occur, the oocyte degenerates within about 24 hours

5. Key features

  • One primary oocyte gives only one ovum (plus two or three polar bodies), whereas one spermatocyte gives four sperm
  • The unequal division of cytoplasm gives the ovum enough food reserve for the early embryo
  • Only about 400–500 oocytes are ovulated in a woman's whole reproductive life

6. Applied importance

  • The long arrest of oocytes increases errors in chromosome separation with age – higher risk of Down syndrome in babies of mothers above 35 years
  • Menopause occurs when the follicles are exhausted
  • Chemotherapy and radiation can destroy oocytes – egg freezing may be offered
  • IVF – mature oocytes are collected after hormonal stimulation

Conclusion Oogenesis begins in fetal life, pauses in prophase I until puberty, produces a secondary oocyte at ovulation and is completed only at fertilisation, giving one ovum and polar bodies from each primary oocyte.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Describe the physiological changes at puberty in boys and girls.
answer_html:
Introduction Puberty is the period during which the reproductive organs mature and secondary sexual characters develop, so that reproduction becomes possible. It usually begins at about 8–13 years in girls and 9–14 years in boys. It is part of adolescence (10–19 years).

1. Hormonal basis

  • The hypothalamus increases the pulsatile secretion of GnRH
  • GnRH → anterior pituitary → FSH and LH
  • In girls, the ovaries secrete oestrogen; in boys, the testes secrete testosterone
  • Adrenal androgens cause pubic and axillary hair
  • Growth hormone rises → growth spurt
  • Adequate body fat and nutrition are needed for puberty to start

2. Changes in girls

  • Breast development (thelarche) – usually the first sign
  • Pubic and axillary hair
  • Growth spurt – earlier than in boys
  • Menarche – about 2–3 years after breast budding
  • Widening of the pelvis; fat deposited on the hips, thighs and breasts – the female body shape
  • Growth of the uterus, vagina and external genitalia; vaginal secretions
  • Oily skin and acne

3. Changes in boys

  • Enlargement of the testes – the first sign; then growth of the penis and scrotum
  • Pubic, axillary and facial hair
  • Growth spurt – later and greater than in girls
  • Deepening of the voice – the larynx enlarges ("Adam's apple")
  • Increase in muscle mass, bone strength and haemoglobin; broad shoulders
  • First ejaculation (spermarche); nocturnal emissions ("wet dreams")
  • Oily skin and acne

4. Psychological and social changes

  • Concern about body image, search for identity and independence
  • Attraction to the opposite sex, mood swings, strong peer influence
  • Risk-taking behaviour

5. Disorders

  • Precocious puberty – before 8 years in girls or 9 years in boys
  • Delayed puberty – no breast development by 13 years in girls, or no testicular enlargement by 14 years in boys

6. Nursing and health education

  • Menstrual hygiene and correct use and disposal of sanitary pads
  • Nutrition – iron-rich diet; weekly iron–folic acid supplementation for adolescents
  • Counselling on body changes, nocturnal emissions, safe behaviour, avoiding tobacco, alcohol and drugs
  • Adolescent-friendly health services under the national adolescent health programme

Conclusion Puberty is driven by GnRH, FSH, LH and the sex hormones; girls show breast development, a growth spurt and menarche, while boys show testicular enlargement, voice change and muscle growth, along with important emotional changes that need guidance.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Explain menopause – its hormonal and physiological changes, with nursing implications.
answer_html:
Introduction Menopause is the permanent cessation of menstruation due to the loss of ovarian follicular activity. It is diagnosed after 12 continuous months without a period. It usually occurs between 45 and 55 years; Indian women often reach it in their mid-to-late forties.

  • Perimenopause (climacteric) – the transition years with irregular cycles before menopause
  • Premature menopause – before 40 years
  • Surgical menopause – after removal of both ovaries

1. Hormonal changes

  • The ovarian follicles are exhausted
  • Oestrogen, progesterone and inhibin fall
  • Loss of negative feedback → FSH and LH rise markedly (a high FSH confirms menopause)
  • After menopause, small amounts of oestrogen (oestrone) are formed in fat tissue from adrenal androgens

2. Physiological changes

  • Menstrual – cycles become irregular, then stop
  • Vasomotor – hot flushes, night sweats, palpitations
  • Genital and urinary – thinning and dryness of the vagina, painful intercourse, itching and infections; urgency, frequency, recurrent urinary infections, stress incontinence; shrinking of the uterus and breasts; weak pelvic floor → prolapse
  • Bones – rapid bone loss → osteoporosis and fractures
