  • Heart and blood vessels – loss of oestrogen's protection; LDL cholesterol rises and the risk of heart disease increases
  • Skin and hair – thin, dry skin; thinning hair
  • Psychological – irritability, mood swings, anxiety, depression, poor sleep and concentration
  • Weight gain around the abdomen

3. Nursing implications

  • Reassure that menopause is a natural phase of life; involve the family
  • Diet rich in calcium, vitamin D and protein; weight-bearing exercise; stop smoking; limit caffeine and alcohol
  • Hot flushes – light cotton clothing, a cool room, avoid triggers such as hot drinks and spicy food
  • Pelvic floor (Kegel) exercises; vaginal lubricants
  • Hormone replacement therapy only on medical advice – it has risks (breast cancer, blood clots)
  • Screening – BP, blood sugar, lipids, bone density, cervical screening and breast examination
  • Postmenopausal bleeding must always be reported – it may indicate endometrial cancer

4. Factors influencing the age of menopause

  • Heredity – age of the mother's menopause
  • Smoking – brings menopause earlier
  • Poor nutrition, chronic illness
  • Chemotherapy, pelvic radiation or removal of the ovaries – early (induced) menopause

5. Role of the nurse in the community

  • Health talks and support groups for women in their forties and fifties
  • Encourage yoga, walking and relaxation for sleep and mood
  • Identify women with severe symptoms, heavy or irregular bleeding, or depression and refer them

Conclusion Menopause results from exhaustion of ovarian follicles, with low oestrogen and high FSH; it brings hot flushes, genitourinary changes, bone loss and cardiovascular risk, which the nurse addresses through education, lifestyle advice and screening.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Describe the physiology of lactation. Add a note on the composition of breast milk and the advantages of breastfeeding. (2 + 3 + 2 + 3)

diagram.caption: Prolactin reflex and milk ejection reflex

answer_html:
(a) Definition and development of the breast (2 marks)

  • Lactation is the secretion and ejection of milk from the mammary glands after childbirth
  • At puberty – oestrogen causes growth of the ducts and fat deposition; progesterone develops the lobules and alveoli
  • During pregnancy – high levels of oestrogen (duct growth), progesterone (alveoli), prolactin, human placental lactogen, cortisol, insulin and growth hormone fully develop the milk-secreting alveoli
  • A little colostrum may be secreted in late pregnancy, but full milk secretion is prevented by the high oestrogen and progesterone, which block the action of prolactin on the breast

(b) Milk secretion (3 marks)

  • Onset – after delivery of the placenta, oestrogen and progesterone fall sharply; prolactin can now act, and milk "comes in" by about the 2nd–4th day
  • Prolactin from the anterior pituitary stimulates the alveolar cells to make milk – lactose, milk proteins (casein, lactalbumin) and fat
  • Prolactin reflex:
    • suckling stimulates nerve endings in the nipple and areola
    • impulses reach the hypothalamus, which reduces dopamine (prolactin-inhibiting hormone)
    • prolactin rises → more milk is made for the next feed
    • prolactin levels are higher at night – so night feeds help milk production
  • Maintenance (galactopoiesis) – depends on frequent, effective suckling and emptying of the breasts – "the more the baby feeds, the more milk is made"; milk left in the breast contains a factor that slows secretion
  • Growth hormone, cortisol, thyroxine and insulin are also needed
  • Prolactin suppresses GnRH → delays ovulation and menstruation (lactational amenorrhoea)
  • Production is about 500–800 ml per day once lactation is established

(c) Milk ejection (let-down) reflex (2 marks)

  • Suckling → impulses to the hypothalamus → posterior pituitary releases oxytocin
  • Oxytocin contracts the myoepithelial cells around the alveoli and ducts → milk is squeezed into the ducts and flows out to the baby
  • It is a neuro-endocrine reflex; it can be conditioned – triggered by the baby's cry or even thinking of the baby
  • It is inhibited by pain, anxiety, worry, embarrassment and fatigue (adrenaline) – so a relaxed, confident mother feeds better
  • Oxytocin also contracts the uterus – helps involution and reduces postpartum bleeding (mothers may feel "after-pains" while feeding)

(d) Composition of breast milk and advantages of breastfeeding (3 marks)

Composition

  • Colostrum – thick, yellow milk of the first 2–4 days; small in volume but rich in protein, antibodies (secretory IgA), white cells, vitamin A and minerals; less fat and sugar; mild laxative – helps pass meconium; called the baby's "first immunisation"
  • Transitional milk – from about day 4 to 2 weeks
  • Mature milk (per 100 ml, approximately):
    • water about 88%
    • energy about 65–70 kcal
    • protein about 1.1 g – mainly whey (lactalbumin), easy to digest
    • fat about 3.5–4.5 g – with essential fatty acids (DHA) for brain development
    • lactose about 7 g
    • vitamins, minerals and protective factors – lactoferrin, lysozyme, bifidus factor, antibodies
  • Foremilk (watery, quenches thirst) and hindmilk (rich in fat, satisfies hunger) – so the baby should empty one breast before moving to the other
  • Cow's milk has about three times more protein (mostly hard-to-digest casein), less lactose and more minerals – a heavy load for the infant's kidneys

Advantages to the baby

  • Ideal nutrition, easily digested, clean, at the right temperature and always available
  • Protects against infections – diarrhoea, pneumonia, ear infections
  • Less allergy; better brain development; lower risk of obesity and diabetes later
  • Promotes bonding

Advantages to the mother

  • Less postpartum haemorrhage; faster involution of the uterus
  • Child spacing – lactational amenorrhoea (reliable only with exclusive breastfeeding, absent periods and a baby below 6 months)
  • Helps return to pre-pregnancy weight; lower risk of breast and ovarian cancer

Advantages to the family and nation: economical, saves time, no preparation and environment-friendly.

Recommended practice

  • Start breastfeeding within one hour of birth; give no pre-lacteal feeds
  • Exclusive breastfeeding for 6 months, then continue with complementary feeding up to 2 years or beyond
  • Feed on demand (8–12 times a day), including at night

Nursing points

  • Teach correct positioning and attachment – baby's chin touching the breast, mouth wide open, lower lip turned out, more areola visible above the mouth than below
  • Manage engorgement and cracked nipples; teach expression of breast milk
  • Ensure the mother gets extra food, fluids and rest, and emotional support

Conclusion Breasts are prepared by oestrogen, progesterone and prolactin; after delivery, prolactin (prolactin reflex) secretes milk and oxytocin (milk ejection reflex) ejects it; breast milk – especially colostrum – gives ideal nutrition and protection, and early exclusive breastfeeding benefits both mother and baby.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Define reflex arc and name its components.
answer_html:
Definition A reflex arc is the pathway along which impulses travel to produce a reflex action – an automatic, quick response to a stimulus.

Components

  1. Receptor – detects the stimulus (e.g. stretch receptors in a muscle, pain receptors in skin)
  2. Afferent (sensory) neuron – carries the impulse to the CNS
  3. Centre – in the spinal cord or brainstem, where the sensory neuron connects (synapses) with the motor neuron, directly or through an interneuron
  4. Efferent (motor) neuron – carries the impulse from the CNS
  5. Effector – the muscle or gland that responds

Example: knee jerk – tapping the patellar tendon → quadriceps contracts → leg kicks forward.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: What is referred pain? Give examples.
answer_html:
Definition Referred pain is pain that is felt in a part of the body away from the actual site of disease, usually in a skin area supplied by the same spinal segment as the diseased organ. The brain wrongly locates visceral pain to the more familiar skin area.

Examples

  1. Heart (angina, MI) – pain in the left arm, shoulder, neck and jaw
  2. Diaphragm (and gall bladder, spleen irritating it) – pain at the tip of the shoulder (C3–C5)
  3. Appendix – early pain around the umbilicus
  4. Kidney and ureter – pain from the loin to the groin
  5. Hip joint – pain felt in the knee

Applied: a nurse must not dismiss arm or jaw pain in a cardiac patient.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: List the functions of the cerebellum.
answer_html:
Introduction The cerebellum ("little brain") lies at the back of the skull, behind the pons and medulla.

Functions

  1. Maintains equilibrium (balance), with the vestibular apparatus
  2. Maintains posture and muscle tone
  3. Coordinates voluntary movements – controls their timing, smoothness, force and accuracy, and corrects errors as movement proceeds
  4. Motor learning – learning skilled movements such as cycling, writing and typing

Applied: damage causes ataxia (unsteady, drunken gait), intention tremor, inability to do rapid alternate movements, slurred (scanning) speech and nystagmus – on the same side as the lesion. Alcohol affects the cerebellum.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Describe the composition and functions of cerebrospinal fluid.
answer_html:
Introduction Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) is a clear, colourless fluid that fills the ventricles of the brain, the central canal of the spinal cord and the subarachnoid space. It is formed mainly by the choroid plexuses (about 500 ml a day) and absorbed into the venous sinuses through the arachnoid villi.

1. Physical properties

  • Volume: about 150 ml in adults
  • Appearance: clear and colourless like water
  • Specific gravity: about 1.005
  • Reaction: slightly alkaline
  • Pressure: about 60–150 mm of water in the lying position (higher in the sitting position)
  • Does not clot

2. Chemical composition (compared with plasma)

  • Water – about 99%
  • Proteins – very low, about 15–45 mg/dl (plasma has about 7 g/dl)
  • Glucose – about 50–80 mg/dl, about two-thirds of blood glucose
  • Chloride – higher than in plasma
  • Sodium – similar to plasma; potassium and calcium – lower
  • Cells – very few, 0–5 lymphocytes per mm³; no red cells

3. Functions of CSF

  1. Mechanical protection
    • Acts as a water cushion and shock absorber that protects the brain and spinal cord from injury
    • Buoyancy – the brain "floats" in CSF, so its effective weight falls from about 1,400 g to about 50 g; this prevents it being crushed under its own weight
  2. Maintains constant intracranial pressure – CSF volume adjusts when blood volume in the skull changes
  3. Nutrition – supplies nutrients (glucose, oxygen) to nervous tissue
  4. Removal of waste – carries away metabolic waste products; acts like lymph for the brain
  5. Chemical environment – keeps the ionic environment of neurons stable; changes in its CO₂ and H⁺ stimulate the central chemoreceptors and regulate breathing
  6. Transport – carries some hormones and other substances within the CNS

4. Applied / nursing importance

  • Lumbar puncture – CSF is examined to diagnose:
    • Bacterial meningitis – turbid fluid, high protein, low glucose, many neutrophils
    • Viral meningitis – clear fluid, lymphocytes, normal glucose
    • Tuberculous meningitis – high protein, low glucose, lymphocytes, cobweb clot
    • Subarachnoid haemorrhage – blood-stained or yellowish (xanthochromic) fluid
  • Lumbar puncture is avoided when there are signs of raised intracranial pressure (risk of brain herniation)
  • After lumbar puncture: keep the patient lying flat as per hospital policy, encourage fluids, watch for headache and leakage
  • CSF leak from the nose or ear after a head injury tests positive for glucose; may show a "halo sign" on gauze; do not pack the nose or ear

Conclusion CSF is a clear fluid low in protein and cells, with glucose about two-thirds of blood glucose; it cushions, supports and nourishes the brain and spinal cord, and its examination is a key test in meningitis.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Explain the events in synaptic transmission.
answer_html:
Introduction A synapse is the junction between two neurons (or between a neuron and a muscle or gland) where the impulse passes from one cell to the next. Most synapses in the body are chemical – a chemical messenger (neurotransmitter) carries the signal across a narrow gap.

1. Structure of a chemical synapse

  • Presynaptic terminal – the end of the axon of the first neuron; contains synaptic vesicles filled with neurotransmitter and many mitochondria
  • Synaptic cleft – a very narrow gap between the two cells
  • Postsynaptic membrane – the membrane of the second neuron (dendrite or cell body) carrying receptors for the neurotransmitter

2. Events in synaptic transmission

  1. Arrival of the impulse – the action potential reaches the presynaptic terminal and depolarises it
  2. Entry of calcium – voltage-gated calcium channels open and Ca²⁺ ions enter the terminal
  3. Release of neurotransmitter – calcium makes the vesicles fuse with the presynaptic membrane and release their neurotransmitter into the cleft (exocytosis)
  4. Diffusion – the neurotransmitter diffuses across the cleft
  5. Binding to receptors – it binds to specific receptors on the postsynaptic membrane, opening ion channels
  6. Postsynaptic potential
    • Excitatory (EPSP) – Na⁺ enters → the membrane is partly depolarised; e.g. acetylcholine, glutamate
    • Inhibitory (IPSP) – Cl⁻ enters or K⁺ leaves → the membrane becomes more negative; e.g. GABA, glycine
  7. Summation – many EPSPs from many synapses (spatial) or in quick succession (temporal) add up; if the threshold is reached at the axon hillock, a new action potential is fired in the second neuron
  8. Termination – the neurotransmitter is removed quickly by:
    • Enzymes – e.g. acetylcholinesterase breaks down acetylcholine
    • Reuptake into the presynaptic terminal – e.g. noradrenaline, serotonin, dopamine
    • Diffusion away from the cleft

3. Properties of synaptic transmission

  • One-way conduction – from presynaptic to postsynaptic neuron only
  • Synaptic delay – about 0.5 ms for each synapse
  • Summation and facilitation
  • Fatigue with repeated rapid stimulation
  • Very sensitive to lack of oxygen, acidosis and drugs

4. Applied / nursing importance

  • Many drugs act at synapses:
    • Antidepressants (SSRIs) block the reuptake of serotonin
    • Benzodiazepines and many anticonvulsants increase the effect of GABA (inhibitory) – cause drowsiness
    • Anaesthetics depress synaptic transmission
  • Parkinson's disease – lack of dopamine; treated with levodopa
  • Tetanus toxin blocks the release of inhibitory transmitters → severe muscle spasms
  • Organophosphorus poisoning – acetylcholinesterase is inhibited; acetylcholine accumulates
  • Hypoxia quickly stops synaptic transmission – unconsciousness within seconds of cardiac arrest

Conclusion At a chemical synapse, an impulse arriving at the presynaptic terminal causes calcium entry and release of a neurotransmitter, which crosses the cleft, acts on postsynaptic receptors and is then quickly removed; many drugs and poisons work by altering these steps.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Elaborate on the parasympathetic nervous system.
answer_html:
Introduction The autonomic nervous system controls the internal organs automatically, without conscious effort. It has two divisions – sympathetic ("fight or flight") and parasympathetic. The parasympathetic system is the "rest and digest" system: it conserves energy, slows the heart and promotes digestion and excretion.

1. Outflow – craniosacral A. Cranial part – through four cranial nerves:

  • Oculomotor (3rd) – to the eye: constricts the pupil and contracts the ciliary muscle
  • Facial (7th) – to the lacrimal, submandibular and sublingual glands
  • Glossopharyngeal (9th) – to the parotid gland
  • Vagus (10th) – carries about 75% of all parasympathetic fibres; supplies the heart, lungs, oesophagus, stomach, intestines up to the middle of the transverse colon, liver, pancreas and kidneys

B. Sacral part – sacral segments S2–S4 of the spinal cord through the pelvic splanchnic nerves; supplies the lower colon, rectum, urinary bladder and reproductive organs

2. Arrangement of neurons

  • Long preganglionic fibres from the brainstem or sacral cord
  • Ganglia lie close to or within the walls of the organs (terminal ganglia)
  • Short postganglionic fibres
  • So parasympathetic effects are localised to individual organs

3. Neurotransmitter

  • Acetylcholine at both the ganglia (nicotinic receptors) and the organs (muscarinic receptors) – the system is cholinergic

4. Effects of parasympathetic stimulation

  • Eye – constriction of the pupil (miosis); accommodation for near vision
  • Glands – increased secretion of saliva, tears, gastric and intestinal juices
  • Heart – slows the heart rate; slows AV conduction
  • Lungs – bronchoconstriction; increased bronchial secretions
  • Gastrointestinal tract – increases peristalsis, relaxes sphincters → digestion and defecation
  • Urinary bladder – contracts the detrusor and relaxes the internal sphincter → micturition
  • Reproductive organs – erection
  • Metabolism – favours storage of energy

5. Comparison with the sympathetic system

Feature Sympathetic Parasympathetic
Outflow thoracolumbar (T1–L2) craniosacral (cranial nerves 3, 7, 9, 10; S2–S4)
Ganglia near the spinal cord near or in the organs
Preganglionic fibres short long
Neurotransmitter at organ mainly noradrenaline acetylcholine
Effect widespread, "fight or flight" localised, "rest and digest"
Heart rate increased decreased
Pupil dilated constricted
Bronchi dilated constricted
Gut movements decreased increased
Bladder retention emptying

6. Applied / nursing importance

  • Atropine (anticholinergic) blocks parasympathetic effects – used to dry secretions before surgery, treat slow heart rate and organophosphorus poisoning; side effects: dry mouth, fast pulse, blurred vision, urinary retention, constipation, flushing
  • Vagal stimulation – straining at stool, tracheal suctioning and pressure on the eyeball can slow the heart sharply; suction briefly and watch the pulse
  • Cholinergic drugs (neostigmine) – used in urinary retention, paralytic ileus and myasthenia gravis
  • Organophosphorus poisoning – excess parasympathetic activity: small pupils, sweating, salivation, diarrhoea, slow pulse, bronchial secretions

Conclusion The parasympathetic system arises from cranial nerves 3, 7, 9 and 10 and sacral segments S2–S4, uses acetylcholine, and acts locally to slow the heart, constrict the pupils and promote digestion and excretion – the body's "rest and digest" system.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Explain the physiology of pain.
answer_html:
Introduction Pain is "an unpleasant sensory and emotional experience associated with actual or potential tissue damage". It is a protective sensation – it warns us of injury and makes us protect the injured part. Pain is now regarded as the fifth vital sign.

1. Pain receptors (nociceptors)

  • Free nerve endings in the skin, muscles, joints, bones and internal organs (the brain itself has none)
  • Stimulated by:
    • Mechanical stimuli – cutting, crushing, stretching
    • Thermal stimuli – extreme heat or cold
    • Chemical stimuli – substances released from damaged tissue: bradykinin, prostaglandins, histamine, potassium, hydrogen ions, substance P
  • Pain receptors do not adapt – pain continues as long as the stimulus does

2. Pain fibres – two types

  • A-delta fibres – thin, myelinated, fast; carry sharp, pricking, well-localised pain ("fast" or first pain)
  • C fibres – unmyelinated, slow; carry dull, aching, burning, poorly localised pain ("slow" or second pain)

3. Pain pathway

  1. Pain fibres enter the spinal cord through the dorsal roots and end in the dorsal horn (substantia gelatinosa); transmitters – substance P and glutamate
  2. Second-order neurons cross to the opposite side and ascend in the lateral spinothalamic tract
  3. They reach the thalamus, where pain is first perceived
  4. Third-order neurons carry it to the somatosensory cortex (localisation and intensity) and to the limbic system and frontal cortex (emotional response and suffering)

4. Modulation of pain A. Gate control theory (Melzack and Wall, 1965)

  • The dorsal horn acts like a "gate"
  • Impulses in large touch fibres (A-beta) – produced by rubbing, massage, vibration, warmth or TENS – close the gate and reduce the pain impulses passing upward
  • Anxiety and attention to pain open the gate; distraction and relaxation help close it

B. Descending pain control

  • Centres in the brainstem (periaqueductal grey, raphe nuclei) send fibres down to the dorsal horn and inhibit pain transmission
  • They release the body's own morphine-like substances – endorphins and enkephalins – and serotonin

5. Types of pain

  • Somatic – from skin (superficial, sharp) or muscles, bones and joints (deep, aching)
  • Visceral – from internal organs; poorly localised; caused by distension, spasm or ischaemia; often with nausea and sweating
  • Referred pain – felt away from the diseased organ
  • Neuropathic pain – from damaged nerves (burning, shooting)
  • Phantom limb pain – after amputation
  • Acute pain (recent, protective) and chronic pain (more than 3 months)

6. Nursing importance

  • Assess pain regularly – site, character, severity (numeric scale 0–10, Wong–Baker faces scale for children), onset, duration, aggravating and relieving factors
  • Pharmacological relief – NSAIDs block prostaglandin formation; opioids act on opioid receptors; local anaesthetics block nerve conduction
  • Non-pharmacological relief – position change, massage, cold or warm application, TENS, distraction, relaxation, guided imagery, reassurance (based on gate control theory)
  • Evaluate the effect of relief measures and document

Conclusion Pain is detected by nociceptors, carried by A-delta and C fibres through the dorsal horn and spinothalamic tract to the thalamus and cortex, and can be modulated at the spinal "gate" and by endorphins – which explains why both drugs and simple nursing measures relieve pain.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Define reflex. Describe the reflex arc, classify reflexes and explain their properties and clinical importance. (2 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 2)

diagram.caption: Reflex arc - knee jerk and withdrawal

answer_html:
(a) Definition (2 marks)

  • A reflex is an automatic, involuntary, rapid and predictable response to a stimulus, brought about through the nervous system without conscious effort
  • Examples: withdrawing the hand from a hot object, blinking when something touches the eye, the knee jerk, salivation when food is in the mouth
  • Reflexes protect the body, maintain posture and regulate many internal functions (heart rate, blood pressure, breathing, micturition)

(b) Reflex arc (2 marks) The reflex arc is the nervous pathway of a reflex. It has five parts:

  1. Receptor – detects the stimulus (muscle spindle, pain receptor in skin)
  2. Afferent (sensory) neuron – carries the impulse to the CNS through the dorsal root; its cell body is in the dorsal root ganglion
  3. Centre – in the spinal cord or brainstem
    • In a monosynaptic reflex the sensory neuron synapses directly with the motor neuron (knee jerk)
    • In a polysynaptic reflex one or more interneurons lie between them (withdrawal reflex)
  4. Efferent (motor) neuron – carries the impulse from the CNS through the ventral root
  5. Effector – skeletal muscle, smooth muscle or gland that produces the response

A reflex fails if any part of the arc is damaged – this is why reflex testing helps locate lesions.

(c) Classification of reflexes (2 marks) 1. According to development

  • Unconditioned (inborn) reflexes – present from birth; e.g. sucking, swallowing, blinking, knee jerk
  • Conditioned (acquired) reflexes – learnt by experience; e.g. salivation at the sight or smell of food (Pavlov's experiment)

2. According to the location of the centre

  • Spinal reflexes – knee jerk, withdrawal reflex
  • Brainstem (bulbar) reflexes – pupillary light reflex, corneal reflex, coughing, sneezing, vomiting, swallowing, gag reflex, baroreceptor reflex
  • Cerebellar and cortical reflexes – posture and righting reflexes

3. According to the number of synapses

  • Monosynaptic – stretch reflexes such as the knee jerk
  • Polysynaptic – withdrawal reflex and most others

4. According to the site of the receptor

  • Superficial reflexes – receptor in skin or mucous membrane: corneal, abdominal, plantar reflexes
  • Deep (tendon) reflexes – receptor in muscle (stretch):
    • Biceps jerk – C5, C6
    • Triceps jerk – C6, C7
    • Knee jerk – L2, L3, L4
    • Ankle jerk – S1, S2
  • Visceral reflexes – pupillary, micturition, defecation, carotid sinus reflexes

5. According to the response

  • Somatic reflexes – effector is skeletal muscle
  • Autonomic reflexes – effector is smooth muscle, heart or gland

(d) Properties of reflexes (2 marks)

  1. One-way conduction – impulses pass only from sensory to motor side
  2. Reflex time (delay) – time taken mainly at the synapses; longer in polysynaptic reflexes
  3. Summation – weak stimuli added together can produce a response
  4. Irradiation (spread) – a stronger stimulus spreads to more motor neurons and more muscles respond
  5. After-discharge – the response may continue briefly after the stimulus stops
  6. Fatigue – repeated stimulation weakens the response
  7. Reciprocal inhibition – when one muscle contracts, its antagonist relaxes (knee jerk: quadriceps contracts, hamstrings relax)
  8. Final common path – many reflexes use the same motor neuron
  9. Adequate stimulus – each reflex responds best to a particular stimulus

(e) Clinical importance (2 marks)

  • Locating nervous system lesions
    • Exaggerated tendon reflexes and clonus – upper motor neuron lesion (stroke, spinal cord compression)
    • Absent or reduced reflexes – lower motor neuron lesion (peripheral neuropathy, poliomyelitis, Guillain–Barré syndrome) or spinal shock
  • Plantar reflex
    • Normal adult – flexor (toes curl down)
    • Extensor (Babinski sign) – big toe goes up and toes fan out – upper motor neuron lesion; normal in infants up to about 1–2 years
  • Newborn reflexes – Moro, rooting, sucking, grasp and stepping reflexes assess the maturity of the newborn's nervous system; Moro reflex disappears by about 4–6 months; persistence or absence is abnormal
  • Brainstem reflexes – pupillary, corneal, gag and doll's-eye reflexes are tested in unconscious patients and in the assessment of brain death
  • Pupillary reaction is part of neurological observation along with the Glasgow Coma Scale

Nursing points

  • Use a reflex hammer correctly, with the limb relaxed; compare both sides
  • Record reflexes as absent (0), diminished (1+), normal (2+), brisk (3+), very brisk with clonus (4+)
  • Protect patients with absent protective reflexes – e.g. eye care (taping lids) when the corneal reflex is lost; position the unconscious patient laterally when the gag reflex is absent

Conclusion A reflex is an automatic response produced through a reflex arc of receptor, sensory neuron, centre, motor neuron and effector. Reflexes are classified by development, centre, synapses and receptor site; their properties and changes in disease make reflex testing a simple but powerful clinical tool.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: What is the blood–brain barrier?
answer_html:
Definition The blood–brain barrier (BBB) is a special barrier between the blood in the brain capillaries and the brain tissue that controls which substances pass from the blood into the brain.

Structure

  1. Tight junctions between the endothelial cells of brain capillaries – the main barrier
  2. Thick basement membrane
  3. End-feet of astrocytes surrounding the capillaries

Passes freely: water, oxygen, CO₂, glucose (by carriers) and fat-soluble substances – alcohol, anaesthetics, nicotine.

Blocks: most proteins, many drugs, toxins and microbes.

Function: protects the neurons and keeps their environment stable.

Applied

  • Kernicterus – the immature BBB of newborns lets bilirubin enter the brain
  • Levodopa (not dopamine) is given in Parkinson's disease because dopamine cannot cross
  • In meningitis the barrier becomes leaky

subject: Applied Physiology
question: What is saltatory conduction?
answer_html:
Definition Saltatory conduction (from the Latin "saltare" – to jump) is the conduction of the nerve impulse in myelinated nerve fibres, in which the impulse jumps from one node of Ranvier to the next.

Mechanism

  • The myelin sheath acts as an insulator
  • Ion exchange (and the action potential) occurs only at the nodes of Ranvier, which have many sodium channels
  • Local current flows to the next node and depolarises it

Advantages

  1. Faster conduction – up to about 120 m/s in large myelinated fibres, compared with 0.5–2 m/s in unmyelinated fibres
  2. Saves energy – fewer ions have to be pumped back

Applied: demyelinating diseases – multiple sclerosis, Guillain–Barré syndrome – slow or block conduction, causing weakness and sensory loss.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Classify nerve fibres.
answer_html:
Introduction Nerve fibres are classified in several ways. The most useful is the Erlanger–Gasser classification, based on diameter and conduction velocity.

1. Type A fibres – myelinated, largest and fastest

  • Aα – motor to skeletal muscle; proprioception (up to about 120 m/s)
  • Aβ – touch and pressure
  • Aγ – motor to muscle spindles
  • Aδ – fast (sharp) pain and cold 2. Type B fibres – thin myelinated; preganglionic autonomic fibres 3. Type C fibres – unmyelinated, thinnest and slowest (0.5–2 m/s); slow (dull, burning) pain, warmth, itch; postganglionic sympathetic fibres

Other classifications

  • Myelinated and unmyelinated
  • Sensory (afferent), motor (efferent) and mixed
  • Cholinergic and adrenergic (by neurotransmitter)

Applied: local anaesthetics block the thin pain fibres before the thick touch and motor fibres.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: What is Wallerian degeneration?
answer_html:
Definition Wallerian degeneration is the degeneration of the part of a nerve fibre distal to a cut or crush, i.e. the part separated from its cell body.

Changes

  1. Within a few days the axon swells and breaks into fragments
  2. The myelin sheath breaks down into fat droplets
  3. Macrophages and Schwann cells clear the debris
  4. The muscle supplied wastes unless it is re-innervated

Regeneration (only in peripheral nerves)

  • Schwann cells multiply and form a tube that guides new sprouts from the proximal stump
  • The axon regrows at about 1–4 mm per day; recovery is better when the cut ends are close (nerve repair)
  • Nerve fibres in the brain and spinal cord do not regenerate effectively – hence spinal cord injuries are usually permanent

Nursing: maintain joint movement and prevent deformities while the nerve regrows.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: What is the reticular activating system?
answer_html:
Definition The reticular activating system (RAS) is a network of neurons in the reticular formation of the brainstem (medulla, pons and midbrain) that projects through the thalamus to the whole cerebral cortex.

Key features

  • Receives branches from all sensory pathways – sound, light, touch and pain

Functions

  1. Maintains wakefulness, alertness and consciousness
  2. Arousal from sleep – by an alarm, a shake or pain
  3. Attention – filters unimportant stimuli
  4. Takes part in the sleep–wake cycle and in muscle tone

Applied

  • Damage to the RAS (brainstem injury, stroke, raised intracranial pressure) → coma
  • General anaesthetics and sedatives depress the RAS; caffeine stimulates it
  • Level of consciousness is assessed with the Glasgow Coma Scale

subject: Applied Physiology
question: What is an electroencephalogram (EEG)? Name the brain waves.
answer_html:
Definition An electroencephalogram (EEG) is a record of the electrical activity of the brain, picked up by electrodes placed on the scalp.

Brain waves

  1. Alpha waves – 8–13 per second; awake, relaxed, eyes closed; disappear on opening the eyes
  2. Beta waves – above 13 per second; alert, eyes open, mental activity
  3. Theta waves – 4–7 per second; children, drowsiness, light sleep
  4. Delta waves – below 4 per second; deep sleep and infants; in an awake adult they suggest brain disease

Uses

  • Diagnosis of epilepsy, sleep disorders and encephalopathy
  • Supporting evidence in brain death

Nursing: wash the hair and keep it free of oil; avoid tea and coffee before the test; sleep deprivation if ordered.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: What is spinal shock?
answer_html:
Definition Spinal shock is a temporary loss of all spinal reflex activity below the level of an acute, severe spinal cord injury (such as transection), due to the sudden loss of facilitating impulses from the brain.

Features (below the level of injury)

  1. Flaccid paralysis with loss of muscle tone
  2. Loss of all sensations and reflexes
  3. Atonic bladder (urinary retention) and bowel (paralytic ileus)
  4. Loss of sweating and vasomotor tone → low BP

Duration: usually days to a few weeks. Its end is shown by the return of reflexes, which later become exaggerated (spastic paralysis with a positive Babinski sign).

Nursing: spinal immobilisation and log rolling, catheter care, bowel care, 2-hourly turning to prevent pressure ulcers, DVT prevention, and monitoring of BP and breathing.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Explain the generation and conduction of the nerve impulse.
answer_html:
Introduction A nerve impulse is an action potential – a brief, self-spreading reversal of the electrical charge across the nerve fibre membrane (depolarisation followed by repolarisation) that carries information along the nerve.

1. Resting membrane potential

  • At rest, the inside of the neuron is negative – about –70 mV
  • Maintained by the Na⁺–K⁺ pump (3 Na⁺ out, 2 K⁺ in), the leakage of K⁺ out of the cell, and large negatively charged proteins inside
  • The membrane is said to be polarised

2. Generation of the action potential A stimulus that brings the membrane to the threshold (about –55 mV) produces an action potential:

  • a. Depolarisation – voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open → Na⁺ rushes in → the potential rises rapidly from –70 mV to about +35 mV (overshoot – the inside becomes positive)
  • b. Repolarisation – Na⁺ channels close; K⁺ channels open → K⁺ moves out → the potential returns towards the resting level
  • c. Hyperpolarisation – K⁺ channels close slowly, so the potential briefly becomes more negative than at rest
  • d. Restoration – the Na⁺–K⁺ pump restores the original ion distribution
  • The whole spike lasts about 1 millisecond

3. Properties of the action potential

  • Threshold – weaker (subthreshold) stimuli give only a small local change
  • All-or-none – once threshold is reached, the size of the spike is always the same
  • Refractory period – absolute (no response at all) and relative (only a stronger stimulus works); limits the frequency of impulses and keeps conduction one-way

4. Conduction (propagation) of the impulse

  • Unmyelinated fibres – the depolarised area sets up local currents with the neighbouring resting area, depolarising it; the impulse travels continuously and slowly (0.5–2 m/s)
  • Myelinated fibres – saltatory conduction, jumping from node to node; fast (up to about 120 m/s)
  • In the body, impulses travel in one direction – from dendrites and cell body along the axon to the terminals

5. Factors affecting conduction

  • Diameter (thicker is faster) and myelination
  • Temperature – cold slows conduction (the basis of cold packs for pain)
  • Pressure, lack of oxygen and local anaesthetics block conduction
  • Electrolytes – low calcium increases excitability (tetany); high potassium depolarises the membrane

6. Applied importance

  • Local anaesthetics (lignocaine) block Na⁺ channels → no impulses → no pain
  • Hypocalcaemia → tetany; potassium imbalance → muscle weakness and cardiac arrhythmias
  • Demyelinating diseases slow conduction
  • Epilepsy – abnormal, excessive discharge of neurons

Conclusion The nerve impulse is generated when threshold is reached: Na⁺ entry depolarises the membrane, K⁺ exit repolarises it and the pump restores the ions; the impulse spreads by local currents in unmyelinated fibres and by saltatory conduction in myelinated fibres.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Explain the properties of nerve fibres.
answer_html:
Introduction Nerve fibres (axons) receive and conduct impulses. Their main properties are excitability, conductivity, refractory period, all-or-none response, summation, accommodation and infatigability.

1. Excitability

  • The ability to respond to a stimulus by producing an action potential
  • The stimulus must have adequate strength and duration
  • Rheobase – the minimum strength of a current that can excite the nerve when applied for a long time
  • Chronaxie – the minimum duration needed to excite the nerve with a current of twice the rheobase; a short chronaxie means high excitability (nerve has a shorter chronaxie than muscle)
  • These values are plotted as a strength–duration curve, used to assess nerve injury

2. Conductivity

  • The ability to transmit the impulse along the fibre
  • Speed depends on diameter and myelination – from about 0.5 m/s (C fibres) to 120 m/s (Aα fibres)

3. Refractory period

  • Absolute refractory period – no second impulse can be produced, whatever the stimulus strength
  • Relative refractory period – a stronger-than-normal stimulus is needed
  • In large nerve fibres it lasts less than a millisecond, allowing hundreds of impulses per second

4. All-or-none law

  • A single nerve fibre responds fully or not at all
  • A whole nerve (a bundle of fibres with different thresholds) gives a graded response as more fibres are stimulated

5. Summation

  • Two or more subthreshold stimuli in quick succession (temporal summation) or at nearby points at the same time (spatial summation) can add up to reach threshold

6. Accommodation

  • If the strength of a stimulus rises very slowly, the nerve adapts and may not fire even at a strength that would normally excite it, because sodium channels become inactivated

7. Infatigability

  • Nerve fibres practically never fatigue, as they use very little energy; fatigue occurs at the synapse or neuromuscular junction, not in the nerve fibre

8. Applied importance

  • Nerve conduction studies – diagnose diabetic and leprosy neuropathy, Guillain–Barré syndrome and carpal tunnel syndrome
  • TENS (transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation) – relieves pain
  • Electrical stimulation in physiotherapy and the strength–duration curve in nerve injury
  • Local anaesthetic nerve blocks

Conclusion Nerve fibres show excitability (rheobase, chronaxie), conductivity, a refractory period, the all-or-none response, summation, accommodation and infatigability; these properties are the basis of nerve conduction studies and electrotherapy.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Differentiate between upper motor neuron and lower motor neuron lesions.
answer_html:
Introduction The voluntary motor pathway has two neurons:

  • Upper motor neuron (UMN) – from the motor cortex through the corticospinal (pyramidal) and corticobulbar tracts to the brainstem and spinal cord
  • Lower motor neuron (LMN) – from the anterior horn cell (or cranial nerve motor nucleus) through the peripheral nerve to the muscle – the "final common pathway"

Differences

Feature UMN lesion LMN lesion
Site motor cortex, internal capsule, brainstem, corticospinal tract in the spinal cord anterior horn cells, nerve roots, peripheral nerves, cranial nerve nuclei
Muscles affected groups of muscles (e.g. one half of the body) individual muscles or those of a segment or nerve
Type of paralysis spastic flaccid
Muscle tone increased (spasticity, "clasp-knife") decreased (hypotonia)
Muscle wasting absent or slight (late disuse) marked wasting
Tendon reflexes exaggerated; clonus may be present diminished or absent
Plantar reflex extensor – Babinski sign positive flexor or absent
Abdominal reflexes absent usually present
Fasciculations absent may be present
Examples stroke (hemiplegia), cerebral palsy, spinal cord injury (after spinal shock), brain tumour, multiple sclerosis poliomyelitis, Guillain–Barré syndrome, peripheral nerve injury, Bell's palsy, leprosy neuropathy

Facial palsy – a useful example

  • UMN facial palsy (stroke) – only the lower part of the face on the opposite side is weak; the forehead is spared
  • LMN facial palsy (Bell's palsy) – the whole half of the face on the same side, including the forehead, is weak

Nursing implications

  • Spastic limbs – positioning to prevent contractures, splints, regular ROM exercises, prevent pressure sores
  • Flaccid limbs – support joints (e.g. a sling to prevent shoulder subluxation in early stroke), passive exercises, skin care
  • Eye care in Bell's palsy (incomplete eye closure)
  • Physiotherapy and rehabilitation

Terms used for the extent of paralysis

  • Monoplegia – one limb
  • Hemiplegia – arm and leg of one side (usually UMN, e.g. stroke)
  • Paraplegia – both lower limbs (spinal cord injury below the neck)
  • Quadriplegia (tetraplegia) – all four limbs (cervical cord injury)

Eliciting the Babinski sign

  • Stroke the outer border of the sole firmly from the heel towards the little toe, then across to the big toe
  • Normal (flexor) response – toes curl down
  • Babinski sign (extensor response) – the big toe goes up and the other toes fan out; indicates a UMN lesion (normal in infants up to about one year)

Conclusion UMN lesions cause spastic paralysis with exaggerated reflexes and a positive Babinski sign but little wasting, while LMN lesions cause flaccid paralysis with wasting, lost reflexes and fasciculations.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Explain the limbic system and its functions.
answer_html:
Introduction The limbic system ("limbus" – border) is a ring of structures on the inner (medial) side of the cerebral hemispheres, around the upper brainstem. It is called the "emotional brain", as it controls emotions, behaviour, memory and motivation.

1. Components

  • Cortical parts – cingulate gyrus, parahippocampal gyrus, hippocampus
  • Subcortical parts – amygdala, septal nuclei, hypothalamus (mammillary bodies), anterior nucleus of the thalamus
  • Connecting pathways – the fornix and others; olfactory connections
  • Papez circuit – hippocampus → fornix → mammillary body → anterior thalamic nucleus → cingulate gyrus → back to the hippocampus; important in emotion and memory

2. Functions

  • Emotions – fear, anger, rage, pleasure and sadness; the amygdala recognises danger and produces fear and aggression; reward and punishment centres
  • Expression of emotion – through the hypothalamus, it produces the bodily signs of emotion: fast heart rate, sweating, rise in BP, facial expression
  • Memory and learning – the hippocampus converts short-term memory into long-term memory
  • Motivation and instinctive behaviour – feeding, drinking, sexual and maternal behaviour
  • Smell – links smell with emotion and memory (a smell can bring back old memories)

3. Applied importance

  • Alzheimer's disease – the hippocampus is affected early → loss of recent memory
  • Korsakoff's psychosis – damage to the mammillary bodies from thiamine deficiency in chronic alcoholism → memory loss and confabulation
  • Temporal lobe epilepsy – strange smells, déjà vu and emotional changes
  • Anxiety, depression and PTSD involve limbic circuits; benzodiazepines and antidepressants act here
  • Addiction – drugs act on the reward pathways
  • Bilateral damage of the amygdala may cause loss of fear and abnormal behaviour

4. Nursing importance

  • Fear and anxiety raise the pulse and BP of patients – a calm environment and therapeutic communication reduce stress
  • Memory aids, routine and orientation for patients with dementia
  • Recognise emotional reactions to illness as normal and provide support

Memory – a brief note

  • Short-term (working) memory – lasts seconds to minutes, e.g. remembering a phone number while dialling
  • Long-term memory – lasts days to years; formed by consolidation, which needs the hippocampus
  • In dementia, recent memory is lost first, while old memories remain till late
  • Anterograde amnesia – cannot form new memories; retrograde amnesia – loss of memories before an injury (common after head injury)

Conclusion The limbic system – cingulate gyrus, hippocampus, amygdala, hypothalamus and their connections – controls emotions and their bodily expression, memory, motivation and instinctive behaviour; its disorders affect memory, mood and behaviour.

subject: Applied Physiology
question: Describe the sensory (ascending) and motor (descending) pathways. (5 + 5)
answer_html:
Introduction Pathways (tracts) are bundles of nerve fibres in the spinal cord and brain that carry impulses up to the brain (sensory, ascending) or down from the brain (motor, descending). Most of them cross to the opposite side, so each half of the body is controlled by the opposite cerebral hemisphere.

(a) Sensory (ascending) pathways (5 marks)

General plan – a chain of three neurons

  • First-order neuron – from the receptor to the spinal cord or medulla; cell body in the dorsal root ganglion
  • Second-order neuron – from the spinal cord or medulla to the thalamus; it usually crosses to the opposite side
  • Third-order neuron – from the thalamus to the sensory cortex (postcentral gyrus)

1. Dorsal column–medial lemniscus pathway

  • Carries: fine (discriminative) touch, vibration, position sense (proprioception), two-point discrimination and recognition of objects by touch
  • Course:
    • first-order fibres enter the dorsal (posterior) column and ascend on the same side – fasciculus gracilis (from the lower body) and fasciculus cuneatus (from the upper body)
    • they end in the nucleus gracilis and nucleus cuneatus in the medulla
    • second-order fibres cross in the medulla (sensory decussation) and ascend as the medial lemniscus to the thalamus
    • third-order fibres go to the sensory cortex
  • Lesion – loss of position and vibration sense → unsteady gait (sensory ataxia), positive Romberg's test; seen in vitamin B₁₂ deficiency and tabes dorsalis

2. Spinothalamic (anterolateral) pathway

  • Lateral spinothalamic tract – pain and temperature
  • Anterior spinothalamic tract – crude touch and pressure
  • Course:
    • first-order fibres end in the dorsal horn
    • second-order fibres cross within one or two segments in the spinal cord and ascend on the opposite side to the thalamus
    • third-order fibres go to the sensory cortex
  • Lesion – loss of pain and temperature on the opposite side below the level of the lesion

3. Spinocerebellar tracts

  • Carry unconscious proprioception from muscles and joints to the cerebellum (same side) for coordination of movement and posture

Applied – hemisection of the spinal cord (Brown-Séquard syndrome)

  • Same side below the lesion: loss of fine touch, vibration and position sense, and UMN paralysis
  • Opposite side below the lesion: loss of pain and temperature

(b) Motor (descending) pathways (5 marks)

1. Pyramidal tracts (corticospinal and corticobulbar)

  • Origin – motor cortex (precentral gyrus) and nearby areas, including the giant Betz cells
  • Course – corona radiata → posterior limb of the internal capsule → midbrain → pons → pyramids of the medulla
  • Pyramidal decussation – in the lower medulla about 80–90% of fibres cross to form the lateral corticospinal tract; the rest descend uncrossed as the anterior corticospinal tract and cross lower down
  • Termination – on anterior horn cells (lower motor neurons), directly or through interneurons
  • Corticobulbar fibres go to the motor nuclei of cranial nerves
  • Functions – voluntary, skilled and fine movements, especially of the hands and fingers
  • Lesion – UMN signs; a bleed in the internal capsule (hypertensive stroke) causes hemiplegia of the opposite side

2. Extrapyramidal tracts

  • Arise from brainstem nuclei, influenced by the basal ganglia, cerebellum and cortex:
    • Rubrospinal tract (red nucleus) – tone of flexor muscles, limb movements
    • Vestibulospinal tract (vestibular nuclei) – tone of anti-gravity (extensor) muscles, balance
    • Reticulospinal tracts (reticular formation) – muscle tone, posture, automatic movements
    • Tectospinal tract (superior colliculus) – reflex turning of the head towards sudden sights and sounds
  • Functions – posture, muscle tone, balance and automatic, associated movements (e.g. swinging the arms while walking); they smooth voluntary movements
  • Disorders – Parkinson's disease (tremor, rigidity, slowness, shuffling gait), chorea

3. Role of the cerebellum and basal ganglia

  • The cerebellum coordinates the timing and force of movements; damage → ataxia and intention tremor
  • The basal ganglia help to plan and start movements and regulate tone

4. Final common pathway

  • All motor commands reach the muscle through the lower motor neuron – anterior horn cell → motor nerve → neuromuscular junction → muscle

Applied and nursing importance

  • Stroke – opposite-side paralysis and sensory loss; positioning, ROM exercises, safety and communication aids
  • Spinal cord injury – loss below the level; cervical injury → quadriplegia, thoracic or lumbar → paraplegia
  • Neurological assessment – motor power graded 0–5; sensation tested with cotton wool (touch), a pin (pain), a tuning fork (vibration) and joint position sense; the level of sensory loss is recorded

Conclusion Sensation reaches the opposite sensory cortex through three-neuron chains – the dorsal column–medial lemniscus pathway (fine touch, vibration, position) crossing in the medulla, and the spinothalamic pathway (pain, temperature, crude touch) crossing in the spinal cord – while voluntary movement is controlled by the crossed pyramidal tracts and posture and tone by the extrapyramidal tracts.
